sections.t: For Xi, international politics is an arena of struggle in which containment and encirclement by a U.S.-led West are a constant, and reunification with Taiwan and the Party's leadership are tasks from which he cannot retreat, however long they take. He prefers building pressure a little at a time, at each opportunity, to a single decisive move; turns other countries' dependence on China into leverage; and, in choosing people, checks loyalty before competence. How he sees the world His tendency to treat outside criticism as interference in China's internal affairs was evident before he reached the top (remarks in Mexico, 2009, C); once in power, he named the all-round containment by "Western countries led by the United States" directly (speech, March 2023, E). Language casting international relations as an arena of "struggle" rather than cooperation was also presented as an achievement in the 2022 Party Congress report. Basis: February 11, 2009 · October 16, 2022 · March 6, 2023 What he wants He has defined Taiwan as a problem that "cannot be passed down from generation to generation" (2019, E) but has set no public deadline. At his 2023 meeting with Biden, he reportedly dismissed U.S. military predictions that he would move on Taiwan in 2025 or 2027 and said he preferred a peaceful path (B, U.S. account). Basis: January 2, 2019 · November 15, 2023 What he thinks works As a local official in 1990, he wrote of the gradualism of "dripping water wearing through stone" (D); in 2020, he called for "assassin's mace" technologies and a capacity to counter outside pressure, turning other countries' dependence on China into a weapon (E). The mineral export controls that began three years later, and their repeated time-limited suspensions, appear to put both ideas directly into practice. Basis: March 1990 · April 10, 2020 · July 3, 2023 · November 7, 2025 People and process The loyalty standard he set for Party members in a 2005 column — readiness to risk everything in times of crisis — was reused as the standard for officials in the 2022 Party Congress report (D→E), and the 2023–2026 purges of the military leadership enforced it. Basis: April 27, 2005 · October 16, 2022 · January 24, 2026 Where his words and decisions diverge He crossed his own 2015 pledge that China did not intend to militarize the South China Sea, and he lifted the zero-COVID policy he had vowed to pursue "unwaveringly" six days after nationwide protests. His external pledges appear to bind him only loosely; under domestic pressure that touches regime stability, he changes course quickly, but he does not appear to say anything that concedes a retreat. Basis: May 2, 2018 · December 7, 2022

sections.h: Relation to the country's strategic culture
sections.t: Xi borrows from China's traditional strategic culture the idea of unification (da yitong, "grand unification") as the highest form of legitimacy, the practice of reading shi (勢, "the momentum or propensity of things") and building pressure gradually, and the memory of humiliation since 1840; but the skeleton of his decisions appears closer to the Leninist organizational culture of Party leadership and loyalty vetting. The gap between his rhetoric of a "peace-loving civilization" and his actual coercive conduct resembles the split between word and deed that Johnston found in the Ming dynasty. Because he has not yet resorted to large-scale force, however, the reading that traditional culture drives him toward offensive war remains unconfirmed. Inherited from the national tradition Xi has inherited the concept of da yitong ("grand unification"), which treats unification as the highest form of legitimacy. At a June 2, 2023, symposium on cultural inheritance and development, he said that the remarkable unity of Chinese civilization means that "national unification is forever the core of China's core interests," and the full text of the same speech published in Qiushi uses the phrase "the tradition of grand unification." His framing of Taiwan's reunification as a task that cannot be put off from generation to generation, and the central government's direct enactment of the Hong Kong national security law, were justified in this language. Basis: January 2, 2019 · June 30, 2020 · May 14, 2026 · June 2, 2023 The second inheritance is the practice of reading shi (勢) and accumulating pressure bit by bit rather than seeking a decisive battle. The strategic style that Kissinger explained through weiqi (the board game known in the West as Go) and the concept of shi appears to connect with Xi's 1990 gradualism of "dripping water wearing through stone," with his view of "profound changes unseen in a century" (bainian weiyou zhi da bianju), first officially confirmed on December 28, 2017, and with his January 11, 2021, judgment that "time and momentum are on our side" (shi yu shi zai women yibian). The step-by-step militarization of the South China Sea's artificial islands and the repeated time-limited suspensions of mineral export controls appear to follow the same pattern. This may, however, be less a distinctively Chinese practice than a delaying strategy commonly chosen by rising powers. Basis: March 1990 · May 2, 2018 · July 3, 2023 · November 7, 2025 · January 11, 2021 The third is the memory that takes the humiliation following the Opium War of 1840 as the starting point of the national story. On November 29, 2012, visiting "The Road to Rejuvenation" exhibition — where he first set out the "Chinese Dream" — Xi called national rejuvenation "the greatest dream of the Chinese people since the advent of modern times." In his July 1, 2021, speech on the Party's centenary, he said that after the Opium War "the country endured intense humiliation, the people were subjected to great pain, and the Chinese civilization was plunged into darkness," then warned that foreign forces attempting to bully China would pay a heavy price. His remarks treating outside criticism as interference also appear to fit within the frame of this memory, though Ford points out that the humiliation narrative draws its force less from actual injury than from a former empire's lofty self-image. Basis: February 11, 2009 · March 6, 2023 · November 29, 2012·July 1, 2021 Roots outside the tradition The Leninist organizational culture in which the Party leads everything and commands the gun has roots distinct from the culture of the traditional dynasties. At an all-army political work conference held in late October 2014 at the site of the 1929 Gutian Conference, Xi called the Party's absolute leadership over the military "the soul of a strong military," and the 19th Party Congress in 2017 wrote Mao Zedong's dictum that "the Party leads everything" into the Party Constitution. Torigian explains that in the political culture of the revolutionary elite that raised Xi, the Party was an object of loyalty that came before personal suffering. The line running from the loyalty standard in his 2005 column to the 2022 standard for officials and on to the 2026 purge of the military leadership appears closer to this root. Basis: April 27, 2005 · October 16, 2022 · January 24, 2026 · July 1, 2021 The Marxist language of struggle and contradiction also has roots distinct from tradition. In his 2022 Party Congress report, Xi held up as an achievement the "fighting spirit" shown against outside containment and blockade, and in his June 2, 2023, speech he cast traditional culture as something to be integrated with the basic tenets of Marxism (the so-called second integration). The pattern appears to be not tradition guiding ideology but ideology selecting from tradition. Basis: October 16, 2022 · March 6, 2023 How history is used selectively This is the practice of selecting only the peaceable passages from the classics to build a narrative of a "peace-loving civilization." In a May 15, 2014, speech, Xi quoted the classical injunction to value harmony and the line that a great power fond of war will perish, and said that the blood of the Chinese nation carries "no gene for invading others or seeking world hegemony" (meiyou qinlüe taren, chengba shijie de jiyin); in 2023 he fixed "peacefulness" as one of the five defining features of Chinese civilization. Since the militarization of the South China Sea and live-fire exercises around Taiwan continued over the same period, this rhetoric appears to be an instance of the selective citation of ancient strategic thought that Ghiselli identifies. Basis: September 25, 2015 · May 2, 2018 · August 4, 2022 · May 15, 2014 The very assessment of tradition has been reversed to suit the Party's needs. Under Mao Zedong, the Party attacked Confucius in the 1973–1976 "Criticize Lin, Criticize Confucius" campaign, whereas Xi, at the Confucius Institute in Qufu on November 26, 2013, said that research on Confucian thought should stand on historical materialism, "make the past serve the present" (gu wei jin yong), and take only its essence. That the same Party has treated the same tradition in opposite ways supports the reading that tradition does less to produce decisions than to supply the Party with parts it can select for justification. Basis: November 26, 2013 · June 2, 2023 Checked against classics and scholarship Henry Kissinger · On China (Penguin Press, 2011; Korean edition, Minumsa, 2012) Conditional Interpretation Comparing Chinese strategy to weiqi (Go), Kissinger argued that rather than seeking decisive victory as in chess, it patiently accumulates relative advantage, pursues strategic encirclement, and reads and exploits shi (勢), the flow of the strategic configuration — a tradition he saw continuing into modern leaders (chapter 1, "The Singularity of China," pp. 5–32). He also examined the worldview of the tributary order, in which China saw itself as the center of civilization and understood foreign relations as hierarchical rather than equal, and how that sense of superiority contributed to its decline in the 19th century (chapters 2–3). Comparison The step-by-step militarization of the South China Sea (2015–2018), the repeated cycle of mineral export controls and time-limited suspensions (2023–2026), exercises around Taiwan that end in about two days after each trigger, and the assessment that "time and momentum are on our side" fit the weiqi-and-shi reading well. But the book appeared in 2011, before Xi took power, and was written on the premise of Deng Xiaoping–style restraint and U.S.-China "co-evolution." Where it falls short The "no limits" Sino-Russian joint statement of February 4, 2022, was a choice to throw in with one camp rather than the weiqi-style flexibility of keeping many moves open, and decisions that cut operational capability, such as the 2026 purge of the military leadership, cannot be explained by a theory of exploiting shi. The "Pacific Community"-style cooperation Kissinger hoped for in his epilogue has also given way to strategic competition. Alastair Iain Johnston · Cultural Realism: Strategic Culture and Grand Strategy in Chinese History (Princeton, 1995) Conditional Interpretation Examining the Ming dynasty's (1368–1644) strategy toward the Mongols and the Seven Military Classics through cognitive mapping and symbolic analysis, Johnston argued that Confucian-Mencian discourse emphasizing virtuous rule and defense remained largely at the level of idealized symbols, while actual decisions followed a hard-line "parabellum" realpolitik that saw conflict as zero-sum and favored offensive force when the balance of power was favorable. He concluded that this realpolitik was rooted more in ideas than in the structure of the international system. Comparison The split between peaceful rhetoric and coercive conduct fits well: missile deployments (2018) followed the 2015 statement that China did not intend to militarize, and encirclement exercises around Taiwan were repeated alongside rhetoric about having "no gene for invasion" (2014) and "peacefulness" (2023). But the parabellum model's central prediction — offensive use of force when the balance favors China — has not materialized as a major war under Xi, whose instruments have stayed below the threshold of war: the coast guard, military exercises, and export controls. Where it falls short Even with China's military stronger than at any time in its history, Xi reportedly expressed a preference for a peaceful path and an open-ended timeline for reunification with Taiwan (November 15, 2023, B), and in negotiations with Washington he suspended rare-earth controls for a fixed period (November 7, 2025). Decisions in which he gave way to domestic pressure, such as the lifting of zero-COVID in December 2022, are also better explained by calculations of regime stability than by strategic culture. Transposing conclusions drawn from the Ming dynasty directly onto an individual 21st-century leader is also a stretch. Yuan-kang Wang · Harmony and War: Confucian Culture and Chinese Power Politics (Columbia, 2011) Conditional Interpretation Drawing on cases from the Song and Ming dynasties, Wang argued that whether China used force depended not on Confucian culture but on relative power, and that Confucianism served less as a cause of decisions than as a language of justification — a structural-realist answer to Johnston's cultural explanation. Comparison The pattern of growing assertiveness in the South China Sea and in export controls as the power gap with the United States narrows, and of retreating into time-limited suspensions when Washington pushes back hard, appears to be adjustment according to power. Where it falls short Structural factors alone cannot explain a legitimacy project such as reunification with Taiwan, which is hard to account for by the balance of power, or domestic decisions that sap national strength, such as the purge of the military leadership. Participants in the review roundtable also raised counterexamples of restraint despite superior power, such as the Ming's relations with Joseon Korea. Strategic culture should be treated not as the cause of Xi's decisions but as a condition that sets the range of his options and the language in which he justifies them. Within the same tradition, Mao Zedong attacked Confucius and chose continuous revolution, while Deng Xiaoping chose restraint and opening; Xi's next decision should therefore not be predicted from an essentialist view that "this is simply how China is."

sections.h: Domestic coalition and room to maneuver
sections.t: Xi holds power not through an electoral coalition but with the backing of a narrow selectorate: the Party's central elite, a purged People's Liberation Army, and the discipline and political-legal apparatus. Since the removal of term limits in 2018 and the makeup of the Standing Committee chosen in 2022, that elite's ability to coordinate collective sanctions against him appears to have weakened sharply. He therefore has wide latitude to make concessions on foreign issues, but on issues such as Taiwan, where the Party's legitimacy and nationalist opinion are at stake, the path to a verbal retreat is closed; on domestic issues, he appears to change course when backlash from urban residents and economic interests grows, while never admitting a retreat. Coalition The Party's central elite (Politburo Standing Committee, Politburo, Central Committee) Party leadership and regime stability, the security of their own positions, and governing legitimacy sustained through growth. A March 11, 2018, constitutional amendment removed the term limit on the presidency, and none of the seven Standing Committee members chosen at the First Plenum of the 20th Central Committee on October 23, 2022 (Xi Jinping, Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi) has been marked as a successor. Formally, this is the body that selects Xi, but its capacity to coordinate collective opposition appears to have declined. The People's Liberation Army (the Central Military Commission and theater commands) Budgets and modernization, a firm stance on Taiwan, and job security for the top brass. Both CMC vice chairmen chosen in 2022 (Zhang Youxia and He Weidong) have been purged (October 17, 2025, and January 24, 2026), and the CMC is reported to consist of only Xi and Zhang Shengmin. The military's power to make collective demands or resist policy has weakened, but the vacuum in operational command appears, conversely, to constrain the feasibility of using force. The discipline, political-legal, and state security apparatus (Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, Central Political and Legal Affairs Commission, Ministry of State Security) A line that puts "political security" first, and the preservation and expansion of their oversight and policing powers. Standing Committee member Li Xi heads the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, and Chen Wenqing, a former minister of state security, has led the Central Political and Legal Affairs Commission since October 28, 2022. These bodies look less like independent constituencies than like instruments Xi uses to control the elite and the military, and their effect appears to be to give security logic more weight in policymaking. Nationalist opinion and urban residents (online opinion, university students, urban homeowning households) Abroad, a hard line toward Taiwan and the United States; at home, a return to normal life and stable home values. They have no way to replace leaders through elections, but they can send signals that shake the regime's legitimacy, as with the disappointment over Pelosi's visit in August 2022 and the zero-COVID protests that November. Because the authorities can stoke or cool this opinion through censorship and propaganda, the size of the constraint appears to be something they can adjust themselves. Decisions that strained the coalition November 2022 After a November 24, 2022, apartment fire in Urumqi killed 10 people, anger spread over claims that lockdown measures had blocked their escape, and protests broke out in Shanghai, Beijing (at Tsinghua University), Nanjing, Wuhan, Urumqi, and elsewhere, with some protesters chanting for Xi to step down. A month earlier, the 20th Party Congress report had declared that China had "tenaciously pursued a dynamic zero-Covid policy." How it was handled · Police dispersed protesters and related posts were deleted, while on December 7, 2022, the "10 new measures" from the State Council's Joint Prevention and Control Mechanism effectively ended mass testing and compulsory quarantine. On March 6, 2023, Xi described this as "dynamically optimizing and adjusting" COVID measures, declining to call it a policy retreat. August 2022 When U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi arrived in Taiwan on August 2, 2022, nationalist hashtags on Weibo drew billions of views, and figures such as Hu Xijin, the former editor of the Global Times, voiced disappointment that the government's military response had been weaker than expected. How it was handled · From August 4, Beijing staged large-scale live-fire exercises around Taiwan, with ballistic missiles landing in Japan's exclusive economic zone. At the same time, Weibo outages were reported, and the Foreign Ministry asked the public for patience, saying the United States and Taiwan would "gradually and persistently feel the countermeasures." November 2020 Shortly after Jack Ma publicly criticized financial regulators, Ant Group's $37 billion initial public offering was halted on November 3, 2020, and the regulatory crackdown on platform companies that followed eroded the confidence of private businesses and investors. The decision ran counter to Xi's record of supporting the private economy as a provincial official. How it was handled · At the Central Economic Work Conference on December 15, 2022, Xi declared, "I have always supported private enterprises." On February 17, 2025, he chaired a symposium with private entrepreneurs, pledging the "two unwaverings" (liangge haobu dongyao) and the removal of obstacles to fair competition (the official report lists six speakers, including Ren Zhengfei and Lei Jun; Jack Ma's attendance is confirmed only by press reports). The Private Economy Promotion Law was passed on April 30, 2025, and took effect on May 20. July 2022 A movement of buyers of stalled presale apartments refusing to pay their mortgages spread to more than 200 projects and at least 80 developers. The housing slump was squeezing both the assets of urban households and local government finances. How it was handled · The China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission instructed banks to meet developers' reasonable funding needs, and a Politburo meeting chaired by Xi on July 28, 2022, wrote "guaranteeing the delivery of homes" (baojiaolou) into its readout for the first time. A September 26, 2024, Politburo meeting called for the property market to "halt its decline and stabilize" (zhidie huiwen) and ordered more lending to "whitelisted" projects, but policy stayed with local-government responsibility and targeted support rather than a large-scale direct bailout. Room to maneuver On Taiwan, Xi appears to have almost no room for verbal concessions. Because the Party's legitimacy and nationalist opinion are both at stake, he cannot take back language such as "the first red line"; but he has wide discretion over how forcefully he acts — choosing the scale and timing of exercises, as in 2022, or substituting coast guard patrols, as in 2026 — and the vacuum in the military leadership appears to narrow his room to harden toward the use of force. On chips, rare earths, and tariffs, he has broad room to concede through time-limited suspensions and extensions, apparently because he can package them in a narrative of "counter capacity" and technological self-reliance and so faces little domestic backlash. On issues where his domestic base has little interest — North Korea, Iran, and Ukraine — his calculations in bargaining with Washington, more than domestic constraints, appear to set the limits. On domestic issues tied directly to the lives of urban households, such as housing and the private economy, he can reverse course abruptly, as with the lifting of COVID controls in 2022, but even then he is likely to avoid any words that admit a retreat. Words before and after a change of office The difference between what Xi said before and after taking power appears small. As vice president, in Mexico on February 11, 2009, he called foreigners who meddle in China's affairs "foreigners with full bellies and nothing better to do," and the loyalty standard in his April 27, 2005, column as Zhejiang Party secretary reappeared almost verbatim in the 2022 Party Congress report; his views of outside criticism and of the Party organization point the same way before and after. What changed was the volume and firmness of his public statements. Before taking power, as a local official and vice president, he rarely spoke on foreign affairs; once in power, he began to speak directly of "struggle" and of containment by "Western countries led by the United States." On the private economy, there was a gap between his record of support in Fujian and Zhejiang and the crackdown of 2020–2021, but since 2022 he has moved to close it, saying he has "always supported" private enterprises. Earlier leaders who faced the same structure In a September 4, 1989, talk with leading members of the Central Committee, Deng Xiaoping laid down the guideline that, on the international situation, China should "observe the situation coolly," "hold our ground," and "act calmly." After the bombing of the Chinese Embassy in Belgrade in May 1999, large anti-American protests were allowed under Jiang Zemin's leadership, and Hu Jintao, then vice president, endorsed the protests in a May 9 televised address as an expression of patriotism while calling on protesters to refrain from "extreme and illegal acts." Checked against theory Jessica Chen Weiss · Powerful Patriots: Nationalist Protest in China's Foreign Relations (Oxford University Press, 2014); supplemented by Weiss and Dafoe, "Authoritarian Audiences and Government Rhetoric in International Crises: Evidence from China" (2018 manuscript) Conditional Interpretation Weiss argues that authoritarian leaders can use anti-foreign protests as signals: allowing them conveys a resolve that cannot back down, while suppressing them conveys a willingness to negotiate. She finds that anti-Japanese protests in 1985, 2005, and 2012 and anti-American protests in 1999 were allowed, that anti-Japanese protests in 1990, 1996, and 2010 and anti-American protests in 2001 were suppressed, and that protests over Taiwan have never been allowed. A follow-up experimental study found that Chinese citizens also think less of leaders who back down after making threats, but that government explanations along the lines of biding one's time sharply reduce that cost. Comparison During Pelosi's 2022 visit, the authorities allowed no street protests and cooled opinion on Weibo, sending a signal of resolve through large-scale exercises instead, and the Foreign Ministry's explanation that the countermeasures would be felt "gradually and persistently" appears consistent with the explanatory effect the experimental study describes. Under Xi, however, protest is rarely used as a signal at all, and public opinion appears to have become less a tool for signaling resolve than a constraint the authorities regulate. Jessica L. Weeks · Autocratic Audience Costs: Regime Type and Signaling Resolve, International Organization 62(1), 2008, pp.35-64 Conditional Interpretation Weeks argues that nondemocratic leaders can also be held accountable at home and can therefore generate audience costs. That depends on three conditions — whether domestic political groups can coordinate to punish the leader, whether they view backing down unfavorably, and whether outsiders can observe the likelihood of punishment — and where elites can solve the coordination problem, such regimes are no worse at signaling than democracies. Comparison By this logic, the more Xi weakens the elite's and the military leadership's capacity for collective coordination by replacing them, the smaller the domestic cost of backing down. His execution of major reversals without elite resistance — the lifting of COVID controls in 2022 and the time-limited suspension of rare-earth controls in 2025–2026 — is consistent with this. The same logic implies, however, that because the likelihood of domestic punishment cannot be observed from outside, his warnings on Taiwan may carry less binding force as signals; no case has yet tested this directly.

sections.h: How he decides: hypotheses and forecasts
sections.t: Patterns drawn from the decision record. Each hypothesis carries a forecast that the next decision can confirm or refute. 1. When Xi withdraws an economic measure that hurts the other side, he does so only through a dated, time-limited suspension that leaves the legal basis intact, and he preserves his leverage by renewing that deadline for short periods at each summit. Evidence and counterexamples Supporting cases: November 7, 2025 (a one-year suspension of expanded rare-earth controls); November 9, 2025 (the ban on exports to the United States suspended until November 27, 2026); and September 24, 2026 (the suspension extended by two months, to January 10, 2027, according to a U.S. announcement). The April 2025 licensing requirement on seven medium and heavy rare earths was not even suspended, and on June 22, 2026, during the suspension, Beijing added 10 U.S. companies to its control list. A possible counterexample is the complete lifting of zero-COVID on December 7, 2022; but that was a domestic policy, and because it was packaged as "dynamic optimization" without any admission of retreat, it can also be read as a variant of the same pattern. What would confirm or refute it If, around the next deadline (January 10, 2027), the Ministry of Commerce again issues a dated suspension or reimposes the controls, the hypothesis holds; if it issues an announcement repealing (feizhi or chexiao) Nos. 61 and 62 or No. 46, it fails. 85% As of June 30, 2027, Ministry of Commerce Announcement No. 61 of 2025 and Announcement No. 46 of 2024 will not have been repealed (they will remain in force or under a time-limited suspension) 2. Large named joint exercises around Taiwan are held briefly, for one to three days, right after specific triggers (a presidential inauguration or speech, a high-level U.S. visit, a large arms sale); while a U.S.-China summit is on the calendar, coast guard "law enforcement" patrols take their place. Evidence and counterexamples Exercises following triggers: August 4, 2022; May 23, 2024; October 14, 2024; April 1, 2025; and December 29, 2025. From January to September 2026, a period of back-to-back summits, no named encirclement exercise was reported; instead, a coast guard "quasi-quarantine" operation in waters east of Taiwan on June 1–6 and monthly rotating coast guard patrols filled the gap. The counterexample is Strait Thunder-2025A in April 2025, which came during the tariff war but before a summit date had been fixed. What would confirm or refute it If, between the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November 2026 and the G20 summit in Miami in December 2026, a large arms sale or a U.S. transit by President Lai is not followed within two weeks by a named exercise, the trigger-exercise link weakens. If a named exercise is held while a summit is on the calendar, the substitution element fails. 75% By December 31, 2027, the PLA Eastern Theater Command will publicly announce at least one named joint exercise around Taiwan 3. In matters of succession and military command, Xi puts confirmation of personal loyalty ahead of continuity in operational capability; he will not name a successor and intends to remain general secretary beyond 2027. Evidence and counterexamples Supporting cases: the 2023 overhaul of the Rocket Force leadership; the October 17, 2025, expulsion from the Party and the military of Vice Chairman He Weidong and eight others; and the January 24, 2026, investigation of Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli, which left the CMC with two members. The loyalty standard of being ready to risk everything in a crisis runs consistently from the 2005 column (D) to the 2022 report (E). Against it: in October 2025, Xi promoted Zhang Shengmin to vice chairman, keeping the CMC minimally functional. What would confirm or refute it If, at the Fifth Plenum on October 26–29, 2026, or at the 21st Party Congress in 2027, someone born in the late 1960s or later is named CMC vice chairman or to a clear succession post, the hypothesis fails; if Xi keeps both the general secretaryship and the CMC chairmanship, it holds. 88% At the First Plenary Session of the 21st Central Committee of the Communist Party of China, held by December 31, 2027, Xi Jinping will be reelected general secretary

Time horizon · Born in June 1953, Xi is 73. His third term as general secretary began at the 20th Party Congress in October 2022. The next milestones are the 21st Party Congress, expected in the second half of 2027, and the March 2028 session of the National People's Congress (NPC), when his term as president expires. A 2018 constitutional amendment removed the term limit on the presidency, and no successor has been named. Before then, the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th Central Committee will meet October 26–29, 2026, with "exercising full and rigorous Party self-governance" on its agenda. Power base · Xi's power rests on his chairmanship of the Central Military Commission (CMC) and his grip on Party discipline and personnel. In January 2026, CMC Vice Chairman Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli, chief of the Joint Staff Department, were placed under investigation; in August, the NPC Standing Committee removed both from the state CMC, and in September they were expelled from the Party and the military. That reportedly leaves only Xi and Zhang Shengmin, a vice chairman who rose through the political-work and discipline system, on the commission. His confirmed inner circle includes Cai Qi, a member of the Politburo Standing Committee and director of the General Office of the Central Committee, who also became president of the Central Party School in June 2026, and Wang Yi, a Politburo member and foreign minister. Possible conflicts with personal interest · The purges make Xi personally more secure, but one analysis (CSIS, February 2026) argues that, by leaving no operational commanders on the CMC, they erode the People's Liberation Army's readiness for joint operations. Declining to name a successor likewise helps him hold on to power but is likely to undermine the regime's ability to manage an orderly succession.

Shows whether what was said publicly before each decision matched the decision itself. Date Decision Matches words? May 2, 2018 Other Anti-ship and anti-aircraft missile systems were first reported on China's artificial islands in the Spratlys (Fiery Cross, Subi, and Mischief reefs); despite Xi's 2015 statement that China did not intend to militarize them, the buildup of military facilities continued. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand At a joint press conference at the White House on September 25, 2015, Xi said that construction in the Nansha (Spratly) Islands did "not target or impact any country, and China does not intend to pursue militarization" (C; verified only in the English interpretation, not in the Chinese original). Alternatives Beijing could have confined the islands to civilian and maritime-rescue uses, or frozen activity after the 2016 arbitral ruling. Cost China lost the arbitration decided by the Permanent Court of Arbitration on July 12, 2016, and the episode stands as a case of Xi breaking his own public pledge to Washington and China's neighbors — one repeatedly cited since as grounds for discounting his statements. Inconsistent June 30, 2020 Other Rather than wait for Hong Kong to legislate on its own under Article 23 of the Basic Law, Beijing had the NPC Standing Committee enact the Hong Kong national security law directly and put it into force the same day. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In a July 1, 2017, speech marking the 20th anniversary of Hong Kong's return, Xi declared that any challenge to the power of the central government "crosses the red line, and is absolutely impermissible" (the Chinese term is dixian, literally "bottom line") (E). Alternatives Beijing could have kept pressing Hong Kong's Legislative Council to pass its own law, or managed the protests with existing public-order laws. Cost The United States ended Hong Kong's special treatment through Executive Order 13936 on July 14, 2020, and Beijing accepted the damage to Hong Kong's reputation as an international financial center. Consistent February 4, 2022 The Russia-Ukraine War Twenty days before Russia invaded Ukraine, Xi signed a joint statement with Putin in Beijing declaring that the friendship between the two states "has no limits" and that there are "no 'forbidden' areas of cooperation," and he did not retract that framing after the war began. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand No separate public statement before the decision was found; the joint statement itself (E) says that strengthened bilateral strategic cooperation "is neither aimed against third countries nor affected by the changing international environment." Alternatives Beijing could have dropped the language opposing NATO enlargement, or distanced itself from the joint statement once the war began. Cost Trust with Europe suffered, and Beijing accepted Western pressure, including the threat of secondary sanctions, over whether it was aiding Russia. Even so, at his November 4, 2022, meeting with Chancellor Olaf Scholz, Xi formally stated China's opposition to the use or threat of nuclear weapons, drawing a line. Largely consistent August 4, 2022 The Taiwan Strait Immediately after U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's visit to Taiwan, Xi approved large-scale live-fire exercises around the island; for the first time, five ballistic missiles landed in Japan's exclusive economic zone. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In a July 28, 2022, call with Joe Biden, Xi warned: "Those who play with fire will perish by it" (wan huo bi zi fen) (E). Alternatives Beijing could have limited itself to diplomatic protests and economic sanctions, or scaled down the exercises. Cost U.S.-China military dialogue was suspended, and Beijing accepted friction with Japan and a sharper crisis in the Taiwan Strait. Consistent December 7, 2022 Other Through the State Council's Joint Prevention and Control Mechanism, Beijing announced the "10 new measures," effectively dropping mass testing and compulsory quarantine and ending the zero-COVID policy. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In his report to the 20th Party Congress on October 16, 2022, Xi said China had "tenaciously pursued a dynamic zero-Covid policy" (jianchi dongtai qingling bu dongyao) (E). On December 1, 2022, according to an EU official, he told European Council President Charles Michel that the protests stemmed mainly from frustration among students (B). Alternatives Beijing could have kept the dynamic zero-COVID policy endorsed at the 20th Party Congress, or raised vaccination rates among the elderly first and then reopened in stages. Cost Reopening abruptly while elderly vaccination rates remained low, Beijing accepted a massive wave of infections in a short period and reversed a policy it had vowed two months earlier to pursue unwaveringly. On March 6, 2023, Xi described the shift as "dynamically optimizing and adjusting" COVID measures, framing it as continuity rather than retreat. Inconsistent July 3, 2023 AI and Chips Through Ministry of Commerce and General Administration of Customs Announcement No. 23 of 2023, Beijing placed exports of gallium- and germanium-related items under licensing, effective August 1. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand At an April 10, 2020, meeting of the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission, Xi called for tightening the dependence of international production chains on China so as to build a powerful capacity to counter and deter any foreign attempt to cut off supply; the speech was published in Qiushi on October 31, 2020 (E). Alternatives Beijing could have answered U.S., Dutch, and Japanese controls on chipmaking equipment with legal steps alone, such as a WTO complaint, or held its scarce-mineral leverage in reserve. Cost Beijing accepted the risk that major importers would hurry to build alternative supply chains, weakening its leverage over the medium to long term. Consistent May 23, 2024 The Taiwan Strait Three days after Lai Ching-te's inauguration as Taiwan's president, Beijing had the Eastern Theater Command stage the two-day Joint Sword-2024A exercise around Taiwan. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In his January 2, 2019, speech (E), Xi said China makes no promise to renounce the use of force; on November 15, 2023, according to U.S. officials, he told Biden that he preferred peaceful reunification but had set no deadline (B). Alternatives Beijing could have limited itself to statements criticizing the new president's inaugural address, or applied economic pressure alone. Cost Beijing accepted the cost of hardening anti-Beijing sentiment in Taiwan and heightening vigilance in Washington and Tokyo. After Lai's National Day speech on October 10 of that year, it staged the one-day Joint Sword-2024B on October 14, cementing a pattern of answering each trigger with an exercise. Consistent December 3, 2024 AI and Chips Through Ministry of Commerce Announcement No. 46 of 2024, Beijing banned in principle the export of gallium, germanium, antimony, and superhard materials to the United States — the day after Washington announced tighter controls on semiconductor exports. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand Xi had set out the idea of a capacity to counter and deter foreign supply cutoffs in his April 10, 2020, speech (E), and on March 6, 2023, he spoke of "all-round containment, encirclement and suppression" by "Western countries led by the United States" (E). Alternatives Beijing could have held off, or settled for symbolic sanctions on a few U.S. companies. Cost As China's first comprehensive export ban aimed at a named country, it deepened international concern about the reliability of Chinese supply chains. Consistent November 7, 2025 AI and Chips After the Busan summit on October 30, Beijing suspended "until November 10, 2026" the rare-earth export controls it had widened on October 9, 2025, to cover extraterritorial application (Nos. 61 and 62, among others), and on November 9 it suspended the ban on exports to the United States (Clause 2 of No. 46) "until November 27, 2026." Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand The October 9, 2025, announcement (E, Ministry of Commerce) defined the measures as a permanent system serving national security. Alternatives Beijing could have withdrawn the controls, or made the suspension open-ended. Cost In exchange for lower U.S. tariffs, Beijing set aside its strongest lever for a year, but it kept the April 2025 licensing requirement on seven medium and heavy rare earths out of the suspension. On June 22, 2026, it added 10 U.S. rare-earth and defense companies to its export control list, continuing to use individual tools even during the suspension. Largely consistent December 29, 2025 The Taiwan Strait Right after Washington announced an $11.1 billion arms sale to Taiwan, Beijing had the Eastern Theater Command stage the two-day Justice Mission-2025 exercise around Taiwan. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand At their November 14, 2022, meeting in Bali, Xi told Biden that the Taiwan question is "the first red line that must not be crossed in China-U.S. relations" (E). Alternatives Beijing could have limited itself to sanctions on the arms makers, or postponed the exercise with the coming 2026 U.S.-China summits in mind. Cost Beijing raised tensions with Washington ahead of a summit and escalated, drawing the exercise zones closer to Taiwan's coast and firing rockets into its contiguous zone. Consistent January 24, 2026 Other Xi had Zhang Youxia, the CMC vice chairman he had elevated, and Liu Zhenli, chief of the Joint Staff Department, placed under formal investigation, followed by their removal from state posts in August and expulsion from the Party in September. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In his report to the Party Congress on October 16, 2022 (E), Xi set the standard that officials "excel in their daily work, step forward at critical moments, and act with courage in times of danger" — wording nearly identical to that of his April 27, 2005, column from his years in Zhejiang (D). Alternatives Xi could have stopped at the 2023 overhaul of the Rocket Force leadership and the October 17, 2025, expulsion from the Party and the military of Vice Chairman He Weidong and eight others, or eased the two men out quietly, citing their age. Cost The CMC is reported to have been reduced to just Xi and Zhang Shengmin, and analysts (CSIS) argue that the absence of operational commanders degrades readiness for joint operations. Consistent April 7, 2026 Iran and Hormuz At the UN Security Council, China joined Russia in vetoing a resolution, submitted by Bahrain with Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, on escorting ships through the Strait of Hormuz. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand The five-point China-Pakistan proposal of March 31, 2026 (E, Foreign Minister Wang Yi), called for a ceasefire and normal passage through the strait, and Xi made the same points himself in an April 20, 2026, call with the Saudi crown prince (E). Alternatives Beijing could have abstained and let the resolution pass, or voted for it on condition of changes to the text. Cost By blocking a resolution sponsored mainly by Gulf states that are major suppliers of China's crude, Beijing accepted a cost in those relationships. There are reports, unconfirmed, that China helped persuade Iran on the same day to accept Pakistan's proposal for a two-week ceasefire. Largely consistent May 14, 2026 The Taiwan Strait At the Beijing summit, Xi agreed with Donald Trump on a new framing of relations — a "constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability" — and accepted an invitation to visit the United States in September, while insisting that the Taiwan question is "the most important issue." Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In the same vein as the "first red line" remark at Bali in 2022 (E), Xi warned this time that if the issue is not handled properly, "the two countries will have clashes and even conflicts" (E). Alternatives Beijing could have made a change in U.S. language on Taiwan a precondition for the summit, or kept up military pressure before and after it. Cost Beijing offered economic concessions, including a reported purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft, but even at the White House meeting on September 24 it did not win any change in the wording of U.S. Taiwan policy. Some analysts note that from January to September 2026, coast guard "law enforcement patrols," rather than named exercises encircling Taiwan, served as the main means of pressure. Consistent June 8, 2026 The Korean Peninsula On a state visit to Pyongyang, Xi agreed with Kim Jong Un to strengthen "strategic communication and coordination" and to expand practical cooperation in the economy, agriculture, and construction, while leaving denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula out of the official readout. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand At his June 20, 2019, talks in Pyongyang, Xi said China would play "a constructive role in the denuclearization of the peninsula and the long-term stability of the region" (E). Alternatives Beijing could have kept "denuclearization of the peninsula" and a "political settlement" in the readout, as in 2019. Cost Beijing accepted criticism from the United States, Japan, and South Korea over weakening enforcement of sanctions on North Korea. CSIS notes that after the September White House meeting, even the White House's own readout made no mention of denuclearization. Inconsistent

January 2, 2019 Makes no promise to renounce the use of force against Taiwan independence and interference by outside forces, and reserves "the option of taking all necessary means" Taiwan has made no formal declaration of independence, and Beijing has answered U.S. arms sales and high-level visits not with force but with named exercises and sanctions (August 2022, May 2024, December 2025). Article 8 of the Anti-Secession Law (2005) provides the legal basis. Untested November 14, 2022 The Taiwan question is "the first red line that must not be crossed in China-U.S. relations" Washington has continued arms sales but has not changed its official policy language, and rather than break off relations, Xi has kept up summit diplomacy; at the September 2026 White House meeting he went no further than asking the United States to maintain its stated opposition to Taiwan independence. Untested July 1, 2017 Any activity in Hong Kong that endangers national sovereignty and security or challenges the power of the central government "crosses the red line, and is absolutely impermissible" After the 2019 protests, Beijing enforced this line by enacting the national security law directly on June 30, 2020. Kept September 25, 2015 Construction in the Spratly Islands does not target any country, and China does not intend to pursue militarization In 2017 and 2018, hardened shelters for surface-to-air missiles and the deployment of anti-ship and anti-aircraft missiles on the artificial islands were confirmed and reported — a case of Xi crossing a line he had drawn himself. Crossed November 4, 2022 Opposes the use or threat of nuclear weapons; a nuclear crisis in Eurasia must be prevented Russia has not used nuclear weapons, and no case was found of China publicly answering Russian nuclear threats with sanctions or adjustments to the relationship. Untested

Statements are graded by reliability and labeled with the speaker's position at the time (in office, public office before taking power, opposition or candidate, private citizen). In forecasting decisions after a change of position, statements from opposition or campaign days carry less weight. Grades: A, said alongside a decision · B, private remarks later made public · C, off-the-cuff remarks · D, writings from before taking power · E, official speeches and documents March 1990 D "Lessons from Dripping Water Wearing Through Stone," an essay from his years as Party secretary of Ningde Prefecture, Fujian (collected in Up and Out of Poverty) · Before taking power: Party secretary of Ningde Prefecture, Fujian Xi wrote that development has no shortcuts and is a gradual process in which quantitative change accumulates into qualitative change. The key line is "dripping water can, in the end, wear through stone" (dishui zhongjiu keyi chuan shi). The idea appears to anticipate his later habit of building pressure a little at a time, at each opportunity, rather than using his levers all at once. April 27, 2005 D "A Party Member Is a Banner," a column in Zhijiang Xinyu (written as Party secretary of Zhejiang) · Before taking power: Party secretary of Zhejiang Arguing that Party members must be loyal to the Party, Xi set the standard that they stand out in ordinary times, step forward at critical moments, and be ready to risk everything in times of crisis (weinan shike neng huo de chulai). Nearly the same wording reappeared as the standard for officials in the 2022 report to the 20th Party Congress. February 11, 2009 C Remarks to the overseas Chinese community in Mexico, as vice president · Before taking power: Vice President of China Criticizing foreigners for telling China what to do, Xi spoke of "foreigners with full bellies and nothing better to do" (chibaole mei shi gan de waiguoren). The off-the-cuff remark showed, before he reached the top, a tendency to treat outside criticism as interference in China's internal affairs. January 2, 2019 E Speech marking the 40th anniversary of the Message to Compatriots in Taiwan · In office Xi said the political differences across the strait "cannot be passed down from generation to generation" (zong bu neng yidai yidai chuan xiaqu), framing reunification as a task with a timetable, and declared that China makes no promise to renounce the use of force. April 10, 2020 E Speech to the seventh meeting of the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission (published in Qiushi on October 31, 2020) · In office Xi directed that China cultivate "assassin's mace" (shashoujian) technologies in industries where it leads, tighten the dependence of international production chains on China, and build a powerful capacity to counter and deter any foreign attempt to cut off supply. The speech appears to be the blueprint for the mineral export controls that began three years later. October 16, 2022 E Report to the 20th National Congress of the Communist Party of China · In office Xi pledged to strive for peaceful reunification with the utmost effort but said China "will never promise to renounce the use of force" (jue bu chengnuo fangqi shiyong wuli), and he held up as an achievement the "fighting spirit" China had shown against "external attempts to blackmail, contain, blockade, and exert maximum pressure." December 1, 2022 B Closed-door meeting with European Council President Charles Michel (account by an EU official, reported by Reuters) · In office Xi reportedly said that people had grown frustrated after three years of COVID, that the protests were mostly by students and teenagers, and that the less lethal Omicron variant opened the way to easing restrictions. Six days later, the lifting of COVID controls was announced, matching his words with a decision. March 6, 2023 E Speech to members of the China National Democratic Construction Association and the All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce attending the CPPCC session · In office Xi named the United States directly, saying that "Western countries led by the United States" (yi Meiguo wei shou de xifang guojia) had subjected China to all-round containment, encirclement, and suppression. In the same speech, he described the lifting of COVID controls as "dynamic optimization." November 15, 2023 B U.S.-China summit at Woodside (account by three current and former U.S. officials, reported by NBC) · In office Xi reportedly told Biden that China would achieve reunification with Taiwan but had not decided on the timing, that U.S. military leaders' predictions that he planned to take Taiwan in 2025 or 2027 were wrong, and that he preferred a peaceful path. The Chinese side also made public the gist — that China "will realize reunification." May 14, 2026 E Chinese readout of the U.S.-China summit in Beijing · In office Xi warned that the Taiwan question is "the most important issue in China-U.S. relations" and that mishandling it would lead to "clashes and even conflicts," while proposing that the two countries overcome the Thucydides Trap and "create a new paradigm of major-country relations."

sections.h: What the government says and does
sections.t: Beijing speaks of denuclearization and peaceful reunification, but its actions embrace North Korea, make pressure around Taiwan routine, and inflict economic retaliation on a neighbor (Japan) over the Taiwan question. No country shows a wider gap between words and deeds. Said September 24, 2026 At the White House summit, Xi pressed Trump to oppose Taiwanese independence. Did September 21, 2026 Expelled Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli from the party and the military, concentrating military decision-making further in Xi's hands. Did June 8, 2026 When Xi visited Pyongyang, Kim Jong Un pledged to make China-North Korea friendship "the most important top-priority strategic work"; denuclearization went unmentioned. Said May 2026 China's foreign ministry did not confirm the White House announcement of a shared goal of denuclearization, speaking only of continuity and consistency. Did March 18, 2026 China-South Korea supply-chain hotline reactivated; cooperation to keep South Korean chip plants running smoothly Did January 15, 2026 Customs told to block H200 imports; companies urged to hold off on purchases Did January 6, 2026 Ban on exports of dual-use items to Japan Did January 2026 Imposed export controls on dual-use items and rare earths bound for Japan in retaliation for remarks about Taiwan. Said January 2026 Ahead of President Lee Jae-myung's visit to China, pressed Seoul to state its position on Taiwan clearly. Did December 29, 2025 Fired 27 rockets into Taiwan's contiguous zone during the Justice Mission-2025 exercises. Did December 2025 Staged large-scale blockade-style exercises around Taiwan (Justice Mission-2025). Did November 7, 2025 Implementation of the October 9, 2025, rare-earth export control announcement suspended until November 10, 2026 Did October 14, 2025 Sanctions on five U.S. subsidiaries of Hanwha Ocean (suspended November 10, 2025) Did 2025 China-North Korea trade rose 25 percent, returning to pre-pandemic levels. Words and deeds: Inconsistent · 14 signals (said: 3 · did: 11)

sections.h: Who decides and who can veto, issue by issue
sections.t: Issue Decides Veto players The Korean Peninsula Xi makes the final call as general secretary, working through the Central Foreign Affairs Commission, while Foreign Minister Wang Yi handles day-to-day diplomacy. The broad direction of relations with North Korea is set directly between the two leaders, as at the June 2026 summit in Pyongyang. No institution in China can effectively block Xi's decisions. Collective decision-making in the Politburo Standing Committee appears to be a formality; the real constraints appear to lie outside China, in North Korea's own choices and in Russia's support for Pyongyang. The Taiwan Strait Article 8 of the Anti-Secession Law (2005) provides that the State Council and the CMC decide on and carry out "non-peaceful means" and report to the NPC Standing Committee; under the CMC chairman responsibility system, the final decision rests with Xi. With the CMC reduced to two members, decision-making appears to be concentrated, in practice, in Xi alone. The NPC Standing Committee is merely informed after the fact and has no legal power to block a decision. There is no institutional veto player; some analysts (CSIS) argue that the command vacuum left by the purges and gaps in operational readiness act as de facto brakes. The Russia-Ukraine War Xi personally sets the direction of relations with Russia; during Vladimir Putin's visit to China in May 2026, he signed an extension of the Sino-Russian friendship treaty and a joint statement. China's real levers are its imports of Russian energy and whether it allows exports of dual-use goods. There is no domestic institutional veto player. As a permanent member of the UN Security Council, China itself holds an international veto. Iran and Hormuz Xi and Foreign Minister Wang Yi decide. On March 31, 2026, China and Pakistan jointly proposed five points calling for a ceasefire and the restoration of normal shipping through Hormuz, and on April 7 China, together with Russia, reportedly vetoed a Bahrain-led resolution on escorting ships. At the U.S.-China summits of May and September 2026, Beijing agreed that Iran must not have nuclear weapons and that Hormuz must stay open. There is no domestic institutional veto player. The interests of the independent refiners that actually process Iranian crude, and of the agencies responsible for energy security, appear to set the pace of policy. AI and Chips Under the Export Control Law (2020), the Ministry of Commerce announces and licenses export controls on rare earths and critical minerals, but major decisions — such as when to impose or suspend controls — have come right after U.S.-China summits and appear to be Xi's. Chinese authorities are also reported to be managing imports of Nvidia's H200 by capping approved volumes and blocking their use for inference (July 2026). There is no domestic institutional veto player. The next decision points are the expiry of the rare-earth suspension on November 10, 2026, and the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November; the interests of domestic chipmakers such as Huawei appear to be slowing any expansion of H200 imports.

As general secretary, Xi personally heads the Central Foreign Affairs Commission, the Central National Security Commission, and the Central Military Commission (under the CMC chairman responsibility system), while day-to-day diplomacy is handled by Wang Yi, a Politburo member who serves as foreign minister and director of the Office of the Central Foreign Affairs Commission. Every year, all Politburo members, the Party groups of the NPC Standing Committee, the State Council, and the CPPCC, and the Party group secretaries of the Supreme People's Court and the Supreme People's Procuratorate submit written work reports "to the Party Central Committee and General Secretary Xi Jinping." The practice was repeated on February 26, 2026, and it formalizes a structure in which reporting converges on one man. Cai Qi, a member of the Politburo Standing Committee, is confirmed to control documents and schedules as director of the General Office of the Central Committee, but public sources do not show how information is actually filtered. As of September 2026, the CMC is reported to consist of only Xi and Zhang Shengmin, so decisions on the use of force against Taiwan appear to rest, in practice, with one man. An EU official (anonymous, traveling with European Council President Charles Michel) · According to the official, Xi said at the December 1, 2022, meeting that the COVID protests arose from three years of frustration and were mostly by students and teenagers, and that the less lethal Omicron variant opened the way to easing restrictions. (Partly corroborated: the lifting of COVID controls was in fact announced six days later (December 7, 2022), in line with the direction of the remarks. The Chinese readout contains no such remarks.) Three current and former U.S. officials (anonymous, reported by NBC) · They said that at the November 15, 2023, meeting at Woodside, Xi told Biden that China would achieve reunification with Taiwan but had not decided on the timing, and that he preferred a peaceful path. (Partly corroborated: Hua Chunying, then the Foreign Ministry spokesperson, made public the gist that China "will realize reunification," but the remarks on timing rest solely on the U.S. account.) Donald Trump, U.S. president · In a Fox News interview on August 15, 2025, Trump said Xi had told him, "I will never do it as long as you're president," while also saying, "I am very patient, and China is very patient." (Not corroborated: a single source, and the Chinese Embassy in Washington merely restated its position of principle without confirming the remarks.) Scott Bessent, U.S. treasury secretary · During Xi's visit to the United States on September 24, 2026, Bessent announced that the U.S.-China trade truce and the suspension of rare-earth export controls would be extended to January 10, 2027. (Partly confirmed: the Chinese readout says only that the two sides agreed on "new joint arrangements" and does not mention rare earths; as of October 2, 2026, no new Ministry of Commerce announcement had been found.)

Assassin's mace (shashoujian, 杀手锏) · A Chinese expression for a secret weapon that overpowers an opponent in a single stroke. Xi Jinping has applied it to core technologies that make other countries dependent on China. ↩ Grand unification (da yitong, 大一統) · The traditional Chinese political idea that all under heaven should be united under a single legitimate dynasty. It originates in the Gongyang Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals. ↩ Shi (勢) · The force and momentum that a configuration of circumstances generates. In Chinese military classics such as Sun Tzu's Art of War, it means reading the potential of a situation and turning it to advantage. ↩ Leninist party organization · The organizing principle under which a vanguard party of professional revolutionaries leads the state and the military, and within the party lower bodies obey the decisions of higher ones (democratic centralism). ↩ Criticize Lin, Criticize Confucius (pi Lin pi Kong, 批林批孔) · A political campaign in China from 1973 to 1976 that attacked Lin Biao and Confucius together. ↩ Parabellum · From the Latin maxim "If you want peace, prepare for war." Alastair Iain Johnston used the term for a hard realpolitik disposition that treats conflict as zero-sum and resorts to force when the balance of power is favorable. ↩ Selectorate · In the theory developed by Bruce Bueno de Mesquita and others, the set of people who can influence the choice of a leader. The core within it that actually keeps the leader in power is called the winning coalition. ↩ Political-legal apparatus (zhengfa, 政法) · The system through which the Chinese Communist Party directs the police, procuratorates, courts, and state security organs together. ↩ Central Military Commission · China's supreme military command body. The party and the state each have a commission with identical membership, and its chairman holds final command authority. ↩ Fifth Plenum · The fifth plenary session of the Chinese Communist Party's Central Committee. Plenums held between party congresses set major policy lines and personnel appointments. ↩ National People's Congress (NPC) · China's highest organ of state power. Its Standing Committee handles legislation when the full congress is not in session. ↩ Anti-Secession Law · A law China enacted in 2005. It sets out the conditions under which Beijing may use non-peaceful means against "secession," such as Taiwanese independence (Article 8). ↩ Thucydides Trap · The hypothesis that a rising power and an established power are prone to collide. The name was coined by Graham Allison. ↩ Veto player · An institution or person that can block or delay a decision-maker's decisions (in the United States, Congress and the courts; in Taiwan, the Legislative Yuan). ↩ Sources · 101 obamawhitehouse.archives.gov Remarks by President Obama and President Xi of the People's Republic of China in Joint Press Conference (Obama White House archives, English interpretation) · 2015-09-25 amti.csis.org A Look at China's SAM Shelters in the Spratlys (CSIS AMTI) · 2017-02-23 cnbc.com China quietly installed missile systems on strategic Spratly Islands in hotly contested South China Sea (CNBC) · 2018-05-02 pca-cpa.org The South China Sea Arbitration (The Republic of the Philippines v.
