For Kim Jong Un, international politics is a world of raw power in which regimes that give up their nuclear weapons collapse, and his goal appears to be to lock in North Korea's status as a nuclear power as an irreversible premise and then face the United States on that footing. He completes displays of capability and legal and institutional steps before entering negotiations; carries out announced deadlines and nonmilitary measures to the letter while holding back on steps that would be costly in relations with China and the United States; and leaves the pressure to Kim Yo Jong while making the decisions himself. How he sees the world Two days after the fourth nuclear test, a KCNA commentary wrote that the regimes of Saddam Hussein and Gaddafi, having given up the foundations of their own nuclear development, "could not escape the fate of destruction," and in 2022 Kim Jong Un declared that there would never be "denuclearization first," daring his adversaries to impose sanctions "for a hundred days, a thousand days" (E). Weeks after the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran that began in late February 2026, he vowed to make North Korea's position as a nuclear state "absolutely irreversible" (E, based on English-language reporting), apparently reaffirming the same lesson. The decision of the plenary meeting at the end of 2019, which framed the U.S.–North Korea standoff after the Hanoi breakdown as a contest between self-reliance and sanctions, appears to spring from the same worldview. Basis: January 6, 2016 · December 31, 2019 · September 8, 2022 · March 23, 2026 What he wants His goal appears to be not denuclearization talks but a relationship in which the United States "respects the present position of our state"—in other words, recognition as a nuclear power (September 2025, February 2026, E). At the same time, he has cut South Korea loose as the other party in "relations between two states hostile to each other" and excluded it permanently from "the category of compatriots" (December 2023, February 2026, E), putting survival and status as a separate state ahead of the reunification championed by his grandfather and father. Basis: December 30, 2023 · September 21, 2025 · February 21, 2026 · March 23, 2026 What he thinks works In his 2018 New Year address, he packed the "nuclear button" threat and the offer to take part in the Olympics into a single speech (E), and he entered negotiations with a testing halt only after declaring the "completion of the state nuclear force." He announced a year-end deadline in April 2019 and enforced it to the letter that December (E), but in June 2020, right after blowing up the liaison office, he suspended the General Staff's plans for military action. He appears to carry out as announced the measures against which adversaries would find direct retaliation difficult, while keeping costly military measures in reserve as instruments of threat. Basis: November 29, 2017 · January 1, 2018 · April 20, 2018 · April 12, 2019 · December 31, 2019 · June 16, 2020 People and process In 2013 he publicly executed his uncle Jang Song Thaek, Pyongyang's channel to Beijing, putting internal control ahead of external costs, and he set the date of the fourth nuclear test himself in a handwritten order. In 2020 and 2026, he sent out pressure and rebuffs in statements in Kim Yo Jong's name and set only the final level himself, and he wrote to President Trump proposing that the two talk directly, without going through President Moon Jae-in (B, not confirmed by North Korea). The structure appears to be one in which one man makes the big decisions while external signaling is split between proxies and direct leader-to-leader dealings. Basis: December 12, 2013 · January 6, 2016 · August 5, 2019 · June 16, 2020 · August 19, 2026 Where his words and decisions diverge He signed the commitment "to work toward complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula" in the 2018 Singapore joint statement (A), but in 2022 he shut the door on denuclearization by law and broadened the conditions for nuclear use beyond his 2018 pledge not to use nuclear weapons first unless North Korea's sovereignty and interests were violated. On the deployment to Russia, he kept silent for more than six months before formally claiming it as his decision in April 2025 (A). Conciliatory words in negotiating phases have often gone unkept, but his words on nuclear possession have been borne out by actual decisions. With costly decisions like the deployment to Russia, he tends to act first and only later declare the decision his own. Basis: January 1, 2018 · June 12, 2018 · September 8, 2022 · October 8, 2024 · April 28, 2025

sections.h: Relation to the country's strategic culture
sections.t: Kim Jong Un inherited as his language of justification Juche and self-reliance, Kim Il Sung's anti-Japanese partisan tradition, and a small state's memory of surviving among great powers by refusing sadae, or deference to the strong. Yet the direct rationale for nuclear weapons appears to come more from lessons of international politics—Iraq and Libya, and in 2026 Iran—and from the Party-centered Leninist organization. He has drawn on tradition selectively, stripping away in 2023–26 the cause of national reunification that his grandfather and father placed at the center of the regime's legitimacy and replacing his father's Songun, or military-first politics, with Party-centered rule, which shows that opposite decisions can emerge from the same tradition. Of the three interpretations, this section judges that Andrei Lankov's account, which puts the rational calculation of regime survival first, fits best, and that B. R. Myers's account, which places pan-Korean racial nationalism at the core, conflicts with the decision to exclude South Koreans from the category of compatriots. Inherited from the national tradition He inherited the language of Juche and self-reliance, which rejects dependence on outsiders. In a speech on December 28, 1955, Kim Il Sung championed Juche while criticizing Soviet-style dogmatism and the sadaejuui, or toadyism, of serving great powers. After the Hanoi breakdown, Kim Jong Un told the December 2019 plenary meeting that the U.S.–North Korea standoff had "now boiled down to a clear stand-off between self-reliance and sanctions" and that North Korea would not count on sanctions relief (per the English version). On his ascent of Mount Paektu in October 2019, too, he called for holding high "the banner of self-reliance." Yet military and economic cooperation with Russia deepened over the same period, which suggests that self-reliance serves less as actual self-sufficiency than as a justification for refusing concessions to outsiders. Basis: December 31, 2019 · September 8, 2022 · October 2019 · December 28, 2019~31 The partisan tradition takes Kim Il Sung's experience in the anti-Japanese guerrilla units in Manchuria as the template for running the state. Wada Haruki characterized the Kim Il Sung system as a "guerrilla-band state" in which the whole population moves like guerrilla fighters. Right after working-level talks broke down in Stockholm, Kim Jong Un rode a white horse up Mount Paektu in October 2019; in December he returned to the revolutionary battle sites in the Mount Paektu area with military commanders in tow, and at a plenary meeting at the end of that month he announced the abandonment of the testing-halt pledge. His December 2015 remark about possessing the H-bomb was made at the Phyongchon Revolutionary Site, where Kim Il Sung set up the first arms factory right after liberation, and it too appears to justify nuclear development as a continuation of the revolutionary tradition of armed self-defense. Basis: December 10, 2015 · January 6, 2016 · December 31, 2019 · October 2019·December 2019 There is also a small state's survival instinct—wedged among China, Russia, Japan, and the United States—to avoid being bound to any one great power, and a rejection of sadae. Kim Jong Un executed Jang Song Thaek, the channel to China who had headed the joint North Korea–China committee, and a May 2017 KCNA commentary (issued under the name Kim Chol, not in Kim Jong Un's name) criticized China by name, declaring that the DPRK "will never beg for the maintenance of friendship with China" (per the English version). During Xi Jinping's visit to the North in June 2026, too, denuclearization was kept out of the readouts. Pompeo recalled Kim saying he needed U.S. forces in Korea to check China (B, unconfirmed), but the 2024 alliance with Russia and the troop deployment amount to leaning heavily on a single great power, which suggests that this tradition does not always produce balancing. Basis: December 12, 2013 · June 8, 2026 · 2018 · May 3, 2017 Roots outside the tradition The direct rationale for nuclear weapons came less from tradition than from lessons of international politics drawn from cases of regime change. During the 2011 air campaign against Libya, North Korea's Foreign Ministry said that "Libya's nuclear dismantlement," as touted by the United States, had "turned out to be a mode of aggression," and two days after the fourth nuclear test a KCNA commentary wrote that the Saddam Hussein and Gaddafi regimes "could not escape the fate of destruction after being deprived of their foundations for nuclear development and giving up nuclear programs of their own accord" (per the English versions). His vow in March 2026, weeks after the strikes on Iran began in late February, to make nuclear status "absolutely irreversible" appears to carry the same lesson forward. This logic appears to point in the same direction as a small state's memory of survival among great powers, the two reinforcing each other. Basis: January 6, 2016 · September 8, 2022 · March 23, 2026 · January 8, 2016 The organizational culture of a Leninist party, which uses Party congresses and plenary meetings as the vehicle for decisions, also has roots distinct from the partisan tradition. In 2016 Kim Jong Un convened a Party congress for the first time in 36 years; he announced the 2018 testing halt, the 2019 abandonment of that pledge, and the 2023 definition of "two hostile states" all as plenary decisions; and the Party Rules as revised in 2021 replaced "Songun politics" with "people-first politics" as the basic mode of politics. He appears to have moved the stage of decision-making from the National Defence Commission and the military-centered rule of his father's era back to the Party. Basis: April 20, 2018 · December 30, 2023 · February 21, 2026 · January 2021 How history is used selectively He kept his grandfather's Paektu-bloodline legitimacy while discarding the reunification legacy of his grandfather and father. In his policy speech of January 15, 2024, Kim Jong Un ordered the removal of the "eye-sore" Monument to the Three Charters for National Reunification, erected in 2001 under Kim Jong Il, and the same speech called for eliminating the concepts of "reunification," "reconciliation," and "fellow countrymen" from the national history and for no longer using expressions such as "80 million compatriots" in domestic life. Yet the same speech also raised the matter of occupying the Republic of Korea and incorporating it into North Korean territory in the event of war, which suggests that he stripped away the national narrative but kept the territorial claim. The "state-first principle," which first appeared in the Rodong Sinmun the day after the November 2017 declaration that the nuclear force was complete, appears to have foreshadowed the shift in the unit of legitimacy from the nation to the state. Basis: December 30, 2023 · February 21, 2026 · November 29, 2017 · January 15, 2024 He drew on his father's Songun and his grandfather's byungjin, or parallel development, as needed. The line of developing the economy and nuclear forces in parallel, adopted at the plenary meeting of March 31, 2013, was presented as carrying the economy-and-defense parallel line of the Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il eras onto a higher stage, and in 2018 he declared that line's "victory" to justify the testing halt and the turn to the economy. In 2021 he dropped "Songun politics," his father's emblem, from the Party Rules, moving away from what Wada Haruki called the "regular-army state" of the Kim Jong Il era. The same ancestral line was used to justify both the nuclear buildup and the testing halt, which suggests that decisions choose the tradition more than the tradition determines the decisions. Basis: April 20, 2018 · September 8, 2022 · March 31, 2013 · January 2021 Checked against classics and scholarship Bruce Cumings · North Korea: Another Country (The New Press, 2004) Conditional Interpretation Cumings argued that U.S. bombing in the Korean War devastated North Korea on a scale comparable to what the Soviet Union and Poland suffered, and, noting that the United States threatened to use nuclear weapons during the war and kept them in South Korea until 1991, he explained North Korea's garrison state and hostile behavior as a response to that memory and that threat. Emphasizing Kim Il Sung's career as an anti-Japanese guerrilla and his distance from the Soviet Union, he saw North Korea not as a satellite but as an anticolonial nationalist state. Comparison His justification of the nuclear forces as "self-defense" and deterrence (December 10, 2015; September 8, 2022), his objections to joint exercises (letter of August 5, 2019, B), and his remark locking in nuclear status right after the strikes on Iran (March 23, 2026) fit the interpretation that he is responding to external threats. Partisan legitimacy and the rejection of sadae also connect to the anticolonial nationalism Cumings emphasized. Where it falls short The 2024 deployment to Russia was not a defensive response but an expeditionary intervention, and the removal of the concept of "compatriots" in 2023–26 runs against the Korean nationalism at the center of Cumings's account. In August 2026, when Washington scaled back joint exercises, Kim held to his conditions and the following month observed a new missile test, so the implication that hostility recedes as threats recede has not been borne out. Andrei Lankov · The Real North Korea: Life and Politics in the Failed Stalinist Utopia (Oxford University Press, 2013) Fits Interpretation Lankov argued that North Korea's leadership is not irrational but acts rationally to ensure regime survival and, because of the lesson of Libya, will not give up its nuclear weapons. He also contended that as long as a prosperous South Korea exists, Chinese-style reform and opening would expose the gap with the South and could bring down the regime, so the leadership avoids reform. Comparison The 2022 law's rejection of any "bargaining chip," the locking in of nuclear status in the 2026 constitution, and the decision not to offer anything beyond Yongbyon in Hanoi match the prediction that the regime will not give up its nuclear weapons. This section judges that the diagnosis that South Korea's existence is a weak point for the regime's legitimacy can serve as a framework for explaining the motives behind the 2024 ban on expressions such as "80 million compatriots" and the 2026 exclusion of South Korea from "the category of compatriots" (whether Lankov himself reads these decisions this way could not be confirmed). Where it falls short Contrary to Lankov's account of extracting aid through calculated escalation, Kim has taken nuclear weapons off the table entirely since 2022, did not respond to the scaled-back U.S. exercises in August 2026, and instead adopted a new mode of bargaining in the troop deployment to Russia. The forecast that the status quo is unsustainable in the long run has not been borne out in the 13 years since the book's publication. B. R. Myers · The Cleanest Race: How North Koreans See Themselves and Why It Matters (Melville House, 2010) Conflicts Interpretation Myers argued that North Korea's ruling ideology is not Marxism-Leninism or Juche but a race-based nationalism inherited from Japanese fascism, with Juche closer to window dressing aimed at foreigners. In later writing, he held that the regime's legitimacy rests on a pan-Korean mission of reunification and that its nuclear program is meant to force the withdrawal of U.S. troops (2017), and he countered that the "two states" declaration of late 2023 was merely propaganda for external consumption, not an abandonment of reunification (2024). Comparison The theory's central proposition is that the regime cannot abandon the idea of "compatriots" and the mission of reunification. Yet Kim Jong Un banned expressions such as "80 million compatriots" not in external propaganda but in domestic political and ideological life, demolished the reunification monument, and erased reunification language from the constitution and the Party Rules in 2026. His raising of the occupation and incorporation of the Republic of Korea in wartime fits Myers's reading that territorial ambitions remain, but because the justification has shifted from the nation to war against a hostile state, this section judges that it conflicts with the central proposition. Where it falls short The Institute for National Security Strategy's finding that the demand for the withdrawal of U.S. forces was deleted in the 2026 revision of the Party Rules runs against the 2017 claim that the nuclear program aims to force a U.S. withdrawal, as does Pompeo's recollection that Kim said he needed U.S. forces in Korea to check China (B, unconfirmed). Whether "two states" is a long-term deception, however, is hard to disprove until a reunification phase returns, and in May 2026 Hyunseung Lee also read it as a tactical redefinition rather than an abandonment. Strategic culture should be seen not as the cause of Kim Jong Un's decisions but as a condition that sets the range of options and the language of justification. On the same Paektu bloodline and Juche tradition, Kim Il Sung put forward the principles of independence, peace, and great national unity in the July 4 South-North Joint Statement of 1972, and Kim Jong Il went to the inter-Korean summit of 2000, whereas Kim Jong Un stripped away the cause of reunification with "two hostile states" in 2023—and he himself had signed the Panmunjom Declaration in 2018. The next decision should therefore not be predicted from the essentialist premise that North Korea is simply like that; cultural explanation appears to gain predictive power only when tradition and the lessons of international politics point the same way, as with nuclear weapons.

sections.h: Domestic coalition and room to maneuver
sections.t: Kim Jong Un controls a small elite at the Party center and the military and security services by drawing on the legitimacy of Paektu-bloodline succession and replacing and purging them at will. What actually narrows his room for decision appears to be less the demands of his support coalition than the logic of nuclear status and regime legitimacy that he himself has formalized. Because the elite's standing depends on him personally, they have virtually no means of sanctioning him for policy failures or reversals, so changes of direction such as resuming dialogue with Washington or deploying troops to Russia carry small domestic costs. Reversing the nuclear status and the exclusion of South Korea that he has written into the constitution and the Party Rules, however, would tear down the legitimacy he has built, a cost high enough that his room to do so appears narrow. Coalition The elite of the Party Political Bureau and Central Committee (core cadres who uphold Paektu-bloodline succession as the basis of legitimacy) Status and personal safety, the preservation of privileges, and the survival of the Kim Jong Un system that guarantees their positions Formally the highest decision-making body, but as the Ninth Party Congress (February 2026) showed—with 161 of the 250 Central Committee members (64 percent) replaced, the Presidium of the Political Bureau reorganized into a five-member body, and veterans such as Choe Ryong Hae, Pak Jong Chon, and Ri Pyong Chol stepping down—its members appear to be pieces that Kim Jong Un swaps out rather than actors who constrain him. The 2013 verdict on Jang Song Thaek, which publicly listed among his crimes turning his department into a "little kingdom" and plotting a coup, served as a public declaration that building an independent power base within the elite is taboo. The Korean People's Army and the security services (the Ministry of State Security and others) Institutional standing and a share of resources, nuclear and missile development and combat experience, and state rewards for meritorious service As holders of coercive power, they have large potential influence, but after the dismissal of Chief of the General Staff Ri Yong Ho in July 2012, the military leadership was replaced in quick succession and Party control of the military through the Party Central Military Commission was reestablished (38 North). The security services appear mainly as instruments for carrying out purges, as when a special military tribunal of the Ministry of State Security handled Jang Song Thaek's trial. After the deployment to Russia, Kim Jong Un publicly expanded rewards for the military, conferring the title of Hero of the DPRK on soldiers killed in action and pledging support for bereaved families, and at the Ninth Party Congress the defense minister, the chief of the General Staff, and the director of the General Political Bureau were named to the leadership. Residents of the capital, Pyongyang, and privileged groups (families of cadres, occupations the regime favors, and families of decorated veterans) Priority in housing and supplies, and keeping the right to live in the capital Moderate, it appears. At the Eighth Party Congress in 2021, the regime made the construction of 50,000 homes in Pyongyang a top priority and announced their completion in February 2026, and it said it had built apartments for the bereaved families of soldiers killed in the Russia deployment across from the memorial museum in Pyongyang. Concentrating visible benefits in the capital even in hard economic times appears to be an allocation aimed at keeping this group from turning away. Ordinary residents (provincial residents who depend on jangmadang market trading and on food supplies) Securing food, freedom to trade in the markets, and better living conditions Weak. With no channel for collective organization, they cannot block decisions directly, but Kim Jong Un acknowledged at a June 2021 plenary meeting that the people's food situation was "getting tense" (per the English translation). Since January 2023, the regime has pushed a state monopoly on grain sales through state grain shops and tightened controls to steer market distribution back toward state-run stores, which suggests that residents' demands are managed through tighter control rather than by changing the direction of policy. Decisions that strained the coalition December 2013 Jang Song Thaek—his uncle by marriage, his former guardian, and director of the Party's Administrative Department—expanded that department and built independent influence over the export of resources such as coal and over personnel appointments, which collided with Kim Jong Un's one-man rule. The verdict said he had massively increased his department's staff and converted it into a "little kingdom," had coal and other underground resources sold off at random, handed over land in the Rason economic and trade zone to a foreign country for 50 years, and plotted a coup using senior military officers. How it was handled · Jang was stripped of all posts and expelled from the Party at an enlarged meeting of the Political Bureau on December 8 and executed after a special military tribunal of the Ministry of State Security on December 12, after which the verdict was published through KCNA. Around that time, a series of personnel moves purged networks tied to Jang Song Thaek and Kim Kyong Hui and installed loyalists (38 North analysis). December 2019 When the Hanoi summit broke down in February 2019 without sanctions relief, the expectation of sanctions easing that underpinned the April 2018 line of concentrating all efforts on economic construction collapsed. Sanctions, the COVID-19 border closure, and typhoon damage in 2020 then combined to leave him unable to deliver the economic results promised at home. How it was handled · At the Fifth Plenary Meeting of the Seventh Central Committee on December 28–31, 2019, he framed the U.S.–North Korea standoff as a contest between self-reliance and sanctions and launched an "offensive for making a breakthrough head-on" with the economy as the main front, acknowledging stagnation across industry—metals, chemicals, power, and coal—and demanding a stepped-up struggle against anti-socialist and non-socialist practices. In his report to the Eighth Party Congress in January 2021, he admitted outright that "almost all sectors fell a long way short of the set objectives" of the five-year strategy and called the preceding five years "the worst of the worst" (per the English translation); as remedies, he put forward greater self-reliance and made the construction of 50,000 homes in Pyongyang a top priority. December 2023 Departing from the national reunification line that his grandfather Kim Il Sung and father Kim Jong Il held up as a pillar of the regime's legitimacy, Kim Jong Un defined inter-Korean ties at the December 2023 plenary meeting as "relations between two states hostile to each other" and called it a mistake to regard South Korea as a partner for reunification. In a system that relies on the continuity of its forebears' instructions and of Paektu-bloodline legitimacy, it was a decision to discard publicly a line laid down by his predecessors. How it was handled · In his January 15, 2024, speech to the Supreme People's Assembly, he defined South Korea as an enemy rather than a partner for reconciliation and reunification and ordered the removal of the "eye-sore" Monument to the Three Charters for National Reunification, a symbol of inter-Korean reconciliation, which was demolished January 19–23 (per the English translation). After the abolition of the agencies handling South Korean affairs (January 2024) and the deletion of reunification language from the Party Rules (June 2024), the constitution as revised in March 2026 deleted the peaceful reunification clause and, for the first time, inserted a territorial clause that excludes South Korea; one analysis finds that the same constitution sharply pared back passages on Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il (KEI). Reports citing inside sources say cadres were told the change was about stabilizing the state system and making diplomatic strategy more realistic (Daily NK). October 2024 Combat units sent to Russia's Kursk front suffered battlefield deaths, but North Korea did not officially acknowledge the deployment itself until April 2025. South Korea's NIS estimated in September 2025 that about 2,000 had been killed; North Korea and Russia have not released casualty figures. How it was handled · On April 28, 2025, he formally declared the deployment his own decision, called all who took part "heroes," and promised to build a monument; in late August, meeting bereaved families, he expressed sorrow at having failed to save precious lives and said that he, the state, and the army would take responsibility for the families (per the English translation). Construction of the Memorial Museum of Combat Feats in Overseas Military Operations began in October 2025, a homecoming ceremony for an engineer regiment and the conferral of the title Hero of the DPRK on the fallen followed in December, and the museum opened on April 26, 2026; it honors about 280 fallen soldiers, far fewer than the NIS estimate. North Korean media said apartments for bereaved families had been built across from the museum. Room to maneuver Because nuclear status has been placed at the center of domestic legitimacy by the 2022 law and by the 2026 Party Congress line and constitutional revision, there appears to be virtually no room for concessions toward denuclearization. Tactical adjustments—accepting a summit with Washington, a testing moratorium, a response to scaled-back exercises—by contrast carry small domestic costs because the elite has no means of sanctioning him, and he appears able to change direction by first declaring an achievement and packaging the shift as victory, as when he halted testing in 2018 after declaring the "completion of the state nuclear force" in 2017. On policy toward the South, having gone as far as rewriting the constitution, he has little room to swing back toward conciliation, but on the hard-line side, too, he has kept to institutional and nonmilitary measures. The casualties of the deployment to Russia have been absorbed through a narrative of heroism and compensation for bereaved families, with no visible domestic backlash, so domestic constraints on either further deployments or a withdrawal appear weak; a worsening food situation is more likely to be managed through tighter control and visible projects centered on the capital than to block decisions. Words before and after a change of office After Kim Jong Un's name first appeared in state media at the Party Conference of September 2010, with the rank of general and the post of vice-chairman of the Party Central Military Commission, no record of public remarks by him has been found before he took power in December 2011, so there is no basis for comparing what he said before and after the change in position. His first public speech was the address of April 15, 2012, marking the centenary of Kim Il Sung's birth, four months after he took power. Instead, his words changed sharply over time in the same position: in the 2012 speech he said the people would never again have to tighten their belts and that he would join hands with anyone who wanted reunification, but in 2021 he called the preceding five years "the worst of the worst," and in 2023 he defined the North and the South as "two states hostile to each other." This shift appears to reflect not a change of position but his management of his base amid changed conditions—the Hanoi breakdown, sanctions, and the border closure. Earlier leaders who faced the same structure After Kim Il Sung's death in July 1994, Kim Jong Il did not immediately take the post of Party general secretary and became head of the Party only in 1997; the 1998 constitutional revision enshrined Kim Il Sung as "eternal president" and made the chairmanship of the National Defence Commission the highest post. In the meantime, hundreds of thousands starved to death in the famine of the late 1990s, and the regime promoted the "Arduous March" and Songun politics (Britannica). Checked against theory Bruce Bueno de Mesquita, Alastair Smith, Randolph Siverson, and James Morrow · The Logic of Political Survival (MIT Press, 2003) Fits Interpretation The theory holds that leaders of systems with a small winning coalition and a large selectorate buy loyalty by distributing private goods to coalition members rather than providing public goods, and that because members stay loyal for fear of losing their places under the next leader, the leader keeps power despite policy failures or the costs of war. Comparison Kim Jong Un acknowledged economic failure himself in 2021 yet moved on by restating the line without holding the leadership accountable, and by replacing 64 percent of Central Committee members at the Ninth Party Congress he showed that coalition members can be replaced at any time. Resources are concentrated on core groups—Pyongyang housing, and apartments and hero titles for the families of soldiers killed in the deployment—while ordinary residents have received an admission of food shortages and controls on the markets. Hanhee Lee (Japanese Journal of Political Science, 2018), applying the theory to the Kim Jong Un system, identified frequent rotation and co-optation of close aides and rule by terror as survival tools, while arguing that rule by terror itself leaves open the possibility of a coup by the selectorate. Yet the regime is also pursuing programs aimed at the provinces, such as the "Regional Development 20×10" policy, so private goods alone do not explain it. Jessica L. Weeks · Autocratic Audience Costs: Regime Type and Signaling Resolve (International Organization 62(1), 2008) Conditional Interpretation The argument is that authoritarian leaders can generate audience costs to signal resolve if domestic elites can coordinate to punish them, but that in personalist dictatorships—where the leader controls the security services, rotates elites frequently, and holds their fate in his hands—audience costs are low and threats are therefore less credible (personalist dictatorships are about 1.8 times as likely as other regimes to meet military reciprocation from their targets). Comparison Elite rotation and control of the security services, as in the execution of Jang Song Thaek (2013) and the replacement of 64 percent of the Central Committee (2026), match the features of personalist dictatorship, and the absence of any sign of domestic punishment for retreats and reversals—the 2018 testing halt, the June 2020 suspension of military action, the abandonment of his predecessors' reunification line—fits the prediction that domestic audience costs are low. Yet Kim Jong Un enforced to the letter the year-end deadline he announced in 2019 and wrote nuclear status into law and the constitution, making his external commitments irreversible by his own hand. This appears to be a way of creating credibility through the logic of his own legitimacy rather than through an elite audience, and it runs against the implication that a personalist dictator's threats are less credible.

sections.h: How he decides: hypotheses and forecasts
sections.t: Patterns drawn from the decision record. Each hypothesis carries a forecast that the next decision can confirm or refute. 1. Just before entering negotiations or summit diplomacy, Kim Jong Un first completes a hard-to-reverse display of capability or a legal and institutional step, then presents the result as a premise that is not up for negotiation. Evidence and counterexamples Support: the declaration of "completing the state nuclear force" on November 29, 2017, followed by the testing halt on April 20, 2018; the codification in law on September 8, 2022; the demand that Washington respect North Korea's "present position" after the February 2026 Party Congress and the March constitutional revision; and the reception of Xi Jinping (June 8, 2026) five days after the June 3, 2026, vow of an "exponential" buildup. Counterexample: the scrapping of Punggye-ri and the testing halt on April 20, 2018, were tangible steps conceded before negotiations. What would confirm or refute it If a U.S.–North Korea, North Korea–Russia, or North Korea–China summit is confirmed, the hypothesis holds if a new strategic weapons test or the unveiling of a nuclear facility comes within 60 days before the meeting, and fails if restraint in testing or acceptance of nuclear-related language comes first. 88% By December 31, 2027, no U.S.–North Korea agreement signed or jointly announced by North Korea will contain the word "denuclearization" 2. Kim Jong Un carries out as announced the measures against which adversaries would find direct military retaliation difficult (cutting ties with the South, institutional changes, enforcing deadlines), but tends to hold back on measures that would be costly in relations with China and the United States (a seventh nuclear test, armed action against the South), even when he has announced or prepared them. Evidence and counterexamples Support: the nuclear test of January 6, 2016, after the remark of December 10, 2015; follow-through on December 31, 2019, after the deadline set on April 12, 2019; the demolition of the liaison office three days after the statement of June 13, 2020; and codification in 2024–26 after the definition of December 30, 2023. Counterexamples and limits: the suspension of the General Staff's military action plans on June 23, 2020; no seventh nuclear test despite assessments since 2022 that preparations are complete; and the deployment to Russia (October 2024), an exception that accepted the risk of retaliation. What would confirm or refute it The hypothesis holds if there is no seventh nuclear test through the end of 2027 and measures against the South stay in the nonmilitary and institutional domain; it fails if Kim Jong Un orders a seventh nuclear test or a direct armed clash along the Northern Limit Line. 80% By December 31, 2027, neither the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO) nor the South Korean or U.S. government will confirm a seventh North Korean nuclear test 3. Kim Jong Un maintains personal rapport with other leaders in his own name, sends rebuffs and pressure out in the name of Kim Yo Jong or the Foreign Ministry, and accepts summits only as a direct decision at the leader level, not as the product of working-level negotiations. Evidence and counterexamples Support: his request in the letter of September 21, 2018, to discuss the issue directly with Trump, "not South Korean President Moon Jae-in"; the leader-level showdown format of Hanoi in 2019; his decision to suspend action after Kim Yo Jong's statements in June 2020; and the pairing of his "good memory" remark on September 21, 2025, with Kim Yo Jong's denial of any communication on August 19, 2026. Counterexample: in his policy speech of April 12, 2019, Kim Jong Un himself applied pressure by setting a deadline. What would confirm or refute it If a U.S.–North Korea summit materializes, the hypothesis holds if it is announced through acceptance in Kim Jong Un's name or a change of tone in a Kim Yo Jong statement, with no prior working-level negotiations made public; it fails if the summit is agreed after lengthy public working-level talks. A rebuff issued in Kim Jong Un's own name would weaken the hypothesis. 30% By June 30, 2027, Kim Jong Un and President Trump will hold an in-person summit (including a brief Panmunjom-style meeting)

Time horizon · He faces no term limits. He was reelected general secretary at the Ninth Party Congress on February 19–23, 2026, and again elevated to chairman of the State Affairs Commission at the First Session of the 15th Supreme People's Assembly on March 22–23 (under the customary five-year cycle, the next Party congress would fall around 2031). The revised constitution removed the Supreme People's Assembly's power to recall the chairman. On succession, South Korea's National Intelligence Service (NIS) told a closed session of the National Assembly Intelligence Committee on February 12, 2026, that it assessed his daughter, Kim Ju Ae, to have entered "the stage of being designated successor." North Korea has made no official announcement, and it has never officially disclosed Kim Jong Un's year of birth. Power base · He is at once Party general secretary, chairman of the State Affairs Commission, and supreme commander of the armed forces, and Article 89 of the revised constitution expressly vests command of the nuclear forces in the chairman of the State Affairs Commission. The Ninth Party Congress expanded the Presidium of the Political Bureau to five members (Kim Jong Un, Premier Pak Thae Song, Jo Yong Won, Kim Jae Ryong, and Ri Il Hwan), and at the Supreme People's Assembly in March, Jo Yong Won replaced Choe Ryong Hae as chairman of the Assembly's Standing Committee while also becoming first vice-chairman of the State Affairs Commission. His sister, Kim Yo Jong, was promoted to Party department director and returned to the Political Bureau as an alternate member, and she continues to issue statements aimed at Washington and Seoul. In the military, Defense Minister No Kwang Chol and Chief of the General Staff Ri Yong Gil kept their posts. Possible conflicts with personal interest · By vesting command of the nuclear forces in the chairman of the State Affairs Commission personally and stripping the Supreme People's Assembly of its power of recall, the constitution appears to have fused national security with the leader's own standing. As a result, taking nuclear status off the agenda appears to carry a heavy political cost for the leader personally, even in negotiations where national economic gains such as sanctions relief are at stake. The deployment to Russia cost some 6,000 casualties by the NIS's estimate, but the combat experience and Russian technical assistance gained in return count as gains for the regime.

Shows whether what was said publicly before each decision matched the decision itself. Date Decision Matches words? December 12, 2013 Other His uncle by marriage, Jang Song Thaek, was stripped of all posts and expelled from the Party at an enlarged meeting of the Party's Political Bureau on December 8 and executed after a special military tribunal of the Ministry of State Security on December 12, KCNA announced on December 13. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand No public statement by Kim Jong Un himself before the execution has been found. Four days earlier, a decision of the enlarged Political Bureau meeting (E, December 8, 2013) had denounced "anti-party, counter-revolutionary factional acts," and the case was then handled exactly as that decision laid out. Alternatives He could have disposed of Jang by means short of public execution, such as quiet dismissal, house arrest, or banishment to a provincial post. Cost Jang had been Pyongyang's channel to Beijing, heading the joint North Korea–China committee on the Rason and Hwanggumphyong economic zones, and the Political Bureau decision of December 8 that preceded his trial charged him with "selling off precious resources of the country at cheap prices," leaving a strain on relations with China. China's foreign ministry confined itself to the pro forma response that the matter was an internal affair. Consistent January 6, 2016 The Korean Peninsula On December 15, 2015, he approved the Munitions Industry Department's report on preparations for an "H-bomb" test, and on January 3, 2016, he ordered in his own handwriting that the test be held on January 6, carrying out the fourth nuclear test. North Korea broadcast the written order on Korean Central Television. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand During a field guidance visit to the Phyongchon Revolutionary Site on December 10, 2015, he described North Korea as "a powerful nuclear weapons state ready to detonate self-reliant A-bomb and H-bomb" (E, per KCNA's English version). Alternatives He could have deferred the test and sought dialogue, or held the Seventh Party Congress in May without a nuclear test. Cost UN Security Council Resolution 2270 (March 2, 2016) imposed broader sanctions than before, including a ban on mineral exports, and China voted for it. Because the order tied the test to the first Party congress in 36 years, the test appears to have put the domestic political calendar ahead of external costs. Consistent September 3, 2017 The Korean Peninsula He conducted the sixth nuclear test, of what North Korea called "a hydrogen bomb for ICBM." The decision followed two ICBM test launches, on July 4 and July 28. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In his 2017 New Year address, he said that "preparations for the test launch of an intercontinental ballistic rocket have reached the final stage" (E; the Korean-language original is in the full text published by the Seoul Shinmun). Alternatives He could have kept testing ICBMs while holding off on a nuclear test. Cost It was the most powerful test to date, and UN Security Council Resolution 2375 (September 11, 2017) imposed a cap on refined petroleum supplies and a ban on textile exports. Consistent November 29, 2017 The Korean Peninsula After launching the Hwasong-15 ICBM, he declared that "the great historic cause of completing the state nuclear force" had been realized, fixing for himself the end point of the development phase. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In his 2017 New Year address, he vowed to keep strengthening the nuclear forces (E). Alternatives He could have kept testing without declaring completion, or moved on to further tests such as a seventh nuclear test or a demonstration of atmospheric reentry. Cost UN Security Council Resolution 2397 (December 22, 2017) cut the cap on refined petroleum supplies further, to 500,000 barrels a year. In return, the completion declaration gave him grounds to present the later halt in testing not as a concession but as a step that was no longer needed. Consistent April 20, 2018 The Korean Peninsula At the Third Plenary Meeting of the Seventh Central Committee, the Party adopted a "new strategic line" that halted nuclear tests and ICBM test launches from April 21, scrapped the Punggye-ri nuclear test site, and concentrated all efforts on economic construction. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In his 2018 New Year address (E), he declared that "the nuclear button is on my office desk all the time" and ordered mass production and deployment, while also signaling willingness to send a delegation to the PyeongChang Olympics. The South Korean government announced that on March 5 he had told its special envoys that the North would not resume testing while dialogue continued (a secondhand account comparable to grade B). Alternatives He could have pressed ahead, as his New Year address had ordered, with the mass production and deployment of nuclear warheads and ballistic rockets, while offering only low-cost gestures of conciliation such as Olympic participation. Cost By halting tests, he gave up opportunities for technical verification, and priority shifted from the munitions sector toward the economy. He did not, however, pledge to dismantle nuclear weapons or halt their production. Largely consistent February 28, 2019 The Korean Peninsula At the Hanoi summit, he offered the permanent dismantlement of the nuclear material production facilities at Yongbyon and a written commitment to the testing halt, in return for lifting the sanctions related to civilian life in five Security Council resolutions adopted in 2016–17. He refused the U.S. demand to include facilities beyond Yongbyon (the so-called big deal), and the summit ended without agreement. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In his 2019 New Year address (E), he warned that if the United States "attempts to unilaterally enforce something upon us," North Korea "may be compelled to find a new way" (per KCNA's English version). In the Singapore joint statement of June 12, 2018 (A), he had signed language under which North Korea "commits to work toward complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula." Alternatives He could have broadened the offer, by declaring facilities beyond Yongbyon or widening the freeze on nuclear material production, to secure a partial deal, or settled on joint statement language and handed the rest to working-level talks. Cost He failed to win the sanctions relief he had been counting on since the first summit and accepted the loss of face of a leader-to-leader showdown that ended empty-handed. At a late-night press conference right after the talks, Foreign Minister Ri Yong Ho said, "Our proposal will never be changed." Largely consistent December 31, 2019 The Korean Peninsula At the Fifth Plenary Meeting of the Seventh Central Committee, he declared that North Korea would no longer be unilaterally bound by its 2018 testing halt and foreshadowed a "new strategic weapon." Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In his April 12, 2019, policy speech to the Supreme People's Assembly (E), he made the deadline public, saying, "we will wait for a bold decision from the U.S. with patience till the end of this year" (per the English translation). Alternatives He could have extended the year-end deadline and kept working-level talks going, or let the deadline pass without any public change of course and waited to see what happened. Cost By formally raising the prospect of renewed testing, he sapped Washington's momentum for dialogue; actual ICBM testing resumed only on March 24, 2022, more than two years after the announcement. Consistent June 16, 2020 The Korean Peninsula Citing leaflet launches into the North, Pyongyang cut all inter-Korean communication lines in early June and on June 16 blew up the inter-Korean joint liaison office in Kaesong. On June 23, however, at a preliminary meeting of the Party Central Military Commission that he chaired, Kim "suspended" the General Staff's plans for military action against the South. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand Kim Jong Un himself made no public statement beforehand. A June 13 statement by Kim Yo Jong, then first vice department director (E), foretold that "a tragic scene of the useless north-south joint liaison office completely collapsed would be seen," and said that she had ordered the next action "by exercising my power authorized by the Supreme Leader, our Party and the state" (full Korean-language text as carried by Minplus). Alternatives He could have stopped at symbolic steps such as cutting the communication lines, or let the General Staff carry out its announced plans to move back into the Demilitarized Zone and take military action. Cost By destroying a symbol of the 2018 Panmunjom Declaration himself, he lost the trust of the South Korean government, and the South's minister of unification offered to resign. His own decision to suspend the plans, by contrast, lowered the risk of armed clashes. Consistent September 8, 2022 The Korean Peninsula He had the Seventh Session of the 14th Supreme People's Assembly adopt the law on the state's policy on nuclear forces, broadening the conditions for nuclear use, including an automatic nuclear strike if the command system comes under attack. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In his policy speech that same day (E), he declared that there would never be any abandonment of nuclear weapons or denuclearization first, and no negotiations or bargaining chips to that end (Korean-language original as carried by Choson Sinbo). Alternatives He could have kept nuclear weapons in practice while postponing their codification in law, leaving room to trade them in future negotiations. Cost By shutting the legal door to denuclearization talks himself, he raised the cost of resuming dialogue with Washington and Seoul; and by setting the threshold for first use lower than his 2018 New Year pledge not to use nuclear weapons "unless hostile forces of aggression violate its sovereignty and interests," he intensified the deterrence competition. Consistent December 30, 2023 The Korean Peninsula At the Ninth Plenary Meeting of the Eighth Central Committee, he defined inter-Korean ties as "relations between two states hostile to each other" and ordered a reorganization of the agencies handling South Korean affairs, including the United Front Department. This led to their abolition in January 2024, the deletion of reunification language from the Party Rules in June 2024, and the constitutional revision of March 2026. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In his concluding remarks at the same meeting (E), he said inter-Korean relations had been completely fixed into "the relations between two states hostile to each other and the relations between two belligerent states" (KCNA original as quoted by the Seoul Shinmun). Alternatives He could have kept the reunification line in name while simply cutting off contact with the South. Cost Discarding the cause of national reunification, handed down since the days of Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il, forced a rewrite of the regime's narrative of legitimacy and closed off, by his own hand, the channel of using the South Korean government as a mediator with Washington. Consistent October 8, 2024 The Russia-Ukraine War He decided to send combat troops to Russia. On October 18, South Korea's NIS announced that Russian navy vessels had carried 1,500 special forces troops to Vladivostok between October 8 and 13 and that a total deployment of about 12,000 was expected. North Korea officially acknowledged the deployment as Kim Jong Un's decision only on April 28, 2025. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand At the North Korea–Russia summit at the Vostochny Cosmodrome on September 13, 2023, he pledged full and unconditional support for Russia's "sacred struggle" (E, based on English-language reporting). On the deployment itself, he made no public statement for more than six months, before or after it began. Alternatives He could have limited his support to supplying weapons such as artillery shells and missiles, without sending troops. Cost The NIS put casualties at about 6,000 in early 2026, and he accepted worsening relations with Europe and South Korea. When it went public, North Korea cited Article 4 of the June 2024 treaty with Russia as its justification. Largely consistent February 21, 2026 The Korean Peninsula In his report to the Ninth Party Congress, he decided on a continued buildup of the nuclear forces and the deployment of ground- and underwater-launched ICBM systems, set respect for North Korea's "present position" and withdrawal of the hostile policy as U.S. preconditions for dialogue, and excluded South Korea permanently from "the category of compatriots." In the revised Party Rules released by the Institute for National Security Strategy in September 2026, language on reunification and the demand for the withdrawal of U.S. troops had been removed, through deletions made in June 2024 and at this congress. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In his September 21, 2025, speech to the Supreme People's Assembly (E), he said that if the United States would "shake off its absurd obsession with denuclearization" and accept reality, there was no reason the two countries could not face each other (original as quoted by the Seoul Shinmun). Alternatives He could have lowered his conditions to open dialogue with the second Trump administration, or responded in part to conciliatory proposals from South Korea's Lee Jae-myung government. Cost By raising his conditions for dialogue above where they stood in September 2025, he lowered the odds of a U.S.–North Korea summit, and he closed off exchanges and economic cooperation with South Korea at the level of law and the Party Rules. Consistent June 8, 2026 The Korean Peninsula Hosting President Xi Jinping on his first state visit to Pyongyang in seven years (June 8–9), he defined relations with China as "the most important top-priority strategic work." Yet neither side's readout mentioned denuclearization, and North Korean media did not report the stronger military exchanges that China had proposed. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand During field guidance at a nuclear material production facility on June 3, 2026 (E), he unveiled plans to beef up the state's nuclear forces "at an exponential rate" (based on English-language reporting). Alternatives He could have accepted some "denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula" language, or some restraint on the nuclear buildup, to secure Chinese economic support. Cost On June 3, five days before the visit, he toured a nuclear material production facility and vowed to beef up the nuclear forces "at an exponential rate," apparently accepting the risk of friction with China, which has kept denuclearization as its official position. He appears to have offset the cost by reaffirming support for the "one-China" principle on Taiwan. Consistent August 19, 2026 The Korean Peninsula After President Trump scaled back the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise and floated a summit before year's end, Pyongyang rebuffed him in a statement issued in Kim Yo Jong's name, denying any communication between the two leaders and warning that Washington would not get its "desired answer" by scaling back the drills alone. On September 20, Kim observed the test of a new hypersonic missile. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In his February 2026 report to the Party Congress (E), he publicly set the conditions that the United States must "respect the present position" of North Korea and withdraw its hostile policy. Alternatives He could have accepted the scaled-back exercise as a goodwill gesture and moved to working-level contacts or talks on scheduling a summit. Cost By failing to respond even to a unilateral concession from the U.S. president, he delayed the chance for dialogue, and the September launch drew protests from South Korea and Japan. Because the rebuff did not come in Kim Jong Un's own name, however, he appears to have left himself a way back. Consistent

September 8, 2022 No negotiation or bargaining over giving up nuclear weapons or denuclearization Reaffirmed in the September 2025 speech, at the February 2026 Party Congress, and in the March constitutional revision, and denuclearization was absent from the readouts of the June 2026 North Korea–China summit as well. Because Washington has never actually offered negotiations with sanctions relief on the table, however, the line has not faced a serious test. Kept January 1, 2018 No first use of nuclear weapons unless North Korea's sovereignty and interests are violated Nuclear weapons have never been used, but the September 2022 law broadened the conditions for use, including an automatic nuclear strike if the command system is attacked, so the pledge itself has been walked back. Untested April 20, 2018 A halt to nuclear tests and ICBM test launches At the December 2019 plenary meeting, he declared that North Korea would no longer be bound by the pledge, and it resumed ICBM testing with the Hwasong-17 on March 24, 2022. There has been no nuclear test since September 2017; South Korea's Defense Intelligence Agency assessed in November 2025 that a seventh test could be conducted at once if Kim decided on it. Crossed April 12, 2019 Wait for a bold U.S. decision only until the end of 2019 Right after the deadline, at the plenary meeting of December 28–31, 2019, he announced the abandonment of the testing halt and a "new strategic weapon." Kept December 30, 2023 South Korea is not a partner for reunification or negotiation (two hostile states) The line led to the abolition of the agencies handling South Korean affairs and the revision of the Party Rules in 2024, the February 2026 Party Congress's permanent exclusion of the South from "the category of compatriots," and the March constitutional revision, and Pyongyang has not responded to proposals from the Lee Jae-myung government. Kept September 21, 2025 Dialogue only if the United States respects North Korea's nuclear status and withdraws its hostile policy In August 2026, even after President Trump scaled back joint exercises, Pyongyang held to its conditions, dismissing the move as inadequate in a statement by Kim Yo Jong; but Washington has never offered a formal concession on the question of nuclear status. Untested

Statements are graded by reliability and labeled with the speaker's position at the time (in office, public office before taking power, opposition or candidate, private citizen). In forecasting decisions after a change of position, statements from opposition or campaign days carry less weight. Grades: A, said alongside a decision · B, private remarks later made public · C, off-the-cuff remarks · D, writings from before taking power · E, official speeches and documents January 1, 2018 E 2018 New Year address · In office He said that the entire U.S. mainland was within range of a North Korean nuclear strike and that "the nuclear button is on my office desk all the time," while in the same speech offering to send a delegation to the PyeongChang Olympics and proposing talks between the authorities of the North and the South. It was the first clear display of his method of changing the dynamics by packing threats and offers into a single speech (full Korean-language text as carried by Daily NK). June 12, 2018 A Joint statement of the U.S.–North Korea summit in Singapore · In office Reaffirming the Panmunjom Declaration, he signed language under which North Korea "commits to work toward complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula." The object is "the Korean Peninsula," not North Korea's nuclear weapons, and the text contains no deadline or verification provision (based on the official English text; the Korean text was not checked). April 12, 2019 E Policy speech at the First Session of the 14th Supreme People's Assembly · In office After Hanoi, he made a deadline public, saying he would wait for a bold decision from Washington "till the end of this year," and enforced it that December when he told a plenary meeting that North Korea would no longer be bound by its testing halt (per the English translation). August 5, 2019 B Letters to President Trump (excerpts published in Bob Woodward's Rage in 2020; full texts released in 2022) · In office He complained that the joint U.S.–South Korean exercises were hard to understand but wrote, "I have no intention to attack South Korea or start a war." In a letter of September 21, 2018, he wrote that he hoped "to have discussions on the denuclearization issue directly with your excellency, not South Korean President Moon Jae-in" (based on the English translation; not confirmed by North Korea). September 8, 2022 E Policy speech at the Seventh Session of the 14th Supreme People's Assembly (adoption of the nuclear forces policy law) · In office He declared that there would never be any abandonment of nuclear weapons or denuclearization first, and no negotiations or bargaining chips to that end, and dared the other side to impose sanctions "for a hundred days, a thousand days, ten years, a hundred years" (Korean-language original as carried by Choson Sinbo). December 30, 2023 E Conclusion of the Ninth Plenary Meeting of the Eighth Central Committee · In office He declared that inter-Korean relations had been fixed into "the relations between two states hostile to each other and the relations between two belligerent states, not the consanguineous or homogeneous ones any more," and said that "it is a mistake we should no longer make" to regard as a partner for reunification an adversary that seeks "unification by absorption" (KCNA original as quoted by the Seoul Shinmun). April 28, 2025 A Remarks on officially acknowledging the deployment to Russia (KCNA) · In office He disclosed that the deployment to liberate Kursk had been his own decision, declared that "they who fought for justice are all heroes," and announced that a monument would be erected in Pyongyang. With these words he formally claimed, after the fact, a decision that had cost lives (based on the English translation; the Korean original was not checked). September 21, 2025 E Speech at the 13th Session of the 14th Supreme People's Assembly · In office He said that "personally" he still had good memories of President Trump, while attaching the condition that Washington must shake off its "absurd obsession with denuclearization" before the two sides could face each other, and declared that reunification with South Korea was not needed. It is a manner of speaking that separates personal rapport from the demands of the state (original as quoted by the Seoul Shinmun). February 21, 2026 E Report on the work of the Central Committee to the Ninth Party Congress · In office He said that if the United States would "respect the present position of our state" and withdraw its hostile policy, there was no reason the two could not get along; that the outlook for relations "depends entirely" on Washington's attitude; and that South Korea would be "excluded forever from the category of compatriots" (original as quoted by Money Today). March 23, 2026 E Speech at the First Session of the 15th Supreme People's Assembly · In office He vowed to "continue to consolidate our absolutely irreversible status as a nuclear power," designated South Korea the "most hostile" state, and told the United States that the choice between confrontation and peaceful coexistence was its own. The speech came shortly after the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, and some analysts argue that the Iran case strengthened his rationale for keeping nuclear weapons (based on English-language reporting).

sections.h: What the government says and does
sections.t: No country's words and deeds align more closely. Pyongyang treats its nuclear arsenal as a given rather than a subject of negotiation and has cut off contact with South Korea. The one opening is that Kim Yo Jong's statement did not name the United States directly, and that opening faces Washington alone. Did September 20, 2026 Has fired ballistic missiles at least nine times in 2026 and tested a new hypersonic missile on September 20. Said September 17, 2026 Kim Yo Jong called North Korea's nuclear status "absolute." Her statement, however, did not name the United States directly. Did June 4, 2026 Kim Jong Un inspected a new nuclear facility and ordered an "exponential" expansion of nuclear weapons production. Said February 2026 The Ninth Party Congress formalized North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state and the two-state doctrine that designates the Republic of Korea a "hostile state." Did February 2026 Tightened information control to the point of punishing the viewing of South Korean dramas with execution (Amnesty International report). Did December 2025 Unveiled a nuclear-powered submarine (Russian technology transfer is suspected). Did 2024~ Sends troops and artillery shells to Russia and receives technology in return. Did September 2023 Wrote the policy of strengthening its nuclear forces into the constitution. Words and deeds: Consistent · 8 signals (said: 2 · did: 6)

sections.h: Who decides and who can veto, issue by issue
sections.t: Issue Decides Veto players The Korean Peninsula Kim Jong Un makes the final call on whether to accept a summit with the United States, on policy toward Seoul and Washington, and on the use of the nuclear forces. Formally, decisions are carried out as resolutions of the Party's Political Bureau (and its Presidium) and Central Military Commission or as orders of the chairman of the State Affairs Commission, and external positions are mostly announced in statements issued in the name of Kim Yo Jong or Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui. There is no institutional veto player at home. The 2026 constitutional revision places the chairman of the State Affairs Commission, as head of state, above the Supreme People's Assembly and removes the Assembly's power to recall him. The real constraints lie abroad: the positions of China, North Korea's largest trading partner, and of Russia, a military ally under a 2024 treaty, appear to shape the timing and terms of any negotiation.

Decisions are announced in the form of meetings of the Presidium of the Party's Political Bureau or the Party Central Military Commission, or as orders of the chairman of the State Affairs Commission. But as the handwritten orders made public in 2016 show (approved on December 15, 2015, with the test date fixed on January 3, 2016), Kim Jong Un personally signs off on major decisions such as nuclear tests, down to setting the date. In external signaling, a sequence in which statements in Kim Yo Jong's name apply pressure first and Kim Jong Un then sets the final level was confirmed in June 2020 (statement, then demolition, then his own suspension of military action); in her statement at the time, Kim Yo Jong said she was acting "by exercising my power authorized by the Supreme Leader, our Party and the state," herself revealing the delegation. In August 2026, too, the rebuff to Washington came in Kim Yo Jong's name, and Kim Jong Un said nothing himself. At the Ninth Party Congress, the Presidium was reshaped into a five-member body (Kim Jong Un, Pak Thae Song, Jo Yong Won, Kim Jae Ryong, and Ri Il Hwan) without Choe Ryong Hae, and public reprimands of officials responsible for implementation are frequent, as in the public dismissal of Vice Premier Yang Sung Ho in January 2026 over sluggish factory construction. Who feeds information to Kim and who filters it cannot be established from public sources. Bolton wrote that in Hanoi Kim appeared to lack the inclination or the latitude to revise his proposal, but that is an observer's interpretation. Chung Eui-yong, director of the National Security Office (chief special envoy to North Korea, March 2018) · He announced on March 6, 2018, that Kim Jong Un had expressed a commitment to denuclearization, saying there would be "no reason to keep nuclear weapons if the military threat is removed and the security of the regime is guaranteed," and that the North would not conduct nuclear or missile tests while dialogue continued. (Partly cross-checked: the testing halt was in fact confirmed by the April 20 plenary decision, and the June Singapore joint statement included language on "denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula." The words "no reason to keep nuclear weapons," however, have never been confirmed in North Korean media as Kim Jong Un's own.) Former President Moon Jae-in (counterpart at the 2018 Panmunjom and Pyongyang summits; memoir From the Periphery to the Center, 2024) · He wrote that Kim Jong Un told him again and again that he did not want "even my daughter's generation to live with nuclear weapons on their heads" and that he had "no intention whatsoever of using" nuclear weapons. A briefing on April 29, 2018, by Yoon Young-chan, senior presidential secretary for public communication, conveyed a remark to the same effect: "If an end to the war and nonaggression are promised, why would we live in hardship holding on to nuclear weapons?" (The sources agree, but they all come from the same government, so this is not independent cross-confirmation. The memoir's author has a stake in defending a policy of engagement with the North, and the 2022 law and Kim Jong Un's later public statements flatly contradict these accounts.) John Bolton, former U.S. national security adviser (present at the Hanoi summit; memoir, 2020) · He wrote that Kim Jong Un demanded the lifting of the Security Council sanctions imposed since 2016 in return for giving up the Yongbyon facilities, that the offer amounted in practice to little more than a freeze and inspections, and that Kim was flustered by the breakdown but appeared to lack the inclination or the latitude to improve his offer. (The terms of the exchange broadly match Foreign Minister Ri Yong Ho's late-night press conference (dismantling Yongbyon in exchange for lifting the sanctions related to civilian life in five Security Council resolutions). President Trump, however, said North Korea "wanted the sanctions lifted in their entirety," so even U.S. accounts differ on the scope of the relief sought; and Bolton opposed any deal in the first place.) Mike Pompeo, former U.S. secretary of state (negotiated in Pyongyang in 2018; memoir, 2023) · He wrote that Kim Jong Un said he needed U.S. forces in South Korea to keep China from treating the peninsula like Tibet and Xinjiang, and that when told China claimed North Korea wanted U.S. troops out, Kim laughed and exclaimed "that the Chinese were liars." (Neither North Korea nor China has confirmed or denied the account. Two pieces of circumstantial evidence are consistent with it, though neither is direct confirmation: in 2018, Moon Chung-in, special adviser to the South Korean president, said Kim had not raised the issue of U.S. forces in Korea at the inter-Korean summit, and the Institute for National Security Strategy found that the demand for the withdrawal of U.S. forces was deleted in the 2026 revision of the Party Rules.) Kim Jong Un's letters (sent to President Trump; disclosed in Bob Woodward's Rage in 2020 and released in full in 2022) · In a letter of September 21, 2018, he said he hoped to discuss denuclearization directly with President Trump rather than with President Moon Jae-in, and in a letter of August 5, 2019, he complained about the joint exercises while writing that he had no intention of attacking South Korea. (The full originals have been released, but North Korea has never confirmed their authenticity. They are consistent with Pyongyang's efforts in 2018–19 to bypass Seoul and negotiate directly with Washington and with its statements condemning the joint exercises in August 2019.)

Plenary meeting · A plenary meeting of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea, which sets the party's major lines and policies. ↩ Hanoi summit · The second U.S.-North Korea summit, held in Hanoi, Vietnam, in February 2019. It ended without an agreement. ↩ Two hostile states · The line Kim Jong Un set out in December 2023, defining inter-Korean relations not as ties between compatriots but as relations between two hostile states. ↩ Juche · North Korea's official guiding ideology. It proclaims independence in thought, self-sufficiency in the economy, and self-reliance in defense. ↩ Partisans · Irregular guerrilla fighters rather than a regular army. North Korea grounds the regime's legitimacy in Kim Il Sung's anti-Japanese guerrilla activity. ↩ Sadae (事大) · Literally "serving the great": a small country deferring to a large one. North Korea condemns it and holds up independence instead. ↩ Leninist party organization · The organizing principle under which a vanguard party of professional revolutionaries leads the state and the military, and within the party lower bodies obey the decisions of higher ones (democratic centralism). ↩ Songun (先軍) · The Kim Jong Il-era line that put the military ahead of all other affairs. ↩ Party Rules · The supreme code setting out a party's aims and organizing principles. In North Korea it is regarded as standing above the constitution. ↩ Policy speech · A speech in which a national leader sets out the direction of state affairs before the legislature. In North Korea it is delivered at the Supreme People's Assembly. ↩ Byungjin line · The line North Korea adopted in 2013 of building its economy and its nuclear forces simultaneously. In 2018 it gave way to a line of concentrating on economic construction. ↩ Central Military Commission · China's supreme military command body. The party and the state each have a commission with identical membership, and its chairman holds final command authority. ↩ Kursk incursion · The August 2024 operation in which Ukrainian forces pushed into Russia's Kursk region. ↩ Selectorate · In the theory developed by Bruce Bueno de Mesquita and others, the set of people who can influence the choice of a leader. The core within it that actually keeps the leader in power is called the winning coalition. ↩ Veto player · An institution or person that can block or delay a decision-maker's decisions (in the United States, Congress and the courts; in Taiwan, the Legislative Yuan). ↩ Sources · 101 38north.org Special Report: The Dramatic Fall of Jang Song Thaek (38 North, Alexandre Mansourov) · 2013-12-09 ncnk.org Traitor Jang Song Thaek Executed (KCNA statement, NCNK archive) · 2013-12-13 thediplomat.com China's Official Response To Jang Song-Thaek's Execution: An Analysis (The Diplomat) · 2013-12 piie.com The Fourth Nuclear Test: The Orders (PIIE, Stephan Haggard) · 2016-01-07 globalsecurity.org N.
