For Putin, international politics appears to be a process in which Western pressure, embodied in NATO expansion, closes in on Russia's borders, and Ukraine is not a foreign country but part of historical Russia that was "given away" when the Soviet Union broke up. His pattern has been to deny his intentions right before a decision, create a fait accompli, and then justify it in long-form speeches; and when the West crosses one of his stated red lines, to choose a calibrated response while avoiding direct hostilities with NATO. How he sees the world After calling the unipolar model "not only unacceptable but also impossible" and NATO expansion "a serious provocation" in his 2007 Munich speech (E), he said in 2008 that what mattered was not NATO's intentions but its capabilities (C). Right after the 2004 Beslan hostage crisis, he said, "We showed ourselves to be weak. And the weak get beaten," adding that some would like "to tear from us a 'juicy piece of pie'" (E). Through his 2014 Crimea speech, with its charge that the West was "trying to sweep us into a corner" (A), his framing of Russia as the encircled party appears to have barely changed in nearly 20 years. Basis: September 4, 2004 · February 10, 2007 · April 4, 2008 · March 18, 2014 What he wants As early as a private meeting with President George W. Bush in June 2001, he described the breakup of the Soviet Union as a loss — "Ukraine, part of Russia for centuries, given away" (B; U.S. record declassified in December 2025, in English translation) — and in his 2021 article he declared that Russia would never accept an "anti-Russia" Ukraine (E). The 2022 annexation of four regions and the June 2024 demands for neutral, non-bloc, and non-nuclear status appear to give concrete form to this aim, which most likely combines gaining territory with denying Ukraine the right to choose the Western camp. Basis: June 16, 2001 · July 12, 2021 · September 30, 2022 · June 14, 2024 What he thinks works Against Georgia (2008) and Ukraine (2014, 2022), neither of them NATO members, he created facts on the ground with large-scale force. Against NATO, by contrast, he has gone no further than nuclear threats such as "This is not a bluff" (2022, A) and calibrated demonstrations such as the single Oreshnik strike (2024). In negotiations, he appears to offer only partial or temporary truces, such as halts to strikes on energy facilities or on capitals, rather than a full ceasefire, using his advantage on the battlefield as leverage. Basis: August 8, 2008 · March 18, 2014 · February 24, 2022 · September 21, 2022 · November 21, 2024 · March 18, 2025 · September 5, 2026 People and process The Security Council meeting of February 21, 2022, took a format in which participants declared their support one by one in a recorded broadcast, and the Federation Council's consent to deployments came on the day of the decision or just before. During the 2023 Wagner mutiny, on the same day he called it "treason," he chose a compromise brokered by Lukashenko over punishment. External negotiating channels are divided among Ushakov, Dmitriev, Medinsky, and Kostyukov (the GRU chief), each of whom appears to report directly to the president — an arrangement that funnels information and decisions to one man. Basis: September 30, 2015 · February 21, 2022 · June 24, 2023 · January 2026 Where his words and decisions diverge His off-the-cuff denials just before military decisions have been reversed again and again. Crimea was annexed two weeks after "No, we do not" (March 4, 2014, C); the full-scale invasion came nine days after "Of course not" (February 15, 2022, C); and four regions were annexed seven months after "our plans do not include the occupation of Ukrainian territories" (February 24, 2022, A). Conversely, the retaliation he threatened for Western actions (the "all available means" warning of September 21, 2022, and the warning of September 12, 2024, that NATO countries would be "at war with Russia") was larger than his actual response. Both his denials about his own actions and his warnings about others' are weak indicators of his decisions; his long-form articles and speeches (E) appear to be better ones. Basis: March 4, 2014 · February 15, 2022 · February 24, 2022 · September 21, 2022 · September 30, 2022 · September 12, 2024 · November 21, 2024

sections.h: Relation to the country's strategic culture
sections.t: Putin appears to have inherited from Russian security culture, as a language of justification, the idea of a buffer zone beyond the border and the "besieged fortress" mindset, the narrative of the "gathering of the Russian lands" to recover lost territory, and the notion that great-power status and a strong state go together. But his methods of decision — denying intent and then creating a fait accompli, and acting through a small circle of aides and tightly held information — look closer to the professional culture of a KGB case officer than to state tradition, and he draws on Eurasianism and the Soviet legacy only selectively. Within the same tradition, Gorbachev withdrew force from Eastern Europe, Yeltsin recognized Ukraine's borders by treaty, and Putin himself in 2002 treated Ukraine's cooperation with NATO as that country's own business. The claim that tradition dictated the 2022 full-scale invasion therefore remains unproven. Inherited from the national tradition He inherited the idea that Russia, having suffered repeated invasions across a plain without natural borders, can be safe only with a buffer zone beyond its frontiers, along with the "besieged fortress" mindset, the belief that outsiders seek to encircle and weaken Russia. Kissinger wrote that Russia learned its geopolitics "from the hard school of the steppe," a terrain with few fixed borders. In his 2004 Beslan address, Putin said that "the weak get beaten" (слабых бьют) and that some would like "to tear from us a 'juicy piece of pie'"; in 2008 he said the problem was NATO's capabilities, not its intentions; and in June 2024 he made Ukraine's renunciation of NATO membership a condition for a ceasefire and neutral, non-bloc status a principle. Yet Finland's accession to NATO (2023), despite its long border with Russia, drew no military response, which suggests the buffer logic does not apply equally to every neighbor. Basis: September 4, 2004 · February 10, 2007 · April 4, 2008 · August 8, 2008 · June 14, 2024 He inherited the narrative of the "gathering of the Russian lands" (собирание земель), in which the Grand Duchy of Moscow built a state by gathering the scattered lands of Rus. In a private meeting with President Bush in June 2001, Putin described the Soviet breakup as "Ukraine, part of Russia for centuries, given away" (B; U.S. English-language record); in his 2014 Crimea speech he called Crimea "an inseparable part of Russia" (A); and in June 2022 he said that Peter the Great had taken nothing but returned what was Russia's — "Taking back and reinforcing. That's what he did" — and that "it looks like it fell on us to take back and reinforce, as well" (C). The annexation of four regions a little over three months later, including areas Russian forces did not control, appears to be a case in which this narrative ran ahead of military calculation. Basis: June 16, 2001 · March 18, 2014 · June 9, 2022 · September 30, 2022 He inherited the notion that binds great-power status to a strong state (державность, государственничество). In a programmatic article published as prime minister on December 30, 1999, the day before Yeltsin resigned, Putin wrote that Russia was and would remain a great power, that for Russians a strong state is "a source and guarantor of order," and that Russia would not become a second edition of the United States or Britain. His rejection of the unipolar order in 2007 and his response to U.S. sanctions in 2025 — that "no self-respecting country" makes decisions under pressure — draw on the same language. Hill and Gaddy see this as his "Statist" identity, which takes state builders such as Peter the Great and Stalin as its models. Basis: December 30, 1999 · February 10, 2007 · August 15, 2025 Roots outside the tradition The professional culture of the KGB case officer has roots distinct from the national strategic tradition. Hill and Gaddy identify the "Case Officer" as central among Putin's six identities, arguing that techniques for handling people and information in order to persuade or coerce, the zero-sum calculus of the Cold War, and his experience of watching East Germany collapse from Dresden in 1989 all showed in how the 2014 Crimea operation was run. A pattern of buying time with denials and then revealing a fait accompli recurs: he called the armed men in Crimea "local self-defence units" and admitted six weeks later that Russian servicemen had stood behind them, and he dodged questions about North Korean troops before officially acknowledging them six months later. Former CIA Director Burns has written that Putin and his advisers, whom he warned in Moscow in November 2021, were "badly overestimating their own position," which suggests that reliance on a small inner circle and security-dominated handling of intelligence may have contributed to the misjudgment of 2022. Basis: March 4, 2014→April 17, 2014 · February 15, 2022 · October 24, 2024→April 28, 2025 · February 21, 2022 How history is used selectively He appears to borrow only as much of the vocabulary of Eurasianism as he needs. Unveiling his plan for a Eurasian Union in a 2011 Izvestia article, Putin wrote that "the idea is not to recreate the Soviet Union in some form" (E), and at a February 2021 meeting with media editors he said he believed in the theory of passionarity (пассионарность), Lev Gumilev's concept (C). By contrast, Alexander Dugin, often called "Putin's brain," holds no official post, no record has been found of Putin quoting him publicly, and some analysts say it is unclear whether the two have even met. Moreover, the 2021 article's thesis that Russians and Ukrainians are "one people" looks closer to the imperial-era idea of an "all-Russian nation" than to Eurasianism, which champions a multiethnic Eurasian civilization, so the reading that treats Dugin's influence as a cause of Putin's decisions rests on weak grounds. Basis: October 4, 2011 · February 14, 2021 · July 12, 2021 He uses the Soviet legacy selectively as well, inheriting the size and power of the state while discarding Bolshevik nationalities policy. In his 2005 address to the Federal Assembly he called the collapse of the Soviet Union "a major geopolitical disaster of the century" (E), yet in 2016 he accused Lenin of having "planted an atomic bomb underneath the building called Russia" (C), and on February 21, 2022, he said modern Ukraine had been created by "Bolshevik, Communist Russia" (A). This framing — rejecting the Soviet national structure that gave the union republics a right to secede while counting the territory and great-power status the Soviet Union held as things lost — appears consistent with the selective use of history that Hill and Gaddy describe as his "History Man" identity. Basis: April 25, 2005 · January 21, 2016 · February 21, 2022 Checked against classics and scholarship Henry Kissinger · World Order (Penguin Press, 2014), chapter 2, section "The Russian Enigma"; op-ed "To settle the Ukraine crisis, start at the end" (Washington Post, March 5, 2014) Conditional Interpretation Kissinger saw Russia as "a uniquely 'Eurasian' power, sprawling across two continents but never entirely at home in either," one that learned its geopolitics on the steppe, a terrain with few fixed borders, and has expanded across the Eurasian landmass since the 16th century, its identity shaped by tsarism, Orthodoxy, and the Byzantine legacy. In his 2014 op-ed he wrote that to Russia, Ukraine "can never be just a foreign country," argued that Ukraine should be a bridge rather than either side's outpost, and proposed as the solution a Finland-style status outside NATO. Comparison The 2008 Georgia operation, the 2021 article's refusal to accept an "anti-Russia" Ukraine, and the June 2024 demand for neutral, non-bloc status fit well with a reading of buffer-zone demands rooted in insecurity and of Ukraine as "not a foreign country." The same reading explains why Putin, in negotiations, has kept limits on Ukraine's choice of camp as a core condition alongside territory. Where it falls short Kissinger's prescription assumed that a neutral Ukraine would satisfy Russia's security demands, but the annexation of September 30, 2022, which included areas Russian forces did not control, went beyond buffer logic. Finland's accession to NATO, despite its long border with Russia, drew no military response, so the account in which insecurity breeds expansion did not fit every case; and Kissinger himself changed his view at Davos on January 17, 2023, saying that the idea of a neutral Ukraine was "no longer meaningful." Dmitry (Dima) Adamsky · The Russian Way of Deterrence: Strategic Culture, Coercion, and War (Stanford University Press, 2024); 「From Moscow with coercion: Russian deterrence theory and strategic culture」(Journal of Strategic Studies, 2018) Conditional Interpretation Adamsky argued that Russia's "strategic deterrence" fuses deterrence, compellence, and coercion, which Western theory treats separately, into a single concept for preserving or changing the status quo and shaping the strategic environment through threats, sometimes accompanied by limited use of force. In his account, it puts concrete action ahead of verbal threats and manages escalation across the nuclear, conventional, and informational domains, and its distinctiveness stems less from universal principles than from Russia's strategic culture, national mentality, military customs, and intelligence traditions. Comparison The nuclear threat issued with the mobilization order on September 21, 2022, the nuclear doctrine revision and single Oreshnik strike on November 21, 2024, and the avoidance of direct hostilities with NATO members fit well with his model of managing escalation by mixing threats with limited demonstrations of force. The pattern of offering only partial or temporary truces in the 2025–2026 negotiations also looks like a way of adjusting coercion step by step. Where it falls short The full-scale invasion of February 24, 2022, was a choice for large-scale war rather than "calibrated coercion," and Charap's 2020 forecast, citing Adamsky, that Moscow would keep a low-intensity conflict going indefinitely also missed at that point. In a book review roundtable, Kofman wrote that as the West crossed one warned-of threshold after another (permission for long-range strikes, the Kursk incursion), Russia's coercive measures could be seen as "partially successful at best," and Roberts noted that nuclear restraint may be better explained by battlefield conditions or fear of retaliation than by culture. Fiona Hill and Clifford Gaddy · Mr. Putin: Operative in the Kremlin (Brookings Institution Press, 2013; expanded edition, 2015) Fits Interpretation Hill and Gaddy analyzed Putin as a figure whose six identities — the Statist, the History Man, the Survivalist, the Outsider, the Free Marketeer, and the Case Officer — interlock according to circumstance to produce policy. At the center are the techniques for handling people and information he learned in the KGB; his goals are the stability of the state and the restoration of great-power status; and underneath lies a distrust that sees Western civil society groups as a foreign-funded "fifth column." The authors warned against either underestimating or overestimating Putin. Comparison The denial and later admission about the armed men in Crimea (2014), the evasion and later official acknowledgment of North Korean troops (2024–2025), and the invasion nine days after "Of course not" (February 15, 2022) fit the case officer's pattern of moving from denial to fait accompli. Drawing on history to justify decisions, as in the 2021 article and the remarks on Peter the Great, fits the "History Man" identity, and language that puts a strong state and great-power status first fits the "Statist" identity. Where it falls short The book's portrait of a risk-calculating pragmatist is at odds with the intelligence failure exposed by the 2022 full-scale invasion (Burns's account). The Survivalist's emergency-reserve thinking, born of the 1990s, also showed its limits when the 2022 freeze of foreign exchange reserves held abroad sharply eroded the reserves' value as insurance. A framework in which six identities shift from situation to situation has strong explanatory power after the fact but little power to anticipate the next decision. Strategic culture should be treated not as the cause of Putin's decisions but as a condition that sets the range of options and the language of justification. Within the same tradition, Gorbachev, in his 1988 UN speech, called freedom of choice "a universal principle to which there should be no exceptions" and withdrew tank divisions from Eastern Europe; Yeltsin, in Article 5 of the 1991 Minsk Agreement, recognized the inviolability of existing borders, Ukraine's included; and Putin himself did not stand in the way of cooperation between Ukraine and NATO in 2002. That Gorbachev nonetheless endorsed the annexation of Crimea in 2014 shows that even when attachment to the land is shared, the decision to use force has differed from leader to leader. Putin's next decision should therefore not be predicted from the essentialist claim that "this is simply how Russia is."

sections.h: Domestic coalition and room to maneuver
sections.t: Putin appears to stay in power, behind the forms of elections, by relying on the loyalty of a small coalition of the security services, the military command, state companies, and the economic elite; after he contained the 2023 Wagner mutiny and purged the Defense Ministry in 2024, the independent forces within this coalition capable of standing up to him have most likely dwindled further. The pressure that narrows his choices therefore appears to come less from elite vetoes than from public opinion. Most Russians favor ending the war but oppose returning annexed territory, and they pushed back hard against the 2022 mobilization. Both extremes — returning territory and mobilizing again — thus appear blocked, leaving the options in between as the real ones: freezing the front, partial truces, and intensified strikes. Coalition The security services (the siloviki, including the FSB) and the prosecutorial and investigative agencies They appear to want regime security, the power to suppress opposition, and a share of the assets seized in wartime. Stanovaya argues that because the security services' performance is measured by the number of arrests and asset seizures, repression is growing from the bottom up, and that arrests have reached the network of former Defense Minister Shoigu, the Defense Ministry leadership, regional deputy governors, and even senior judges. High (judgment). Holding the means to punish other elites, and having carried out the suppression of the mutiny and the purge, they appear to be the most influential group in practice. Whether they are pushing to continue or to end the war in the peace negotiations, however, cannot be confirmed from public sources. The military command (the Defense Ministry and the General Staff) They appear to want troops, budgets, and latitude on the battlefield, and to escape blame for failures of command. In June 2023 Prigozhin launched his mutiny demanding the dismissal of Defense Minister Shoigu; Deputy Defense Minister Ivanov was arrested on April 23, 2024, Shoigu was replaced on May 12 by the economic official Belousov, and in May generals including Popov and Shamarin were charged with bribery one after another. Medium to low (judgment). Since the 2024 shake-up, the Defense Ministry has been run by an economic official and its generals have become targets of corruption investigations, making it look more like an executive agency than an independent political force. A single-source report that the military command's optimistic battlefield reports shaped negotiating decisions in September 2026, however, suggests it retains influence as a supplier of information. Economic elites of state companies and big business (including oligarchs) They appear to want sanctions relief, recovery of assets abroad, relief from heavy taxes and high interest rates, and protection of property rights. Stanovaya argues that, with business squeezed by successive tax increases and high interest rates, Central Bank Governor Nabiullina has become the least popular figure among part of the elite, and that large-scale asset seizures targeting Russians living abroad, critics of the war, and underperforming companies are under way. Low (judgment). Because they could themselves become targets of seizure, open opposition is rare, and they have no visible collective means of blocking decisions. Their interests overlap, however, with the agenda of sanctions relief and Russia-U.S. economic cooperation pursued through special envoy Dmitriev, and they appear to be used in defining what Russia would gain from a deal. Public opinion: hard-line nationalist bloggers ("turbo-patriots") and the general public Hard-liners have demanded victory without concessions and escalation (general mobilization, strikes on government buildings in Kyiv, and, for some, nuclear use). As for the general public, in a Levada Center survey in August 2026, 68 percent supported the military operations while 59 percent said it was time to move to peace talks; in September 2025, 80 percent said they would support Putin ending the war immediately, but that fell to 33 percent if the condition was returning annexed territory; and in January 2026, if no agreement could be reached, 59 percent chose intensifying strikes and 21 percent further concessions. Medium (judgment). Hard-liners moved the agenda in 2022 — the replacement of commanders, mobilization, and strikes on infrastructure — but were punished when they targeted Putin directly. The public has no institutional means to replace him but reacts when costs reach daily life, as when his approval rating fell from 83 percent to 77 percent after the 2022 mobilization; this reaction appears to be one reason the Kremlin has avoided another mobilization. Decisions that strained the coalition September 2022 When he announced a partial mobilization of reservists on September 21, protests broke out in which more than 1,300 people were detained that day (according to OVD-Info), and large numbers of men crossed the border to avoid the draft. Even the pro-government RT editor-in-chief Margarita Simonyan criticized how it was carried out, and Putin's approval rating in Levada Center surveys fell from 83 percent in August to 77 percent in September. How it was handled · At a Security Council meeting on September 29, Putin, citing the wrongful call-up of fathers of large families and people with chronic illnesses, said "it's necessary to correct all the mistakes," but he held neither Defense Minister Shoigu nor regional officials to account. On October 28 Shoigu reported that the mobilization of 300,000 had been completed; from then on, the ranks were filled by sharply raising signing bonuses for contract soldiers, and in June 2026 Putin did not publicly back the hard-liners' calls for general mobilization. October 2022 After the collapse of the Kharkiv front in September and the withdrawal from Lyman on October 1, Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov publicly denounced Central Military District commander Alexander Lapin as "a mediocrity," and military bloggers pointed to troop shortages and delays in striking infrastructure. The withdrawal from the city of Kherson on November 9 was announced on television by Defense Minister Shoigu and the overall commander, Sergei Surovikin. How it was handled · Lapin was reported to have been removed from command in late October but returned in January 2023 as chief of staff of the Ground Forces. The Kremlin tolerated criticism aimed at generals and adopted measures the hard-liners had demanded, such as mobilization (September) and strikes on infrastructure (October), and it was the military command, not Putin, that announced the Kherson withdrawal. By contrast, Igor Girkin, who denounced Putin directly as a "cowardly mediocrity," was arrested in July 2023 and on January 25, 2024, sentenced to four years in prison for inciting extremism. June 2023 On June 23–24, Prigozhin of the Wagner Group, claiming the Defense Ministry had attacked a Wagner camp, demanded the dismissal of Defense Minister Shoigu and sent armed units marching to within about 200 kilometers of Moscow. How it was handled · In a June 24 address, Putin branded the mutiny "treason," but the same day, through President Lukashenko's mediation, he agreed that Prigozhin would move to Belarus, that participants would be spared prosecution, and that fighters who had not joined the mutiny could sign contracts with the Defense Ministry; he did not dismiss Shoigu at the time. On August 23 the plane carrying Prigozhin crashed; the next day Putin described him as "a talented man" who had "made serious mistakes in life," and on May 12 of the following year Shoigu was moved from defense minister to secretary of the Security Council. June 2026 After the Anchorage summit in August 2025, pro-war bloggers called a meeting on U.S. soil a "humiliation" and argued that any exchange of territory would violate the constitution. After Ukrainian drones struck a Moscow oil refinery in June 2026, the nationalist businessman Konstantin Malofeyev asked why nuclear weapons were not being used, and bloggers demanded an end to talks with Washington and general mobilization. How it was handled · According to a Reuters analysis, Putin neither broke off talks with Washington nor publicly endorsed nuclear use or general mobilization; the response went no further than the Defense Ministry publishing the addresses of sites it identified as European drone factories and the Foreign Ministry warning of systematic strikes on Kyiv. On September 5, 2026, too, he agreed only to a 72-hour halt to strikes on capitals and conceded nothing on core issues such as territory. He appears to have managed the hard-liners by continuing to negotiate while withholding the concessions they object to. Room to maneuver In ending the war in Ukraine, his room for concession appears narrowest on the legal status of the four annexed regions. Support for ending the war immediately stands at 80 percent but falls to 33 percent if that requires returning annexed territory (Levada Center, September 2025), and since hard-liners spoke of "humiliation" over the Anchorage summit alone, giving territory back would likely carry a heavy cost with both the elite and the public. By contrast, a deal that combines a freeze of the front in Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, partial or temporary truces, and sanctions relief tied to economic cooperation appears to leave relatively wide room, since it fits public support for negotiations (59 percent in August 2026) and the interests of the economic elite. In the hard-line direction, there is wide room for intensifying long-range strikes (59 percent favored more strikes if talks fail, January 2026), but even under hard-liner pressure in June 2026 he did not choose another mobilization or nuclear use, given the backlash against the 2022 mobilization and the risk of direct conflict with NATO. On the Korean Peninsula and Iran, no clear demands from his domestic coalition have been identified, so his latitude appears to depend more on external calculations than on domestic ones. Words before and after a change of office The gap between what he said before and after taking power runs in the opposite direction from the usual case. In a BBC interview on March 5, 2000, as acting president and a candidate, he said of Russian membership in NATO, "Why not? Why not?" and did not rule out the possibility "in the case that Russia's interests will be reckoned with, if it will be an equal partner." In a speech to the German Bundestag on September 25, 2001, he declared that "the Cold War is done with" and presented Russia as "a friendly European nation." From his 2007 Munich speech onward, however, he cast NATO expansion as "a serious provocation," and in 2021–2022 he made Ukraine's approach to NATO the justification for invasion. Because his rhetoric hardened while he held the same office, the gap did not arise from a change of position. The condition of being "an equal partner" in 2000 and the 2001 complaint that "decisions are often taken, in principle, without our participation, and we are only urged afterwards to support such decisions" were already there, so what changed most appears to be not the substance of his demand (an equal status that takes Russia's interests into account) but his judgment of whether that condition was being met, and his tone. That his early audiences were Western (the BBC, the German parliament) and that his support coalition tilted toward the security services from the mid-2000s are also candidate explanations, but no material directly supporting them was found. Earlier leaders who faced the same structure On August 31, 1996, Security Council Secretary Alexander Lebed signed the Khasavyurt Accord with Chechnya's Aslan Maskhadov, postponing a decision on Chechnya's status until the end of 2001; President Yeltsin reportedly approved it through Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin without making any public statement. In August 1991, the heads of the security services and the military, including KGB Chairman Vladimir Kryuchkov and Defense Minister Dmitry Yazov, placed Gorbachev under house arrest at his dacha in Crimea and tried to seize power, but failed within three days. Checked against theory Bruce Bueno de Mesquita, Alastair Smith, Randolph Siverson, and James Morrow · The Logic of Political Survival (MIT Press, 2003) Conditional Interpretation Leaders survive by satisfying the winning coalition that sustains them within the nominal selectorate. When the winning coalition is small and the selectorate large, leaders hand out private benefits to coalition members rather than public goods, and members, fearing they will be pushed out of the coalition, become more loyal, so leaders tend to hold on for a long time even when their policies fail. Comparison The structure — a small coalition of the security services, the military command, and the economic elite sitting atop a large nominal group, the whole electorate — and the facts that his hold on power did not waver after the 2022 retreats from Kharkiv and Kherson or the 2023 mutiny, and that the coalition did not crumble when he replaced Shoigu's network and the Defense Ministry leadership in 2024, fit the theory's loyalty norm. But the biggest threat in 2023 came not from the public but from inside the coalition (Wagner), and the backlash against the 2022 mobilization — a public cost to which the leader of a small coalition should be relatively insensitive — appears to have kept him from mobilizing again, so the public's effect on his latitude is likely larger than the theory predicts. Clarke and Stone have criticized the book, arguing that its statistical findings on war do not hold once democracy is controlled for. Jessica Weeks · Autocratic Audience Costs: Regime Type and Signaling Resolve (International Organization 62(1), 2008) Fits Interpretation She argued that authoritarian leaders, too, can incur audience costs, but only if domestic elites have the ability and incentive to coordinate to punish the leader, if a backdown is observable, and if the audience views backing down unfavorably. She held that audience costs are large in single-party and military regimes and small in personalist dictatorships, where the leader controls the security services and can punish dissent. Comparison When his stated red lines were crossed — "This is not a bluff" (September 21, 2022) and permission for long-range strikes as NATO's entry into the war (September 12, 2024) — Putin did not use the threatened means, yet he was not punished at home. Hard-liners called the retreats and summits a "humiliation," but Girkin, who targeted Putin directly, was jailed, and the Wagner mutiny, the only organized challenge, was contained within a day and its leader died two months later. This comes close to the conditions of a personalist dictatorship, in which the channels for elites to coordinate punishment are blocked. His public warnings should therefore be read as weak signals not backed by domestic costs, which also fits the earlier observation, in "Where his words and decisions diverge," that his warnings were larger than his actual responses.

sections.h: How he decides: hypotheses and forecasts
sections.t: Patterns drawn from the decision record. Each hypothesis carries a forecast that the next decision can confirm or refute. 1. Putin will not accept a full ceasefire along the current line of contact until Russia controls all of the Donetsk region (or Ukraine agrees to withdraw from it); he offers only partial or temporary truces as bargaining tools. Evidence and counterexamples Supporting: March 18, 2025 (accepted only a 30-day halt to strikes on energy facilities); May 11, 2025 (counterproposed talks instead of a ceasefire); August 15, 2025 (demanded withdrawal from Donetsk and Luhansk without a ceasefire); September 5, 2026 (accepted only a 72-hour halt to strikes on capitals). Against: on August 15, 2025, he reportedly softened his demands on Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, so his territorial demands are not fixed, and he has pulled back when the battlefield turned against him, as in the withdrawal from the Kyiv axis in March 2022. What would confirm or refute it Holds if, from October on, only partial truces (covering energy or the air, for example) are agreed at the trilateral talks in the UAE or elsewhere, or if Russia keeps demanding withdrawal from Donetsk as a condition for a ceasefire. Fails if Russia signs a full ceasefire along the current line of contact while Ukrainian forces still hold part of the Donetsk region. 85% By December 31, 2026, no ceasefire covering the entire front (lasting 30 days or more, or open-ended) and officially confirmed by both the Russian and Ukrainian governments will have taken effect 2. When the West crosses one of his stated red lines, Putin responds not with direct hostilities against NATO members but with calibrated, asymmetric moves: demonstrations of new weapons, doctrinal revisions, and gray-zone incursions. Evidence and counterexamples Supporting: November 21, 2024 (he had called permission for long-range strikes "war," but responded only with a single Oreshnik strike and a doctrinal revision); no nuclear use after Ukraine's August 2024 entry into Kursk, despite his "all available means" warning of September 21, 2022; and the drone incursion into Polish airspace on September 10, 2025 (Russia denied intent). Against: against Georgia (August 8, 2008) and Ukraine (March 18, 2014, and February 24, 2022), neither of them NATO members, he reversed his prior denials and actually used large-scale force. What would confirm or refute it Holds if, even after Tomahawks are supplied or Western troops deployed, Russia's response stays within strikes on Ukrainian territory or demonstrations of new weapons. Fails if Russia deliberately attacks a target on the territory of a NATO member and acknowledges doing so. 92% By December 31, 2027, the Russian government will not officially acknowledge attacking a target on the territory of a NATO member, nor will NATO formally invoke Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty against Russia 3. Putin rewards a partner that has shared the costs (North Korea) with a treaty and public acknowledgment, but takes on no new military risk for partners that have not (Iran, the Assad regime). Evidence and counterexamples Supporting: June 19, 2024 (mutual military assistance treaty with North Korea); official acknowledgment of North Korean troops' participation in the war, with thanks, on April 28, 2025; March 2, 2026 (no military intervention in the Iran war); the omission of a defense clause from the January 2025 treaty with Iran; and no military rescue when the Assad regime collapsed in December 2024. Against: the intervention in Syria on September 30, 2015, in which Russia took on the risk first, before its partner had borne any cost. What would confirm or refute it Holds if Kim Jong Un visits Russia and military-technical and economic cooperation keeps expanding in the open, and if cooperation with North Korea does not come up as a concession in negotiations with the United States. Fails if Russia votes for new sanctions on North Korea or again signs a document that explicitly calls for North Korea's denuclearization. 45% By June 30, 2027, Kim Jong Un will visit Russia and hold a summit with President Putin

Time horizon · His current term began with his inauguration on May 7, 2024, and ends in May 2030; the next presidential election is scheduled for March 2030. Under the 2020 constitutional amendments (Article 81(3.1)), his earlier terms are not counted, so he can run once more in 2030 and serve until 2036. Born on October 7, 1952, he turns 74 in October 2026. No official successor has been named; under the constitution, if the president is unable to serve, the prime minister (Mikhail Mishustin) acts in his place. Power base · The Security Council, which the president chairs, is the main consultative body. Its permanent members include Security Council Secretary Sergei Shoigu, Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev, Defense Minister Andrei Belousov, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Federal Security Service (FSB) Director Alexander Bortnikov, Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) Director Sergei Naryshkin, Interior Minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev, Chief of Staff of the Presidential Executive Office Anton Vaino, and presidential aide Nikolai Patrushev (based on attendance at meetings in May and August 2026). In the Ukraine negotiations, foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov has served as the channel to Washington, special envoy Kirill Dmitriev has handled economic talks, and Igor Kostyukov, head of military intelligence (GRU), led the delegation to the 2026 trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi. In the State Duma elections of September 18–20, 2026, United Russia won 349 of 450 seats, further tightening the Kremlin's grip on parliament. Possible conflicts with personal interest · The International Criminal Court (ICC) issued a warrant for his arrest on March 17, 2023, over the alleged forced deportation of Ukrainian children, which restricts his travel to states parties to the Rome Statute. His personal legal exposure may therefore weigh on the choice of summit venues and on peace negotiations independently of Russia's national interests in those talks. The 2020 constitutional amendments also prohibit ceding territory, including annexed territory, so a territorial concession would likely damage both the regime's constitutional legitimacy and his own political standing.

Shows whether what was said publicly before each decision matched the decision itself. Date Decision Matches words? August 8, 2008 Other A military operation triggered by fighting in South Ossetia pushed into Georgia proper. In 2012 Putin said he had approved the operation's plan in 2007 (at the time, President Dmitry Medvedev was formally the decision-maker and Putin was prime minister). Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand After the NATO-Russia Council meeting in Bucharest on April 4, 2008, he said, "The appearance of a powerful military bloc along our borders would be taken in Russia as a direct threat to the security of my country" (C). Alternatives Russia could have limited itself to reinforcing its peacekeepers in South Ossetia, or left the matter to mediation by the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) and the EU. Cost Moscow accepted a chill in relations with the West and the suspension of the NATO-Russia Council, but Georgia's push for NATO membership effectively stalled. The war was followed by Russia's recognition of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states (August 26, 2008). Consistent March 18, 2014 The Russia-Ukraine War Two days after the referendum, he signed the treaty incorporating Crimea and Sevastopol into the Russian Federation. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand At a March 4, 2014, press conference, he called the armed men in Crimea "local self-defence units" and, asked whether Russia considered the possibility of Crimea joining it, answered, "No, we do not" (Нет, не рассматривается) (C). On April 17, during his annual "Direct Line," he acknowledged that Russian servicemen had stood behind the Crimean self-defence forces (C). Alternatives Russia could have stopped at expanded autonomy for Crimea or recognition of it as an independent state, or negotiated guarantees for the Black Sea Fleet's base with Ukraine's new government. Cost Moscow accepted the West's first sanctions against Russia, suspension from the G8, and a rupture with Ukraine. Inconsistent September 30, 2015 Other On the same day the upper house (the Federation Council) authorized the use of troops abroad, Russia began airstrikes in Syria, coming to the military aid of the Assad regime. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In a CBS interview aired on September 27, 2015, he said, "Russia will not take part in any field operations on the territory of Syria or in other states; at least, we do not plan it for now" (C). Alternatives Russia could have kept to supplying arms and military advisers, or confined itself to proposing joint counterterrorism operations with the U.S.-led coalition. Cost Moscow accepted the costs of its first large-scale expeditionary operation outside the former Soviet Union and the risk of clashes with Turkey and others. In March 2016 it declared the mission largely accomplished and announced the withdrawal of its main forces, limiting the scale of its own intervention. Largely consistent February 24, 2022 The Russia-Ukraine War On February 21 he recognized the independence of the Donetsk and Luhansk "people's republics," and on February 24 he ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine (the "special military operation"). Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand At a February 15, 2022, news conference with Chancellor Olaf Scholz, asked whether Russia wanted war, he replied, "Of course not" (Конечно, нет) (C). His July 12, 2021, article (E), by contrast, declared that Russia would "never accept" an "anti-Russia" Ukraine; the long-form text, not the denial, matched the decision. Alternatives Russia could have kept its forces only in the two recognized regions, or continued negotiating with the United States and NATO over its December 2021 draft treaties. In a February 20 call with President Emmanuel Macron, Putin had even agreed in principle to a summit with President Joe Biden. Cost Moscow accepted sweeping sanctions, the freezing of its foreign exchange reserves held abroad, and enormous loss of life, and it drove Finland and Sweden into NATO. Inconsistent September 21, 2022 The Russia-Ukraine War Right after the collapse of the Kharkiv front, he ordered a "partial mobilization" of reservists. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In his International Women's Day greetings on March 8, 2022, he said that "conscripts aren't and won't be taking part in hostilities, and there will be no additional call-up of reservists from the reserve" (E). Alternatives Russia could have stopped at expanding the recruitment of contract soldiers, or shortened the front and sought negotiations. Cost He accepted the political cost of breaking his promise at home that the war would be fought by professional soldiers alone, along with social unrest that included a mass exodus abroad of men eligible for call-up. Inconsistent September 30, 2022 The Russia-Ukraine War He signed treaties incorporating four regions — Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson — including areas Russian forces did not control. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In his February 24, 2022, address announcing the invasion, he said that "our plans do not include the occupation of Ukrainian territories" (в наши планы не входит оккупация) (A). Alternatives Russia could have kept administrative control of the occupied territories while holding back legal incorporation as a bargaining chip. Cost Combined with the constitutional ban on ceding territory, the move narrowed his own room for compromise in peace talks, and soon afterward Russia lost Lyman and the city of Kherson, publicly suffering the loss of "Russian territory." Inconsistent June 24, 2023 Other On the day he branded the Wagner mutiny "treason," he accepted a deal brokered by President Alexander Lukashenko under which Yevgeny Prigozhin would move to Belarus and be spared prosecution. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In a televised address that morning, he called the mutiny "treason" (измена) and "a stab in the back of our country and our people," and promised a harsh response (E). Alternatives He could have crushed the mutinous units by force, or punished their leaders as he had vowed. Cost The public saw the state's monopoly on force shaken, and he paid the political cost of abandoning the harsh punishment he had promised. The Federal Security Service (FSB) closed its criminal case into the mutiny on June 27. Inconsistent June 19, 2024 The Korean Peninsula In Pyongyang, he and Kim Jong Un signed the Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, which includes a mutual military assistance clause (Article 4). Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand At the Vostochny summit on September 13, 2023, asked about military cooperation with North Korea, he said Russia "complies with all the restrictions" but that "all questions will be discussed" (C). Alternatives Russia could have kept its ammunition and arms deals covert and avoided a formal alliance document. Cost As a permanent member of the Security Council, Russia accepted the burden of openly contradicting the North Korea sanctions regime, along with worsening relations with South Korea. Asked in October 2024 about North Korean troop deployments, Putin sidestepped confirmation, saying that "what we do within the framework of this article [Article 4] is our business"; Russia officially acknowledged the deployment only on April 28, 2025. Inconsistent November 21, 2024 The Russia-Ukraine War Right after U.S.-made ATACMS missiles struck Russian territory, he approved a revised nuclear doctrine (November 19) and struck a military plant in Dnipro with Oreshnik, a new intermediate-range ballistic missile. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand On September 12, 2024, he said that permission to use long-range weapons would mean that NATO countries, the United States and European countries, "are at war with Russia" (воюют с Россией) (C). Alternatives Russia could have retaliated directly against NATO members, as it had threatened, or let the strikes pass without a response. Cost Moscow accepted the risk of escalation and the international criticism that came with the first combat use of an intermediate-range missile, but it avoided direct hostilities with NATO members. Largely consistent March 18, 2025 The Russia-Ukraine War In a call with President Donald Trump, he rejected the 30-day general ceasefire Washington had proposed and accepted only a 30-day mutual halt to strikes on energy facilities. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In a June 14, 2024, speech at the Foreign Ministry, he said a ceasefire order would be issued "that very moment" once Kyiv began withdrawing its troops from the four regions and notified Moscow that it was abandoning its plans to join NATO (E). Alternatives He could have accepted the 30-day general ceasefire, or rejected the U.S. proposal outright. Cost He kept up the offensive at the front at the price of being blamed for rejecting a ceasefire and facing pressure from further U.S. sanctions. The Kremlin readout named "the complete cessation of foreign military aid and the provision of intelligence information" to Kyiv as the key condition. Consistent May 11, 2025 The Russia-Ukraine War Instead of the 30-day ceasefire European leaders had demanded, he proposed direct talks in Istanbul on May 15 "without any preconditions," then stayed away himself and sent his aide Vladimir Medinsky to lead the delegation. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In the same statement, he said the aim of the talks was "to eliminate the root causes of the conflict" (первопричины) (E). Alternatives He could have accepted the 30-day ceasefire, or agreed to a summit with President Volodymyr Zelensky. Cost He accepted further European sanctions but shifted the agenda of the talks from a ceasefire to addressing the "root causes" of the conflict. Consistent August 15, 2025 The Russia-Ukraine War At the Russia-U.S. summit in Anchorage, he did not agree to a ceasefire; he reportedly demanded that Ukrainian forces withdraw from all of Donetsk and Luhansk while offering to freeze the front lines in Zaporizhzhia and Kherson. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand He had demanded withdrawal from all four regions on June 14, 2024 (E), and at the joint news conference right after the summit he again made eliminating "all the root causes" of the conflict a precondition for a lasting settlement (E). Alternatives He could have accepted a ceasefire along the current line of contact, or held to his June 2024 demand for withdrawal from the four regions up to their administrative borders. Cost The price of disappointing President Trump was the collapse of the planned October summit in Budapest and sanctions on Rosneft and Lukoil (October 22). Putin responded that "no self-respecting country and self-respecting people make any decisions under pressure." Largely consistent March 2, 2026 Iran and Hormuz After the U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28 and the death of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, he chose a diplomatic response — calling, together with China, for an emergency Security Council meeting — and provided no direct military support to Iran. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand The Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership signed with Iran on January 17, 2025, contains no mutual defense clause (E). In a message of condolence published by the Kremlin on March 1, 2026, he went no further than condemning Khamenei's killing as committed "in cynical violation of all norms of human morality" (E). Alternatives As Iran's treaty partner, Russia could have openly provided military support such as air defense systems. Cost Moscow accepted Iranian discontent and a reputation as an "unreliable partner," but surging oil prices sharply increased its oil revenue. The calculation appears to have been to protect its channel to Washington on Ukraine. Consistent September 5, 2026 The Russia-Ukraine War After meeting U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, he agreed to a 72-hour halt to strikes on each other's capitals but made no concessions on the core issues, including the front line and territory. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In Bishkek on November 27, 2025, he said that if Ukrainian troops did not withdraw, "we will achieve it by military means" (добьёмся этого вооружённым путём) (C). On September 25 he said Russia would decide on resuming talks based on its own interests (C). Alternatives He could have accepted the U.S. peace plan, or the partial ceasefire covering energy and the air that Ukraine had requested. Cost The choice appears to rest on his battlefield advantage while accepting further U.S. pressure (including a $400 million military aid package for Ukraine announced in June 2026). A Kremlin source said there could be no agreement on the front line before Russia captured the rest of Donetsk, but this is a single source. Consistent

April 4, 2008 Ukraine or Georgia joining NATO, or NATO military infrastructure approaching Russia's borders neither country has joined; Putin decided on the 2008 war in Georgia and the 2022 full-scale invasion before membership became a real prospect. He made no military response to the accession of Finland (2023) or Sweden (2024). Untested September 21, 2022 If Russia's territorial integrity is threatened, it will use "all available means," nuclear weapons included Ukrainian forces entered the Kursk region in August 2024 and stayed until April 2025, but Russia responded with conventional counteroffensives and North Korean troops. Crossed September 12, 2024 Allowing Western long-range weapons to strike Russian territory would mean NATO is at war with Russia ATACMS missiles struck the Bryansk and Kursk regions in November 2024, but the response went no further than a revised nuclear doctrine and a single Oreshnik strike inside Ukraine; no NATO member was attacked. Crossed September 30, 2022 Residents of the four annexed regions are Russian citizens "forever" (no return of annexed territory) in every negotiation in 2025–2026, Moscow demanded recognition of the annexations and withdrawal from the rest of Donetsk. In August 2025, however, it reportedly signaled that it could accept a freeze of the front lines in Zaporizhzhia and Kherson. Kept June 20, 2024 South Korea supplying lethal weapons to Ukraine would be "a very big mistake" as far as can be confirmed, South Korea has not directly supplied lethal weapons to Ukraine. Untested September 5, 2025 Western troops deployed in Ukraine would be "legitimate targets" as of October 2, 2026, no official deployment of Western troops had been confirmed. Untested October 2, 2025 Supplying Tomahawks would mean "a qualitatively new stage of escalation," including in relations between Russia and the United States as of October 2, 2026, no official confirmation had been found that Tomahawks were delivered to Ukraine. Untested

Statements are graded by reliability and labeled with the speaker's position at the time (in office, public office before taking power, opposition or candidate, private citizen). In forecasting decisions after a change of position, statements from opposition or campaign days carry less weight. Grades: A, said alongside a decision · B, private remarks later made public · C, off-the-cuff remarks · D, writings from before taking power · E, official speeches and documents February 10, 2007 E Speech at the Munich Security Conference · In office He declared the unipolar model "not only unacceptable but also impossible in today's world" and called NATO expansion "a serious provocation that reduces the level of mutual trust" (серьезно провоцирующий фактор). It is the prototype of a framing of the problem that he would repeat for nearly 20 years. April 4, 2008 C Press conference after the NATO-Russia Council meeting in Bucharest · In office He said a powerful military bloc appearing on Russia's borders "would be taken in Russia as a direct threat to the security of my country," adding that what mattered was not NATO's intentions but its capabilities. The remark "Ukraine is not even a state," reportedly made in a closed session of the same meeting, comes from a single anonymous source and has not been confirmed. March 18, 2014 A Address on the incorporation of Crimea (to the Federal Assembly) · In office He declared that "Crimea has always been an inseparable part of Russia" (неотъемлемой частью России) and said the West was "constantly trying to sweep us into a corner," but "there is a limit to everything." The words came with a costly decision: the annexation itself. July 12, 2021 E Article "On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians" · In office He wrote that Russians and Ukrainians are "one people" and that "true sovereignty of Ukraine is possible only in partnership with Russia." Declaring that Russia would "never accept" the "anti-Russia" Ukraine the West had built (никогда не смиримся), he laid out the justification for the invasion seven months in advance. February 21, 2022 A Address recognizing the independence of Donetsk and Luhansk · In office Asserting that "modern Ukraine was entirely created by Russia or, to be more precise, by Bolshevik, Communist Russia" (целиком и полностью была создана Россией), he announced the recognition of the two "people's republics." He called Ukraine's accession to NATO "a direct threat to Russia's security." February 24, 2022 A Address launching the "special military operation" · In office He said Russia would "seek the demilitarization and de-Nazification of Ukraine," said that "our plans do not include the occupation of Ukrainian territories," and warned outside powers that interfered that "the consequences will be such as you have never faced before in your history." The annexation of four regions that September reversed the first of those pledges. September 21, 2022 A Address announcing partial mobilization · In office He said, "If the territorial integrity of our country is threatened, we will use all available means to protect our people – this is not a bluff" (Это не блеф). The nuclear threat came with a costly decision, the mobilization order, yet nuclear weapons were not used when Ukraine later invaded the Kursk region. June 14, 2024 E Speech to the senior officials of the Russian Foreign Ministry · In office He said a ceasefire order would be issued "that very moment" if Ukrainian forces withdrew "from the entire territory of these regions within their administrative borders" and Kyiv notified Moscow that it was abandoning plans to join NATO. Reaffirming neutral, non-bloc, and non-nuclear status and demilitarization as principles, the speech became the baseline for Russia's negotiating demands in 2025–2026. October 2, 2025 C Q&A at the plenary session of the Valdai Discussion Club · In office He said Tomahawks would not change the battlefield, but because they cannot be used without the direct involvement of U.S. military personnel, supplying them would mean "a qualitatively new stage of escalation." He dismissed claims that Russia intends to attack NATO as "nonsense." November 27, 2025 C Q&A with Russian media during a visit to Bishkek · In office He said, "If Ukrainian forces leave the territories they hold, then we will stop combat operations. If they don't, then we will achieve it by military means." He added that Russia's lack of any intention to attack Europe could be put in writing.

sections.h: What the government says and does
sections.t: Moscow has effectively accepted North Korea's nuclear arsenal and keeps Pyongyang close through the mutual defense treaty, its Security Council veto, and military-technical assistance. As long as the war continues after the collapse of the 32-hour ceasefire in April, this policy of embracing North Korea will not change. Did 2025~ Suspected of providing technical help for North Korea's nuclear-powered submarine. Did 2024~ Sends North Korean troops to the front line and pays North Korea in technology and money in return. Did June 2024 Signed a mutual defense treaty with North Korea. Did March 2024 Vetoed the renewal of the UN Security Council's panel of experts monitoring sanctions on North Korea. Said 2024 Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said North Korean denuclearization is a "closed issue." Words and deeds: Consistent · 5 signals (said: 1 · did: 4)

sections.h: Who decides and who can veto, issue by issue
sections.t: Issue Decides Veto players The Russia-Ukraine War Under Articles 80 and 86 of the constitution, the president directs foreign policy and, as supreme commander-in-chief, has the final say on the terms of a ceasefire or a peace settlement. Negotiations are conducted on his instructions by aide Ushakov (the channel to Washington), special envoy Dmitriev (economics and sanctions), and GRU chief Kostyukov (head of the delegation to the trilateral talks); the Security Council is a consultative body. A peace treaty would require ratification by the State Duma and the Federation Council (Article 106), but with United Russia holding 349 Duma seats, a meaningful check appears unlikely. The ban on ceding territory added in 2020 (Article 67(2.1)) and review by the Constitutional Court are legal obstacles to any agreement that returns annexed land. The real constraints appear to come from how the military command and the security services view the war's aims, from wartime finances and oil prices, and from the United States and the EU, which hold the power to lift sanctions. The Korean Peninsula The president has the final say on Russia's policy toward the Korean Peninsula — military cooperation with North Korea, implementation of the treaty, and votes in the UN Security Council — and the Foreign Ministry (Minister Lavrov and Deputy Minister Rudenko) carries it out. As a permanent member of the Security Council, Russia can veto new sanctions on North Korea under Article 27(3) of the UN Charter, and in March 2024 it vetoed the renewal of the panel of experts assisting the Security Council's North Korea sanctions committee. There is effectively no institutional check at home on North Korea policy; the 2024 treaty with Pyongyang passed parliamentary ratification without notable dissent. The real constraints appear to come from the position of China, which shares a border with North Korea, and from the possibility that cooperation with Pyongyang could become a bargaining chip in negotiations with Washington.

The formal consultative body is the Security Council, chaired by the president. Before major decisions, as on February 21, 2022, it has met in recorded, broadcast sessions in which members voice their support one after another (confirmed by the Kremlin transcript and by Meduza and Interfax reports). Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that meeting was aired from a recording and that some remarks had been cut for security reasons. The Federation Council's consent to deployments abroad (September 30, 2015, and February 22, 2022) came on the day of the decision or just before it, amounting in effect to after-the-fact endorsement. Former CIA Director William Burns has written that Putin and his advisers, whom he went to Moscow to warn in November 2021, were "convinced that their window for dominating Ukraine was closing," and a September 2026 report citing Kremlin sources said the military command's optimistic battlefield reports had shaped negotiating decisions, though it rests on a single source. External negotiating channels are divided among aide Ushakov (the United States), special envoy Dmitriev (economics and sanctions), aide Medinsky (Istanbul in 2025, Geneva in February 2026), and GRU chief Kostyukov (Abu Dhabi in 2026), all of whom appear to report directly to the president. Angela Merkel, former chancellor of Germany (memoir Freedom, 2024) · She wrote that Putin told her, "You will not be chancellor forever. And then they (Ukraine and Georgia) will become NATO members. And I want to prevent that." In her assessment, Putin took the membership pledge made at the 2008 Bucharest summit as a "declaration of war." (A single memoir account, and the timing of the remark is not specified. It is consistent, however, with Putin's public statements in April 2008 (NATO on Russia's borders as a security threat).) An anonymous representative of a NATO member state (reported by Kommersant, April 2008) · Said that in a closed session in Bucharest, Putin told President George W. Bush that "Ukraine is not even a state." (Not cross-checked. A single anonymous source; Spokesman Peskov declined to confirm it, and Bush's side has not confirmed it either. The remark resembles the arguments of the 2021 article and the February 2022 address, but it is weak evidence that the private remark itself was made.) William Burns, former director of the CIA (visited Moscow in November 2021) · He wrote that it is always a mistake to underestimate Putin's fixation on controlling Ukraine, and that Putin and his advisers were "convinced that their window for dominating Ukraine was closing" while "badly overestimating their own position." (A public essay by the sitting CIA director (January 2024), with no Russian confirmation. It fits the July 2021 article and the February 2022 decision.) Emmanuel Macron, president of France (recording of a February 20, 2022, call, aired by France 2 in June 2022) · In a call four days before the invasion, Putin described the Maidan protests as a "bloody coup" but agreed in principle to a summit with President Biden. (Cross-checked (recording). Foreign Minister Lavrov criticized the unilateral release but did not dispute the recording's authenticity.) Boris Johnson, former prime minister of the United Kingdom (BBC documentary, January 2023) · Claimed that in a February 2022 call Putin threatened him: "Boris, I don't want to hurt you, but with a missile, it would only take a minute." (Contested. Spokesman Peskov called the claim "a lie," saying Putin had been describing a security concern: that NATO missiles deployed in Ukraine could reach Moscow within minutes.) Naftali Bennett, former prime minister of Israel (mediation in Moscow on March 5, 2022) · Said Putin promised, "I won't kill Zelensky," and agreed to drop his demand that Ukraine disarm. (A single account. The Ukrainian side (presidential adviser Mykhailo Podolyak) dismissed it as fiction, and the Kremlin did not immediately comment.) Alexander Lukashenko, president of Belarus (mediated during the Wagner mutiny in June 2023) · Said Putin had initially made the harsh decision to "wipe out" the mutineers, but turned to negotiation after Lukashenko urged him to talk. (A single account, from a mediator with a motive to inflate his own role. The Kremlin did not comment, but the account fits the public sequence of events: a hard-line address followed by a deal the same day.) Steve Witkoff, U.S. special envoy (interview with Tucker Carlson, March 2025) · Said of Putin, "I think he was honest with me," and recounted that Putin had prayed for Trump after the assassination attempt and had given him a portrait of Trump. Asked whether Russia might march on Europe, he answered, "100% no." (The Kremlin confirmed the gift of the portrait. The judgment of honesty is a subjective impression, and it is at odds with how the negotiations later turned out (Trump's remarks of October 22, 2025).) Donald Trump, president of the United States (exchange with reporters at the White House, October 22, 2025) · Said, "every time I speak with Vladimir, I have good conversations and then they don't go anywhere." The same day, he called off the Budapest summit and announced sanctions on Rosneft and Lukoil. (Cross-checked (official U.S. presidential record). It matches the pattern in the decision record from March 2025 to September 2026: accepting talks while conceding nothing on the core issues.)

Oreshnik · A new intermediate-range ballistic missile that Russia first used in November 2024, in a strike on Dnipro, Ukraine. ↩ Wagner mutiny · The June 2023 episode in which the private military company Wagner, led by Yevgeny Prigozhin, marched on Moscow and halted within a day. ↩ Buffer zone · An intermediate zone that prevents direct clashes between great powers. Russia has long viewed the countries along its borders this way. ↩ Besieged fortress · A theme of Russian political rhetoric: the sense of being encircled by external enemies, used to justify internal cohesion and hard-line responses. ↩ Gathering of the Russian lands · A historical concept for the process by which the Grand Principality of Moscow built a state by reassembling the scattered lands of Rus. ↩ Eurasianism · A school of thought that sees Russia as a distinct civilization, neither European nor Asian. ↩ Kursk incursion · The August 2024 operation in which Ukrainian forces pushed into Russia's Kursk region. ↩ Siloviki · Russia's power group drawn from the security services, the military, and the prosecutor's office. ↩ Levada Center · An independent Russian polling organization. ↩ Milbloggers · Russian military bloggers. They report on the fighting independently and at times criticize the military leadership. ↩ Khasavyurt Accord · The 1996 ceasefire agreement between Russia and Chechnya that halted the First Chechen War. ↩ Selectorate · In the theory developed by Bruce Bueno de Mesquita and others, the set of people who can influence the choice of a leader.
