President Lee has described South Korea as a country that must manage its security and economic vulnerabilities together, caught between U.S.-China rivalry and the demands of its alliance, and he has set out three external goals side by side: peaceful coexistence with North Korea, staying out of conflicts Seoul does not choose, and building up self-reliant defense. In his decisions, he appears to take de-escalatory steps toward the North without waiting for a response, and to accept Washington's broad framework while drawing his lines at the terms of implementation and at what the law and National Assembly consent allow. How he sees the world Lee has said that if the United States and China pull at the same time, Korea could end up "a shrimp caught in the middle," but that it can widen its room for action through coordination and mediation (in-flight press conference, November 23, 2025, C). Taken together with his remark that the alliance with the United States is the foundation of Seoul's diplomacy but Korea cannot cut itself off from China (August 24, 2025, C), his warning that a lump-sum cash investment could bring on a situation like the 1997 financial crisis (September 21, 2025, C), and a speech saying that security that leans on others' strength wavers when circumstances change (September 30, 2026, E), he appears to see the external environment as a problem of vulnerability in which security and the economy are bound up together. Basis: August 24, 2025 · September 21, 2025 · September 30, 2026 What he wants In his UN General Assembly address, he said Seoul would not pursue unification by absorption and has no intention of engaging in hostile acts (September 23, 2025, E); at his New Year press conference, he said peaceful coexistence comes first even if unification has to wait (January 21, 2026, C); and on Liberation Day, he proposed multilateral talks among the parties concerned to turn the armistice into a peace regime (August 15, 2026, E). To these he has added a principle of non-intervention, "no deployment of troops to be involved in or intervene in a war" (September 18, 2026, A), and the self-reliant defense goals of building nuclear-powered submarines by the mid-2030s and regaining wartime operational control (September 30 and October 1, 2026, E). Basis: September 23, 2025 · January 21, 2026 · August 15, 2026 · September 18, 2026 · September 30, 2026 What he thinks works Toward North Korea, he has acted first without requiring the other side to move, halting loudspeaker broadcasts a week after taking office (June 11, 2025) and expressing regret over the drone incursion (April 6, 2026). With the United States, he accepted a $350 billion investment total but secured a term of implementation, the $20 billion annual cap (November 14, 2025), and in answer to demands for a Hormuz contribution, he drew his lines at "the scope that our laws and basic policy can bear" (August 19, 2026, C) and at National Assembly consent, going no further than a fact-finding team and a review of stronger protection for merchant ships (September 8 and 18, 2026). As when he praised the U.S. president's order to scale back combined exercises as creating conditions for dialogue (August 19, 2026), he also tends to accept a counterpart's decision as a rationale that fits his own goals. Basis: June 11, 2025 · November 14, 2025 · April 6, 2026 · August 19, 2026 · September 8, 2026 · September 18, 2026 People and process National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac coordinates foreign and security decisions, but the president has repeatedly announced conclusions himself at press conferences or in X posts, with Cheong Wa Dae filling in the interpretation the next day (August 19, 2026; September 18–19, 2026). The dismissal of Trade Minister Yeo Han-koo, who led trade negotiations (August 15, 2026), and the acceptance of Chief of Staff for Policy Kim Yong-beom's resignation (September 1, 2026) came quickly and without public explanation, and on North Korea policy, disagreements have been reported over Unification Minister Chung Dong-young's phrase "peaceful two states." Basis: August 19, 2026 · September 18, 2026 Where his words and decisions diverge In January 2017, as mayor of Seongnam and a contender in the opposition's presidential primary, he wrote that Seoul should demand the withdrawal of THAAD and lower cost-sharing and be prepared even for a U.S. troop withdrawal (January 22, 2017, D). Calls to withdraw or reconsider THAAD were not unusual in the opposition at the time (among them Choo Mi-ae, then running for Democratic Party leader, in July 2016 and Seoul Mayor Park Won-soon in January 2017), but no other case was found of anyone raising the prospect of a U.S. troop withdrawal. As president, in an office responsible for managing the alliance, he made strengthening the alliance with the United States a diplomatic principle of his inaugural address, and when U.S. Forces Korea relocated THAAD interceptors, he only conveyed his objection and then accepted it (March 10, 2026). His warning that a cash investment could trigger a financial crisis (September 21, 2025, C) prevailed only in part, in a deal with an annual cap (November 14, 2025), and although he pledged in August 2025 to "take proactive, gradual steps to restore" the September 19 Military Agreement, it had not been restored as of May 2026 amid caution in the defense ministry. Positions he took before coming to power carry little weight in forecasting his decisions; in office, many of his decisions appear to follow the constraints of the alliance and of institutions. Basis: January 22, 2017 · September 21, 2025 · November 14, 2025 · March 10, 2026

sections.h: Relation to the country's strategic culture
sections.t: President Lee invokes, unprompted, Korea's historical memory of being a small country wedged between great powers ("when whales fight, the shrimp's back is broken") but recasts it as room to widen Seoul's scope for action through coordination and mediation. In the broad frame of his decisions, he appears to have inherited both the postwar tradition of treating the alliance with the United States as the foundation and the line of reconciliation with North Korea that dates from the Kim Dae-jung government. Yet he picks from these traditions across camps: he takes the Roh Moo-hyun government's principle of non-intervention without using its label of "balancer," and he places Park Chung Hee and Roh Moo-hyun together in a lineage of self-reliant defense. On the same traditions, Roh chose to send troops to Iraq, the Moon Jae-in government chose an independent deployment to Hormuz, and Yoon Suk Yeol chose to institutionalize trilateral cooperation with the United States and Japan and to suspend the September 19 Military Agreement. The judgment of this section, therefore, is that strategic culture is less a cause of his decisions than a condition that sets the range of options and the language of justification. Inherited from the national tradition The historical memory of a small country wedged between great powers. At an in-flight press conference on the way home from the G20 on November 23, 2025, Lee said that if the United States and China pull at the same time, Korea "could end up a shrimp caught in the middle" but can widen its room for action through coordination and mediation. As a presidential candidate on December 5, 2021, he attributed the defeat at the Battle of Ugeumchi in 1894 to a lack of science, technology, and weapons, that is, of national strength, and said Korea must become a leading nation so that the same thing never happens again. On September 30, 2026, he said that security that leans on others' strength wavers when circumstances change. On the other hand, former Foreign Minister Yoon Young-kwan argued on March 11, 2026, that Korea should move beyond the idea of the shrimp whose back breaks between two whales, consolidate trilateral cooperation with the United States and Japan, and widen its horizons to the world, a reminder that the same memory can yield different prescriptions. Basis: September 21, 2025 · September 30, 2026 · December 5, 2021 · November 23, 2025 He has inherited the postwar tradition of treating the alliance with the United States as the foundation of security. His inaugural address (June 4, 2025, based on the English full text) pledged to strengthen the alliance with the United States, bolster Korea-U.S.-Japan cooperation on that basis, and manage relations with neighboring countries from the standpoint of national interest and pragmatism, and on August 24, 2025, he again called the alliance the foundation of Seoul's diplomacy. His decisions have likewise stayed within the broad frame of the alliance: the $350 billion investment agreement (November 14, 2025), signing the U.S.-led Pax Silica supply-chain declaration (December 12, 2025), and accepting the relocation of THAAD interceptors by U.S. Forces Korea (March 10, 2026). But his reservation that strategic flexibility is "not an issue we can easily agree to" also suggests a tendency to keep the alliance's scope centered on the defense of the Korean Peninsula. Basis: August 24, 2025 · November 14, 2025 · December 12, 2025 · March 10, 2026 · June 4, 2025 He continues the Kim Dae-jung government's line of reconciliation with North Korea (the Sunshine Policy). In his inaugural address on February 25, 1998, President Kim set out three principles: no tolerance of armed provocation, no intention to harm or absorb the North, and reconciliation and cooperation starting from areas where they are possible. In his Liberation Day address on August 15, 2025, President Lee said Seoul respects the North's current system, "will not pursue any form of unification by absorption," and has no intention of engaging in hostile acts. The halt to loudspeaker broadcasts (June 11, 2025) and the expression of regret over the drone incursion (April 6, 2026) appear to be decisions that carried out this line first, without a response from the other side, and he accepted domestic criticism that he was giving up means of pressure on the North for nothing. Large-scale economic cooperation of the kind pursued under Kim Dae-jung is blocked by UN sanctions, however, so what he has inherited seems closer to the language of easing tensions and recognizing the North's system than to economic exchange. Basis: June 12, 2020 · June 11, 2025 · September 23, 2025 · April 6, 2026 · August 15, 2025 Roots outside the tradition The memory of the 1997 financial crisis and a trading nation's sense of economic security have roots different from the geopolitical tradition of survival among great powers. Lee likened the $350 billion cash investment Washington demanded to the 1997 crisis and used the comparison as an argument for refusing it (September 21, 2025), and right after the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran he ordered the swift execution of a 100 trillion won market-stabilization program (March 5, 2026). In his address on the 17th anniversary of former President Kim Dae-jung's death on August 18, 2026 (read on his behalf by Chief of Staff Kang Hoon-sik), he singled out for praise not Kim's North Korea policy but his overcoming of the financial crisis and his building of a high-speed information and communications network. His way of weighing security issues together with financial and trade vulnerabilities appears closer to this experience. Basis: September 21, 2025 · March 5, 2026 · August 18, 2026 His habit of treating law and procedure as the boundaries of a decision also appears to have roots other than strategic culture, and seems tied to his career as a lawyer, a city mayor, and a provincial governor. As governor of Gyeonggi Province, he stopped leaflet launches by designating danger zones under the Framework Act on the Management of Disasters and Safety (June 12, 2020); as president, he treated the tariff memorandum of understanding as not subject to ratification by the National Assembly and took the route of a special act (November 14, 2025); and on a Hormuz contribution, he made "the scope that our laws and basic policy can bear" and National Assembly consent his criteria (August 19 and September 18, 2026). These criteria appear also to have served as a way of limiting a counterpart's demands while avoiding the word "no." Basis: June 12, 2020 · November 14, 2025 · September 8, 2026 · September 18, 2026 How history is used selectively From the Roh Moo-hyun government's legacy, he takes the principle of non-intervention but not the label of "balancer." At the Air Force Academy commencement on March 8, 2005, President Roh said the Korean people would not be drawn into conflicts in Northeast Asia against their will, and at the commencement of the Korea Army Academy at Yeongcheon on March 22, 2005, he spoke of "the role of a balancer for peace and prosperity in Northeast Asia." President Lee's remarks on staying out of the Taiwan dispute (January 12, 2026) and his ruling out a deployment to intervene in war (September 18, 2026) overlap with the first of these principles, but as far as this research found, he uses "coordination and mediation" and "pragmatic diplomacy centered on the national interest" instead of "balancer," and he included strengthened cooperation with the United States and Japan in his inaugural address. In 2005, Kim Tae-hyo, then a professor, and others criticized the balancer idea as liable to be read as a signal that Seoul was drifting away from Washington and Tokyo; no material was found in which Lee himself explained why he avoids the term. Basis: January 12, 2026 · September 18, 2026 · June 4, 2025 · November 23, 2025 He draws on a lineage of self-reliant defense that cuts across political camps. In his Armed Forces Day address on October 1, 2026, he invoked both President Park Chung Hee, who launched the defense industry with the aim of making even a single rifle at home, and President Roh Moo-hyun, who pushed defense reform and the transfer of wartime operational control, and pledged to build nuclear-powered submarines by the mid-2030s and to regain wartime operational control. Roh called regaining wartime operational control "putting the nation's sovereignty right" on August 15, 2006; Lee said on September 30, 2026, that "self-reliant defense is sovereignty." As far as this research found, however, he has not repeated since taking office his talk as mayor of Seongnam of being prepared for a U.S. troop withdrawal (January 22, 2017), and the language of self-reliant defense came after the scaling back of combined exercises (August 2026) and the pressure over Hormuz (September 2026). It therefore appears to serve less as a line that replaces the alliance than as a language of justification running alongside it. Basis: January 22, 2017 · September 30, 2026 · October 1, 2026 Checked against classics and scholarship Victor D. Cha · Alignment Despite Antagonism: The United States-Korea-Japan Security Triangle (Stanford, 1999); supplemented by Powerplay: The Origins of the American Alliance System in Asia (Princeton, 2016) Conditional Interpretation Cha proposed a "quasi-alliance" model in which South Korea and Japan cooperate when their fears of abandonment and entrapment by the United States are symmetrical and clash when they are asymmetrical, and tested it against the periods of the Nixon Doctrine (1969–71), détente (1972–74), and Carter's troop-withdrawal plan (1975–79). In his 2016 book, he traced Washington's choice of bilateral alliances in Asia to a desire to restrain risk-taking by allied leaders such as Syngman Rhee and Chiang Kai-shek. Comparison The framework's basic proposition, that the side fearing entrapment keeps its alliance commitments weak, fits Lee's staying out of the Taiwan dispute (January 12, 2026), his ruling out a deployment to intervene in war (September 18, 2026), and his reservations on strategic flexibility for U.S. Forces Korea (August 24, 2025). The U.S. president's de facto unilateral reduction of combined exercises (August 2026) and relocation of THAAD interceptors (March 2026) also appear to echo the 2016 book's argument about control exercised through alliances. Where it falls short By the model, mounting fear of abandonment should lead Seoul to strengthen its alliance commitments or widen cooperation with Japan. Yet even after the U.S. president raised the size of U.S. Forces Korea and cut combined exercises, Lee ruled out sending combat troops, and his response ran less toward stronger commitments than toward the language of self-reliant defense (September 30, 2026) and higher defense spending. This research could not establish Japan's fear of abandonment or the level of Korea-Japan security cooperation in the same period, so the hypothesis about Korea-Japan cooperation was not tested. There are also limits to applying a model built on Cold War evidence to an individual leader in 2026. David C. Kang · China Rising: Peace, Power, and Order in East Asia (Columbia, 2007); supplemented by "Between Balancing and Bandwagoning: South Korea's Response to China," Journal of East Asian Studies 9(1), 2009, pp. 1–28 Conditional Interpretation Kang argued that East Asian states have seen more benefit than danger in China's rise and so have chosen accommodation over balancing, and that historically the China-centered hierarchical order kept the peace through norms as well as power. Of South Korea, he argued that it sees China more as an economic opportunity than a military threat and has deepened interdependence while barely changing its military posture or alliance structure (2009 article abstract). Comparison The agreement on a "full restoration" of Korea-China relations (January 5, 2026), the position describing "one China" in terms of "respect" rather than "principle" (January 2, 2026), staying out of the Taiwan dispute (January 12, 2026), and the remark that Korea cannot cut itself off from China (August 24, 2025) fit Kang's model of accommodating China while maintaining the alliance. Where it falls short Signing the U.S.-led Pax Silica supply-chain declaration (December 12, 2025) was a decision to reduce non-market practices and dependence, and the push to build nuclear-powered submarines (the November 2025 fact sheet; the October 1, 2026, address) runs against the observation that Seoul has barely changed its military posture. Lee also justifies relations with China in the language of economics and pragmatism rather than hierarchy or cultural affinity, which seems closer to an explanation based on calculations of interest than to Kang's cultural and hierarchical account. A review by Jenny Kim also criticizes the 2007 book for having been written before China's assertiveness became pronounced. Min-hyung Kim · Hedging between the United States and China? South Korea's ideology-driven behavior and its implications for national security, International Relations of the Asia-Pacific 23(1), 2023, pp.129-158 Conditional Interpretation Kim argued that South Korea's behavior between the United States and China cannot be explained by hedging theory alone, and that domestic ideology divides its decisions: conservatives prioritize the alliance and a hard line toward the North, progressives autonomy and engagement with the North. As examples he cited the Moon Jae-in government's "three noes" on THAAD, its hint at terminating the Korea-Japan General Security of Military Information Agreement (GSOMIA), its push for the transfer of wartime operational control, and its reluctance to join the Indo-Pacific strategy. Comparison The halt to loudspeaker broadcasts (June 11, 2025), the regret over the drone incursion (April 6, 2026), the priority on peaceful coexistence (January 21, 2026), the pledge to regain wartime operational control (October 1, 2026), and staying out of the Taiwan dispute (January 12, 2026) overlap with the cluster the article identifies as characteristic of progressive ideology. Where it falls short But Lee has also made alliance-first decisions that the article attributes to conservatives, such as strengthening Korea-U.S.-Japan cooperation in his inaugural address, signing Pax Silica (December 12, 2025), accepting the relocation of THAAD interceptors (March 10, 2026), and the $350 billion U.S. investment (November 14, 2025), and he has named President Park Chung Hee as the starting point of self-reliant defense. Structural conditions, namely dependence on the alliance and trade pressure, rather than ideology appear to have narrowed the range of his decisions. This section does not adopt the article's normative assessment of the Moon Jae-in government's decisions. Strategic culture should be seen not as what caused President Lee's decisions but as a condition that sets the range of options and the language of justification. On the same traditions, President Roh Moo-hyun, who spoke of a "balancer," sent engineering and medical units to Iraq with the National Assembly's consent on April 2, 2003; the Moon Jae-in government, which had set out the "three noes" on THAAD (Foreign Minister Kang Kyung-wha's answer in the National Assembly on October 30, 2017), extended the Cheonghae Unit's area of operations to Hormuz on January 21, 2020, opting for an independent operation; and President Yoon Suk Yeol signed the Camp David joint statement of the United States, Japan, and South Korea, which named the Taiwan Strait, on August 18, 2023, and suspended the September 19 Military Agreement on June 4, 2024. President Lee's next decision should therefore not be forecast from an essentialist claim that Korea has always walked a tightrope between great powers.

sections.h: Domestic coalition and room to maneuver
sections.t: President Lee was elected in June 2025 with 49.42 percent of the vote, and he stands on the support of the Democratic Party, which holds a majority of 161 seats in the National Assembly; the camp favoring engagement with North Korea within the party and the government; organized labor, including the Federation of Korean Trade Unions, and progressive civic groups; and centrist and independent voters he courted by describing his party as "center-right." Reconciliation with the North and non-intervention in war match the demands of his core supporters, so he can push them hard. On the alliance and trade, however, he appears to have repeatedly leaned toward centrist voters and U.S. pressure, accepting opposition from his core supporters, and on deployments, which require National Assembly consent, opposition within the ruling party appears to act as a real brake. Coalition The Democratic Party and its majority in the National Assembly (161 seats, after the June 2026 by-elections) It wants to win the April 2028 general election and keep the government's approval up, and on politically costly votes such as deployments and the U.S. investment, its members want the views of their districts and support bases heard. In the September 2026 debate over a Hormuz contribution, members including Lee Ki-heon, Kim Byung-joo, and Song Young-gil publicly opposed a deployment, while Park Jie-won said sending non-combat personnel was unavoidable, splitting the party; the leadership issued no official position before the government's decision. Likely the greatest. Consent to overseas deployments (Article 60(2) of the Constitution), the Special Act on Investment in the United States, and the budget all go through the National Assembly. With Kim Min-seok, reported to have had the president's backing, taking over the party in August 2026, the chance of a clash between the party and Cheong Wa Dae has fallen, but on issues such as a deployment, where defections by members have been aired in public, a ruling-party majority does not appear to guarantee passage. The engagement and autonomy camp on North Korea within the party and the government (Unification Minister Chung Dong-young, National Intelligence Service Director Lee Jong-seok, former party leader Jung Chung-rae, and former officials such as Jeong Se-hyun and Moon Chung-in) It wants inter-Korean relations put ahead of coordination with Washington, de facto recognition of the North's system under the "peaceful two states" formula, and a change to the arrangement under which the Ministry of Foreign Affairs leads consultations with the United States on North Korea policy. In December 2025, Jung Chung-rae, then party leader, sided with Minister Chung, saying that inter-Korean relations would be constrained if every step had to "get Washington's sign-off." Likely large on North Korea. The May 2026 Unification White Paper included the phrase "peaceful two states oriented toward unification," and the direction matches decisions such as the halt to loudspeaker broadcasts and the regret over the drone incursion. But because the president also employs alliance-minded figures such as National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac, its influence on the alliance and trade appears limited. Organized labor and progressive civic groups (the Federation of Korean Trade Unions, the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, and peace and antiwar groups such as the People's Solidarity for Participatory Democracy) At an extraordinary convention of delegates on April 29, 2025, the Federation of Korean Trade Unions (FKTU) voted with 89.73 percent to back the Democratic Party and signed a policy agreement with it, while the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions (KCTU) endorsed no candidate. On October 21, 2025, 574 organizations, including the KCTU, demanded a full review of the U.S. investment, telling the government it "must not give away anything more," and in September 2026, the People's Solidarity for Participatory Democracy (PSPD) and other groups opposed any form of deployment to Hormuz and demanded that the president declare a refusal. Appears moderate. These groups have influence in street mobilization and in shaping public opposition to a deployment, but in August 2026 the president, braving the KCTU's anger, ordered that the scope of labor disputes under the Yellow Envelope Law be set by enforcement decree, and he went ahead with the U.S. investment deal, so on economic and trade issues their demands do not appear to have constrained his decisions. Centrist and independent voters They appear to prioritize economic stability and management of the alliance and to keep their distance from North Korea policy language that seems to unsettle the constitutional commitment to unification. As party leader on February 19, 2025, Lee targeted them by saying that "the Democratic Party is at heart a center-right party that values growth," which drew objections from some in the party, including former Prime Minister Kim Boo-kyum. Likely large on alliance and trade decisions. Lee won with less than a majority of the vote (49.42 percent), his job approval in Gallup Korea polling fell in the third week of September 2026 to 37 percent, the lowest of his presidency, and decisions such as the $350 billion investment deal and acceptance of the THAAD interceptor relocation have been closer to these voters' preference for stability than to the wishes of his core supporters. Decisions that strained the coalition December 2025 When the Ministry of Unification said it would stay out of the Korea-U.S. consultations on North Korea policy led by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and hold separate talks with Washington, Jung Chung-rae, then Democratic Party leader, sided with Minister Chung Dong-young at a meeting of the party's Supreme Council, saying it would be hard to find a way to unlock inter-Korean relations if every step had to "get Washington's sign-off." Earlier, in September and October 2025, the disagreement had become public when National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac rebutted Minister Chung's "peaceful two states" remarks, saying the government does not accept a two-state theory. How it was handled · At the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Unification policy briefings on December 19, 2025, the president took neither side, saying "it helps for each ministry to have its own position," and ordered the creation of a meeting of security-related ministers bringing together the foreign, unification, and defense ministries. The May 2026 Unification White Paper included the phrase "peaceful two states oriented toward unification," and the Ministry of Unification explained that this did not mean recognizing North Korea as a state in law. March 2026 When U.S. Forces Korea shipped out six THAAD launchers and other equipment from the Seongju base for the Iran operation, civic groups that have long campaigned against the THAAD deployment, including the Peace Council for THAAD Withdrawal, said this showed THAAD had never been essentially about defending against North Korea and demanded that the remaining radar be withdrawn as well. The demand points in the same direction as the THAAD withdrawal the president called for in 2017 as mayor of Seongnam. How it was handled · The president conveyed his objection but did not block the relocation, and Cheong Wa Dae said the movement of some U.S. Forces Korea assets abroad reflected strategic flexibility, adding, with reference to the size of the defense budget and the level of the defense industry, that people "need not worry too much." As far as this research found, the government did not ask for the radar to be withdrawn. September 2026 As the government weighed sending a fact-finding team and non-combat options in response to President Trump's demand for a Hormuz contribution, Democratic Party members including Lee Ki-heon, Kim Byung-joo, and Song Young-gil publicly opposed a deployment, and Kim Joon-hyung of the Rebuilding Korea Party alleged that the government had already decided on a deployment and was merely testing public opinion. On September 16, a coalition of civic groups including the PSPD demanded that the president declare at his September 18 press conference that he would refuse to deploy. How it was handled · On September 18, the president declared that there would be "no deployment of troops to be involved in or intervene in a war," largely meeting the demands of opponents within the party, but he left open a review of stronger protection of merchant ships by the Cheonghae Unit, and the next day Cheong Wa Dae explained that he had not rejected the U.S. request. On September 23, the same coalition of civic groups judged the statement insufficient, saying it left room for a workaround. August 2026 When the president repeatedly instructed the labor minister at Cabinet meetings to set, by enforcement decree, the criteria for what may be the subject of labor disputes under the amended Trade Union Act (the Yellow Envelope Law), the KCTU denounced this as "siding with business and overstepping authority." After the labor ministry issued enforcement guidelines in September that excluded performance bonuses and plant relocations and sales from mandatory bargaining, the KCTU began a two-week sit-in on September 7 in front of the Seoul Regional Employment and Labor Office. How it was handled · The president did not withdraw his instruction, saying that setting the details needed to implement a law is a power the Constitution gives the executive, and the labor ministry implemented the guidelines unchanged. Room to maneuver On North Korea, his core supporters demand engagement, so he has ample room to go further toward easing tensions, but centrist voters and the debate over Articles 3 and 4 of the Constitution appear to constrain him from cementing "two states" as legal recognition or rushing to restore the September 19 Military Agreement. On Hormuz, public opposition from ruling-party lawmakers and civic groups, public opposition to a deployment reported at 55 percent, and the requirement of National Assembly consent combine to leave very little room to yield toward involvement in combat; an adjustment of the Cheonghae Unit's role centered on protecting merchant ships appears to be the ceiling. On the U.S. investment and semiconductor tariffs, his core supporters' opposition has not constrained his decisions, so there is room to concede more on totals and the finalizing of projects; but after President Trump announced projects on October 1, 2026 (nuclear power plants and Alaska LNG), the Progressive Party demanded they be nullified and the People Power Party demanded an explanation, saying they differed from what had been reported to the National Assembly, so commitments beyond what has been reported to the Assembly look costly. Lee has said he will not seek a second term, but the party still has its interests ahead of the 2028 general election, so if his job approval falls further, he may harden toward his supporters' positions on alliance issues. Words before and after a change of office Differences in his words as his office changed are large on the alliance and U.S. Forces Korea and small on Taiwan and engagement with North Korea. On January 22, 2017, as mayor of Seongnam and a contender in the opposition primary, he wrote that Seoul should demand lower cost-sharing and the withdrawal of THAAD "even if prepared for a U.S. troop withdrawal" (D). As president, however, he made strengthening the alliance a diplomatic principle in his inaugural address, only conveyed his objection when THAAD launchers were shipped out in March 2026, and, as far as this research found, did not take up civic groups' demand that the radar be withdrawn. His 2017 position appears to have been not unusual in the opposition at the time: Choo Mi-ae, then running for Democratic Party leader, said on July 16, 2016, that the opposition naturally opposed the THAAD deployment and demanded National Assembly consent; Seoul Mayor Park Won-soon called for a full reconsideration of the deployment on January 16, 2017; and former party leader Sohn Hak-kyu opposed THAAD in February 2017, saying it would heighten tensions and an arms race. No other contender, however, was found to have gone as far as speaking of being prepared for a U.S. troop withdrawal, and Lee's own position shifted even as a candidate: in late 2016 he floated a compromise of a "time-limited deployment" before returning to calls for withdrawal in January 2017. By contrast, his remark on non-intervention in cross-strait issues as opposition leader (March 22, 2024) carried over into his statements in office on "respecting one China" and staying out of the Taiwan dispute (January 2026), so the gap there is small. Earlier leaders who faced the same structure President Roh Moo-hyun's motion to send troops to Iraq passed on April 2, 2003, by 179 to 68, with nine abstentions, but the 96 members of the ruling Millennium Democratic Party split 49 in favor, 43 against, and four abstaining; in March 2007, Kim Geun-tae, a former chairman of the ruling party, and Chun Jung-bae, who had left it, went on hunger strike to demand a halt to the Korea-U.S. FTA negotiations. President Moon Jae-in went ahead with the deployment of four additional THAAD launchers on September 7, 2017, drawing criticism from Kim Jong-dae of the Justice Party that a promise had been trampled within two months, and on January 21, 2020, he decided on an independent deployment that extended the Cheonghae Unit's area of operations to Hormuz. Checked against theory Robert D. Putnam · Diplomacy and Domestic Politics: The Logic of Two-Level Games, International Organization 42(3), 1988, pp.427-460 Conditional Interpretation An international agreement is possible only within the set of agreements that can be ratified at home (the win-set), and a small domestic win-set can be a bargaining advantage: "I'd like to accept your proposal, but I could never get it accepted at home" (p. 440). Conversely, pressure from the other country can sway domestic opinion and widen the win-set ("reverberation," p. 455), and a negotiator may use international negotiations to shift the domestic balance of power toward the policies he prefers (p. 457). Comparison On Hormuz, ruling out involvement in combat (September 18, 2026) by citing "the scope that our laws and basic policy can bear" (August 19, 2026), the requirement of National Assembly consent, and public opposition from ruling-party lawmakers fits the logic of using a small win-set as a bargaining asset. But with the ruling party holding 161 seats, the signal that "the Assembly won't accept it" has little credibility in Washington's eyes, and indeed Washington kept up the pressure by scaling back combined exercises (August 2026). On the U.S. investment, he accepted the total despite opposition from civic groups and the Progressive Party and took the route of a special act instead of ratification, appearing to narrow the scope of domestic ratification rather than use domestic constraints as a bargaining asset. Bruce Bueno de Mesquita et al. (Bruce Bueno de Mesquita, Alastair Smith, Randolph M. Siverson, James D. Morrow) · The Logic of Political Survival (MIT Press, 2003) Conditional Interpretation The authors argue that a leader's survival depends on the support of the winning coalition within the selectorate that keeps him in power, and that in democracies, where the winning coalition is large, handing out private benefits to a few is too costly, so leaders seek support through policies that provide public goods. Comparison Cases in which the president, in a country with a large winning coalition, chose policies aimed at the broad electorate, such as economic stability and management of the alliance, over the demands of core groups such as organized labor (the KCTU) or antiwar civic groups (the August 2026 order on an enforcement decree for the scope of labor disputes, the March 2026 acceptance of the THAAD relocation, the November 2025 U.S. investment deal) fit this framework. But the theory's central motive, the leader's own reelection, does not operate under the single five-year term (Article 70 of the Constitution) and his pledge not to seek another term, so the survival incentive appears to work indirectly, through the ruling party that must face the 2028 general election, rather than through the president himself.

sections.h: How he decides: hypotheses and forecasts
sections.t: Patterns drawn from the decision record. Each hypothesis carries a forecast that the next decision can confirm or refute. 1. Faced with U.S. demands for a military contribution, Lee avoids the word "no" while ruling out involvement in combat, substituting non-combat or indirect contributions within the bounds of the law and National Assembly consent, and so buys time. Evidence and counterexamples Supporting cases include March 10, 2026 (objection to the THAAD relocation, then acceptance), August 19, 2026 (the condition of staying within the law), September 8, 2026 (fact-finding team and cooperation with France), and September 18, 2026 (no deployment to intervene in war, followed by Cheong Wa Dae's explanation that this was "not a rejection"). Against it: on November 14, 2025, he accepted the broad outline of U.S. demands, agreeing to a defense-spending target of 3.5 percent of GDP and a large investment package. What would confirm or refute it The hypothesis fails if, even before a ceasefire, he places Korean warships under a U.S.-led operation or decides to support strikes or combat against Iran. It holds if he wins National Assembly consent for a Cheonghae Unit mission limited to protecting merchant ships and Korean nationals, or joins a multinational mission led by Britain and France after a ceasefire. 40% By June 30, 2027, the National Assembly will pass a motion consenting to a deployment of the armed forces that names the Strait of Hormuz or the Persian Gulf as the area of operations (including a motion to extend or modify the Cheonghae Unit's deployment) 2. On North Korea, Lee takes steps to ease tensions first, even without a response from the North, and does not reverse them; he publicly backs the U.S. president's attempts at dialogue with Pyongyang and justifies the costs within the alliance as serving dialogue. Evidence and counterexamples Supporting cases include June 12, 2020 (blocking leaflets), June 11, 2025 (halting loudspeaker broadcasts), April 6, 2026 (regret over the drone incursion), and August 19, 2026 (support for scaling back Ulchi Freedom Shield). Against it: although he pledged in August 2025 to restore the September 19 Military Agreement, it had not been restored as of May 2026 amid caution in the defense ministry, and he has paired these steps with a stronger deterrent, including an 8.2 percent increase in defense spending and a push for nuclear-powered submarines. What would confirm or refute it The hypothesis fails if, after a seventh North Korean nuclear test or an armed provocation against the South, he turns to countermeasures such as resuming loudspeaker broadcasts or asking for expanded combined exercises. It holds if he keeps existing de-escalation steps in place and repeats offers of dialogue even after a provocation. 85% Through December 31, 2027, the South Korean military will not resume loudspeaker broadcasts toward North Korea 3. On trade and semiconductors, Lee accepts the totals and principles of U.S. demands but holds out on the terms of implementation (annual caps, commercial rationale, corporate judgment), and he signs on to U.S.-led supply-chain frameworks while also restoring relations with China. Evidence and counterexamples Supporting cases include November 14, 2025 (accepting the total with an annual cap), December 12, 2025 (signing Pax Silica), January 5, 2026 (visit to China and full restoration of ties), and September 18, 2026 (deferring to corporate judgment and rejecting pressure). Against it: after Washington threatened in January 2026 to raise tariffs again, the government rushed the special act through in March, moving quickly when pressure turned into actual tariffs. What would confirm or refute it The hypothesis fails if, to secure an exemption from semiconductor tariffs, the government commits in an intergovernmental agreement to a specific amount of additional U.S. investment by a particular company, or, accepting the risk of Chinese retaliation, joins U.S. export controls on chipmaking equipment for China with its own regulations. It holds if negotiations continue in which Seoul cites voluntary corporate investment to demand treatment "no less favorable than competitors." 30% By June 30, 2027, an intergovernmental agreement between Seoul and Washington (including a joint fact sheet) will specify an amount of new U.S. semiconductor investment by Samsung Electronics or SK Hynix together with semiconductor tariff terms

Time horizon · Lee took office on June 4, 2025. Under Article 70 of the Constitution, the president serves a single five-year term, so his ends in early June 2030, and under Article 128(2) any constitutional amendment extending the term would not apply to him. He has said repeatedly, in May 2025 and again at a press conference on September 18, 2026, that he has no intention of seeking a second term. The next National Assembly elections are in April 2028. Should the office fall vacant, Article 71 makes the prime minister acting president; the post has been held since July 1, 2026, by Han Seong-sook. Born in 1963 (December 1964 in the family register), he is 62 as of October 2026. Power base · The ruling Democratic Party kept its majority in the National Assembly after the June 2026 by-elections, with 161 seats to the People Power Party's 109 (as of October 5, 2026), and won 12 of the 16 metropolitan mayor and provincial governor races in the June 3 local elections. On August 17, Kim Min-seok, a former prime minister reported to have had the president's backing, was elected party leader. Foreign and security policy rests with National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun, Unification Minister Chung Dong-young, National Intelligence Service Director Lee Jong-seok, and Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul (in office since September 22, 2026, succeeding Ahn Gyu-back), while Chief of Staff Kang Hoon-sik oversees appointments and public announcements. Trade is handled by Minister of Trade, Industry and Resources Kim Jung-kwan and Trade Minister Park Jeong-seong (appointed August 21, 2026, after Yeo Han-koo was dismissed), and economic policy by Chief of Staff for Policy Ha Joon-kyung (appointed October 1, 2026). Lee's job approval in Gallup Korea polling fell to 37 percent in the third week of September 2026, the lowest of his presidency. Possible conflicts with personal interest · No evidence was found, on any of the four issues, that the interests of the state or the government diverge from the president's personal interests.

Shows whether what was said publicly before each decision matched the decision itself. Date Decision Matches words? June 12, 2020 The Korean Peninsula As governor of Gyeonggi Province, he announced that the province would invoke the Framework Act on the Management of Disasters and Safety to designate border areas of Gimpo, Goyang, Paju, and Yeoncheon as danger zones, blocking the launch of leaflets into North Korea, and that violators would be arrested in the act. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand The same day, he called leaflet launches "an act that threatens peace on the Korean Peninsula" and said they could never be tolerated (D, June 12, 2020). Alternatives He could have asked the police for cooperation or left the response to the central government. Cost He accepted controversy over infringement of free expression and the limits of a provincial government's powers; in September 2023, the Constitutional Court struck down the leaflet-ban provision enacted by the National Assembly. Consistent June 11, 2025 The Korean Peninsula He ordered the military to stop its loudspeaker broadcasts toward North Korea immediately, at a time when the North had mounted no notable provocation. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand Halting the loudspeaker broadcasts was one of his campaign pledges (D, during the 2025 presidential campaign). Alternatives He could have first demanded a reciprocal step, such as an end to the North's noise broadcasts, or scaled the broadcasts back in stages. Cost He accepted domestic criticism that he was giving up a means of pressure on the North for nothing in return. North Korea was reported to have stopped its noise broadcasts toward the South the next day. Consistent November 14, 2025 AI and Chips He announced a joint fact sheet under which South Korea would invest $350 billion in the United States ($150 billion in shipbuilding and $200 billion in cash, capped at $20 billion a year) in exchange for lowering reciprocal tariffs to 15 percent, treatment on semiconductor tariffs no less favorable than that of competitors, and approval to build nuclear-powered submarines, and the government concluded that the memorandum of understanding did not require ratification by the National Assembly. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In a Reuters interview on September 21, 2025, he said that paying $350 billion in cash without a currency swap would bring on a situation like the 1997 financial crisis (C). Alternatives He could have accepted the lump-sum cash investment Washington demanded, dragged the negotiations into the following year, or submitted the memorandum to the National Assembly for ratification. Cost He took on an overseas investment commitment that is large relative to GDP and accepted the opposition's charge that bypassing ratification was unconstitutional (Article 60(1) of the Constitution). When President Trump threatened in January 2026 to raise tariffs back to 25 percent over delays in implementation, the government pushed the special act through in March. Largely consistent December 12, 2025 AI and Chips He sent Second Vice Foreign Minister Kim Jina to sign Pax Silica, a U.S.-led declaration on AI and semiconductor supply-chain cooperation. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand At an in-flight press conference on August 24, 2025, he said that while the alliance with the United States is the foundation of Seoul's diplomacy, Korea cannot live by cutting itself off from China (C). Alternatives With a restoration of ties with China in the offing, he could have delayed signing or stayed on as an observer. Cost Although it did not name China, the declaration aimed at curbing non-market practices and reducing dependence on any single country, so he accepted the risk of a backlash from Beijing a month before his visit there. Largely consistent January 5, 2026 The Taiwan Strait At a moment of rising tension between China and Japan over Taiwan, he made a state visit to China, agreed with President Xi Jinping on a "full restoration" of bilateral relations, and signed 14 memorandums of understanding; on Taiwan, he described Seoul's position on "one China" as one of "respect" rather than a "principle." Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In a CCTV interview on January 2, 2026, he said Seoul respects "one China" (C), and at a campaign rally on March 22, 2024, while he was party leader, he asked why Korea should get involved in cross-strait issues (D). Alternatives He could have postponed the visit until the China-Japan dispute subsided, or adopted the "principle" wording Beijing prefers. Cost He accepted the risk of giving Japan and the United States the impression that Seoul was tilting toward China, and on the issue of Chinese structures in the Yellow Sea he obtained only a pledge of "continued constructive consultations." Eight days later he met Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi to restore the balance. Consistent March 5, 2026 Iran and Hormuz Shortly after the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran (February 28), he ordered the swift execution of a 100 trillion won market-stabilization program, while the Ministry of Foreign Affairs neither criticized nor endorsed the strikes and urged all parties to ease tensions. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand On being briefed on the strikes on February 28, 2026, he ordered a review of countermeasures with the safety of Korean nationals in the region as the top priority (E). Alternatives He could have stated support for or criticism of the strikes, or held off on intervening in the markets. Cost He took on a fiscal and financial burden and, by withholding a position on an ally's military action, accepted the risk of displeasing Washington. Consistent March 10, 2026 Iran and Hormuz He conveyed his opposition to U.S. Forces Korea moving THAAD interceptors from Seongju and Patriot assets for the Iran operation (Epic Fury), but did not block the move and accepted it. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand On August 24, 2025, he said Washington's demand for strategic flexibility of U.S. Forces Korea was "not an issue we can easily agree to" (C). Alternatives He could have refused publicly, or slowed the relocation by demanding consultations under the Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) or the Mutual Defense Treaty. Cost He accepted concerns about a gap in air defense against North Korea and the burden of acknowledging in public that Seoul has no means of saying no. Largely consistent April 6, 2026 The Korean Peninsula At a Cabinet meeting, he disclosed the findings of a government investigation that a National Intelligence Service employee and an active-duty soldier had been involved in the January drone incursion into North Korea, and expressed regret to the North. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In his address to the UN General Assembly on September 23, 2025, he said Seoul respects the North's system and has no intention of engaging in hostile acts (E). Alternatives He could have treated the incursion as the deviant act of civilians, or said nothing. Cost He acknowledged findings at odds with the government's initial explanation that civilians were responsible, and accepted domestic criticism that he was being too soft on the North. Kim Jong Un, through Kim Yo Jong, called the step "a manifestation of a frank and broad-minded man's attitude," but the next day North Korea's Ministry of Foreign Affairs dismissed hopes of improved relations. Consistent August 19, 2026 The Korean Peninsula When President Trump ordered Ulchi Freedom Shield scaled back (from 11 days to five, with seven of 14 field training exercises postponed), citing South Korea's refusal to cooperate on Iran, Lee publicly backed the move in an X post, paying tribute to Trump's decision. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand At the White House summit on August 25, 2025, he said that if President Trump became the "peacemaker," he would be the "pacemaker" (C). Alternatives He could have voiced concern about weakened readiness or asked that the cut be reversed. Cost He accepted concerns about weaker combined readiness and criticism that he was covering over the U.S. president's own description of the cut as retaliation for Seoul's absence from the Iran effort by presenting it as an opening for dialogue with the North. Consistent September 8, 2026 Iran and Hormuz He sent a Ministry of National Defense fact-finding team to the United Arab Emirates to assess the situation, and the same day, in Paris, agreed with President Emmanuel Macron to cooperate on freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz (the defense ministry said the team did not presuppose a deployment). Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand In an X post on August 19, 2026, he said he supports freedom of navigation in Hormuz "within the scope that our laws and basic policy can bear" (C). Alternatives He could have considered joining a unilateral U.S. operation, or ruled out any contribution at all. Cost He drew a Korean-language warning from Iran's foreign ministry (September 7) and accepted a backlash from domestic civic groups who saw the step as a prelude to deployment. Consistent September 18, 2026 Iran and Hormuz At a press conference, he declared that there would be "no deployment of troops to be involved in or intervene in a war," and said Seoul would consider only strengthening the Cheonghae Unit's protection of merchant ships and Korean nationals. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand This followed his X post of August 19, 2026 (C), Cheong Wa Dae's position in March 2026 that it would "review carefully," and National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac's remark on July 31, 2026, about building consensus in the National Assembly and the public (C). Alternatives He could have submitted a consent motion to the National Assembly to send warships to Hormuz, as Washington had requested, or committed to non-combat support such as P-8 patrol aircraft and mine-countermeasure assets. Cost Having already drawn President Trump's public criticism and the cut in combined exercises, he accepted the risk of further penalties; the next day Cheong Wa Dae explained that he had not rejected the U.S. request. Consistent September 18, 2026 AI and Chips Responding to U.S. demands that Korean chipmakers expand their American plants and to pressure from Section 232 tariffs, he said that the scale of any expansion was for companies to judge and that projects under the U.S. investment deal would not proceed under pressure or coercion. Said beforehand · alternatives · cost Said beforehand When announcing the fact sheet on November 14, 2025, he said investment would be made "only at a level our economy can bear" (E). Alternatives The government could have committed companies to additional U.S. investment in exchange for a tariff exemption. Cost He accepted the risk of tariff penalties after U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick declared that "if you don't build here, expect to pay to enter the greatest market in the world." Consistent

September 18, 2026 No deployment of troops to be involved in or intervene in the war (the war with Iran, Hormuz) As of October 2, 2026, the Cheonghae Unit remains on its Gulf of Aden mission, and the government has gone no further than sending a fact-finding team and reviewing non-combat options. In an X post on August 19, 2026, he had already set the condition "within the scope that our laws and basic policy can bear." Kept August 15, 2025 No pursuit of unification by absorption and no hostile acts against North Korea A drone incursion in January 2026 involved a National Intelligence Service employee and an active-duty soldier, but the government disclosed this through its own investigation and the president expressed regret on April 6. The same principle carried through to his UN address of September 23, 2025, and the 2026 Unification White Paper. Kept September 21, 2025 No investment in the United States beyond what the economy can bear (no lump-sum cash investment) Cash investment was capped at $20 billion a year (November 2025), and on September 18, 2026, he again said Seoul would not rush to agree on individual projects, citing commercial rationale. Kept March 22, 2024 No deep involvement in cross-strait issues Since taking office he has made the same point in a CCTV interview (January 2, 2026) and an NHK interview (January 12, 2026), but there has been no Taiwan Strait contingency or specific U.S. request. Untested

Statements are graded by reliability and labeled with the speaker's position at the time (in office, public office before taking power, opposition or candidate, private citizen). In forecasting decisions after a change of position, statements from opposition or campaign days carry less weight. Grades: A, said alongside a decision · B, private remarks later made public · C, off-the-cuff remarks · D, writings from before taking power · E, official speeches and documents January 22, 2017 D Facebook post as mayor of Seongnam · Before taking power: Mayor of Seongnam Arguing for an independent, balanced diplomacy, he wrote that against the Trump administration's "America First," Seoul should demand lower cost-sharing for U.S. troops and the withdrawal of THAAD, "prepared for a U.S. troop withdrawal." March 22, 2024 D Campaign rally in Dangjin, South Chungcheong Province, as party leader · Opposition or candidate He said Korea need only say "xie xie" (thank you) to China and to Taiwan alike, and asked why it should get involved in cross-strait issues. August 24, 2025 C Press conference aboard the presidential plane from Tokyo to Washington · In office He called strategic flexibility for U.S. Forces Korea "not an issue we can easily agree to" while saying a discussion of a future-oriented transformation was needed, and said that although the alliance is the foundation, Korea cannot live by cutting itself off from China. September 21, 2025 C Reuters interview · In office He said that investing $350 billion in cash, as Washington demanded, without a currency swap would put South Korea in a situation like the 1997 financial crisis (as reported in English). September 23, 2025 E Address to the 80th session of the UN General Assembly · In office He set out the END initiative (Exchange, Normalization, Denuclearization) and a phased approach to North Korea's nuclear and missile programs, from "stop" through "reduction" to "dismantlement," and said Seoul would not pursue unification by absorption and has no intention of engaging in hostile acts. January 12, 2026 C NHK interview (at Cheong Wa Dae) · In office He said the dispute over Taiwan is a matter between China and Japan in which Korea should not become deeply involved, and that in affairs beyond one's own borders it is better to respect one another and avoid getting unnecessarily deep. January 21, 2026 C New Year press conference · In office He said denuclearization would be ideal but asked whether North Korea would give up its nuclear weapons, proposing to begin with negotiations on a "stop" and move through arms reduction toward denuclearization, and said peaceful coexistence comes before unification. August 15, 2026 E Address on the 81st anniversary of Liberation Day · In office He proposed multilateral talks among the parties concerned to turn the armistice into a peace regime, and said that in the process they could also discuss practical steps to halt the advance of North Korea's nuclear program. September 18, 2026 A Press conference at the Cheong Wa Dae State Guest House · In office Saying there would be "no deployment of troops to be involved in or intervene in a war," he pledged to keep upholding the principle of non-involvement and non-intervention, and said investment in the United States would not be made under pressure or coercion. September 30, 2026 E Remarks at the launch of the destroyer Daeho Kim Jong-seo, Ulsan · In office Saying that security that leans on others' strength wavers when circumstances change, he declared that "self-reliant defense is sovereignty"; the next day, in his Armed Forces Day address, he pledged to build nuclear-powered submarines with indigenous technology by the mid-2030s and to regain wartime operational control.

sections.h: What the government says and does
sections.t: On wartime operational control, words (the goal of completing verification of full operational capability at the Security Consultative Meeting in November) and deeds (verification under the transition plan) point in the same direction. On engagement with North Korea, words (humanitarianism first) also match deeds (a UN sanctions exemption for medical equipment aid). On the Strait of Hormuz, the official line remains that no decision has been made, but continued visits to coastal states and participation in multinational consultations have raised suspicion in the National Assembly that preparations are running ahead of the government's words. Said October 4, 2026 In an address marking the 19th anniversary of the October 4 inter-Korean summit declaration (read on his behalf by the vice unification minister), the president said, "Only by breaking the vicious cycle of hostility and confrontation can we create a virtuous cycle of peace and prosperity." Source Did October 1, 2026 A special bill on nuclear-powered submarines was approved at a Cabinet meeting. Said September 17, 2026 The first vice foreign minister said, "Whatever concrete course is taken on Hormuz, it will be our own independent decision" (Foreign Affairs and Unification Committee). Source Said September 17, 2026 The unification minister said "humanitarianism comes before ideology" and that the government is preparing medical equipment aid for North Korea (Foreign Affairs and Unification Committee). Source Said September 10, 2026 Asked about a contribution in the Strait of Hormuz, the prime minister said, "So far, no decision has been made on any concrete, substantive way to contribute" (questions to the government, National Assembly plenary session). Source Said September 10, 2026 The acting minister of national defense said the government is "working toward the goal of completing verification of full operational capability (FOC) at this year's SCM" (questions to the government, National Assembly plenary session). Source Said September 10, 2026 The prime minister said, "I cannot agree with the view that it does not matter who makes the decision," framing the transfer of wartime operational control as a question of self-reliant defense (questions to the government, National Assembly plenary session). Source Did September 2026 Obtained a UN sanctions exemption for medical equipment aid to North Korea (166 types of equipment), as confirmed in the unification minister's answer to the National Assembly on September 17. sections.h: Who decides and who can veto, issue by issue
sections.t: Issue Decides Veto players The Korean Peninsula The president decides as head of state and commander in chief of the armed forces (Articles 66 and 74 of the Constitution), after deliberation in the National Security Council (Article 91; run day to day by National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac). Concluding and ratifying inter-Korean agreements, and suspending or restoring them, are presidential powers (Articles 21 and 23 of the Development of Inter-Korean Relations Act). Restoring the September 19 Military Agreement, suspended in full by a Cabinet decision in June 2024, is likewise the president's decision after deliberation by the State Council (Article 89). The scale of combined exercises, U.S. Forces Korea, and extended deterrence are matters for agreement between Seoul and Washington, but in some cases, such as the scaling back of Ulchi Freedom Shield in August 2026, the U.S. president has in effect decided alone. The National Assembly must consent to the ratification of inter-Korean agreements that impose a significant fiscal burden or touch on matters of legislation (Article 21(3) of the Development of Inter-Korean Relations Act) and reviews the budget, including the Inter-Korean Cooperation Fund (Article 54 of the Constitution); with the ruling party holding 161 seats, however, its power to block appears weak. The Constitutional Court can intervene through judicial review of laws and constitutional complaints (Article 111); its September 2023 ruling striking down the ban on leaflets to North Korea is the precedent, and the "peaceful two states" line faces a constitutional challenge under the territorial clause (Article 3) and the peaceful-unification clause (Article 4). Externally, the U.S. president (who controls combined exercises and the posture of U.S. Forces Korea) and UN Security Council sanctions constrain the decision. The Taiwan Strait South Korea's response to a Taiwan Strait contingency (its diplomatic stance, rear-area support, or a deployment of troops) would be decided by the president after deliberation in the National Security Council, with declarations of war, peace settlements, and other major foreign-policy matters going to the State Council (Article 89, Item 2 of the Constitution). Washington decides how U.S. Forces Korea would be used in a Taiwan contingency; in the 2006 agreement on strategic flexibility, the United States said only that it "respects" South Korea's position that it will not be drawn into a regional conflict in Northeast Asia against the will of the Korean people. Dispatching the armed forces abroad and declaring war require the National Assembly's consent (Article 60(2) of the Constitution). But the relocation of THAAD interceptors in March 2026 confirmed that Seoul cannot stop U.S. Forces Korea from moving its assets, so South Korea appears to have no practical means of vetoing how U.S. forces are used. Iran and Hormuz The president decides after deliberation in the National Security Council. Widening the Cheonghae Unit's area of operations or sending a new deployment requires a proposal from the defense minister, deliberation by the State Council, and the consent of the National Assembly. In March 2026, then-Defense Minister Ahn Gyu-back told the National Assembly that the combat waters of Hormuz were an entirely different matter from the Gulf of Aden and would require the Assembly's consent; non-combat steps such as sending a fact-finding team are being pursued by the executive alone. The National Assembly holds the power to consent to overseas deployments of the armed forces (Article 60(2) of the Constitution). In January 2020, however, the government widened the area of operations without fresh consent, citing a clause in the existing consent motion on "waters designated in an emergency," so whether the Assembly can be bypassed is a live question. Public opposition to a deployment has been reported at 55 percent, and from outside, the U.S. president (whose levers include scaling back combined exercises) and Iran (which warned of "serious consequences" on September 7, 2026) press on the decision. AI and Chips The president sets the direction, and the trade minister (Park Jeong-seong) and the minister of trade, industry and resources (Kim Jung-kwan) negotiate and implement; export licenses for strategic items (Article 19 of the Foreign Trade Act) and approval of exports of national core technologies (Article 11 of the Industrial Technology Protection Act) are the latter minister's powers. The $350 billion investment in the United States is carried out by the Korea-U.S. Strategic Investment Corporation under the Special Act on Investment in the United States, and each project must be reported to the National Assembly's Finance, Economy and Planning Committee before consultations with Washington. The National Assembly, through its Finance, Economy and Planning Committee, must consent to investments that lack commercial rationale (under the Special Act on Investment in the United States), and it reviews the budget and tax laws. In November 2025, the People Power Party argued that the tariff memorandum of understanding required ratification under Article 60(1) of the Constitution, but the government concluded that it did not. Actual investment decisions are made by companies such as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, and the president has explicitly committed to "respecting the views of companies." Externally, the United States (through annual licenses for shipping equipment to Korean plants in China and Section 232 tariffs on semiconductors) and China (which sanctioned Hanwha Ocean's U.S. subsidiaries in October 2025, then suspended the sanctions for a year in November) constrain the decision.

Foreign and security decisions are coordinated by National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac, who has said any Hormuz contribution would be decided not by the government alone but after building consensus in the National Assembly and among the public (July 31, 2026). A pattern has recurred in which the president announces a conclusion himself at a press conference or in an X post and Cheong Wa Dae fills in the interpretation the next day (August 19, 2026; September 18–19, 2026), and on North Korea policy, disagreements have been reported over Unification Minister Chung Dong-young's phrase "peaceful two states." On the trade side, Trade Minister Yeo Han-koo was dismissed on August 15, 2026, with no reason given, and the resignation of Chief of Staff for Policy Kim Yong-beom was accepted within a day on September 1, suggesting that decisions to replace negotiators are made quickly at the president's level. Kim Yo Jong, vice department director of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea (at the time; statement on South Korea) · In a statement on August 19, 2025, she acknowledged South Korean steps such as the halt to loudspeaker broadcasts but said that "Lee Jae-myung is not a figure who can change the course of history" and that South Korea cannot be a diplomatic counterpart. (The wording itself is confirmed by the original text of the official North Korean statement (full text carried by Tongil News). As a public statement intended for propaganda, however, it should be read as a declaration of the North's line toward the South rather than a personal assessment.) Kim Jong Un, general secretary of the Workers' Party of Korea (as relayed in a statement by Kim Yo Jong) · He described President Lee's expression of regret over the drone incursion on April 6, 2026, as "a manifestation of a frank and broad-minded man's attitude" while warning of a heavy price if it happened again; the next day, First Vice Foreign Minister Jang Kum Chol dismissed hopes of improved relations as a "pipe dream." (Several outlets, including the Korea JoongAng Daily and the Seoul Shinmun, cited the KCNA report. The words are Kim Yo Jong's account of Kim Jong Un's view, not his own, and North Korea treats personal assessments separately from relations between states.) Donald Trump, President of the United States · On August 16–17, 2026, he claimed that when he asked Lee to "give us a little hand" on Iran, Lee answered "No thanks," and he brought up the size of U.S. Forces Korea; at the same time, he called Lee a very nice man. (Unresolved. A South Korean foreign ministry official said that, as far as Seoul knew, no such call took place, and the last confirmed call between the two leaders was on May 17, 2026. Al Jazeera reported that Lee declined during the May call, but this differs from the South Korean government's account.) Donald Trump, President of the United States · Hours before their August 25, 2025, meeting, he posted that the situation in South Korea "Seems like a Purge or Revolution," then softened his tone after hearing Lee's explanation at the meeting, saying it was likely a misunderstanding. (Both the post and his remarks at the meeting are on the public record (Axios reporting and the White House transcript). It appears to be a case in which Lee eased his counterpart's suspicions at a first meeting by explaining in person.)

Wartime operational control (OPCON) · The authority to command South Korean forces in wartime. It is held by the commander of the ROK-U.S. Combined Forces Command, a U.S. four-star general. ↩ THAAD · Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, a missile defense system. U.S. Forces Korea deployed it in Seongju, North Gyeongsang Province, in 2017. ↩ Northeast Asian balancer · The idea, put forward by the Roh Moo-hyun government in 2005, that South Korea would act as the balancer of power in Northeast Asia. ↩ Battle of Ugeumchi · The 1894 battle at Ugeumchi, near Gongju, in which the Donghak peasant army suffered a crushing defeat at the hands of Joseon government troops and the Japanese army. ↩ Pax Silica · A U.S.-led declaration on semiconductor and AI supply-chain cooperation, adopted at its first meeting on December 12, 2025. South Korea is a signatory. ↩ Strategic flexibility · The concept that U.S. Forces Korea can be used in conflicts beyond the Korean Peninsula. Seoul and Washington agreed on the principle in 2006. ↩ Sunshine Policy · The Kim Dae-jung government's policy of reconciliation and cooperation with North Korea. ↩ Entrapment and abandonment · The two fears of alliance theory: entrapment is being dragged into an ally's conflict; abandonment is being deserted by an ally when it is needed. ↩ Yellow Envelope Act · The popular name for amendments to South Korea's trade union law that widen subcontracted workers' right to bargain with the principal contractor and limit damage claims against strikes. ↩ Cheonghae Unit · A South Korean naval unit deployed to the Gulf of Aden and other waters since 2009 to fight piracy and escort ships. ↩ Win-set · In Robert Putnam's two-level game theory, the range of international agreements that domestic constituencies will accept. The narrower the range, the less room a leader has to make concessions. ↩ Selectorate · In the theory developed by Bruce Bueno de Mesquita and others, the set of people who can influence the choice of a leader.
